Visitors outfoxed by footwear thieves at provincial park in Sask.
Skulk of foxes swipes dozens of shoes from campers and cottagers
Cunning and furry thieves are outfoxing campers and cottagers at Great Blue Heron Provincial Park.
Sonnet McGuire, manager of the park located about 50 kilometres north of Prince Albert, says she started getting reports about shoes going missing in early July.
Visitors found single shoes left in bushes, on the side of the road, or even at the boat launch.
The culprits: a group — sometimes known as a skulk — of sly foxes with a taste for footwear.
“We have five foxes that are moving about the campground and they seem to love stealing people's shoes,” McGuire said.
The behaviour isn’t new, but this year the thieves are more active.
“We knew it was gonna be foxes because we've had this before, the odd time, just not to this level,” McGuire said.
At first, the park kept the lost shoes in the back of the campground office, but it quickly had to upgrade to outdoor storage bins to hold them. So many shoes.
McGuire said there were about 70 in the bin on a recent day, but she suspects over 100 have passed through it this summer.
“It's kind of like a scavenger hunt in the campground because as you're walking around the campground on the trail or wherever you might be, people are just finding shoes," she said.
“We had one story where people were walking down the street and they saw one fox sitting on the road and the other one kind of on the edge of the campsite. And it was almost like the one fox was on lookout and the other one went into the campsite, stole a shoe, and then they both took off running.”
Camper Brenda Andres said she’s also seen the furry criminals at work.
“We just turned onto the first highway and a little fox ran across the road, and sure enough, he had a little shoe in his mouth,” Andres said.
She’ll be keeping her shoes inside during her camping trip.
‘Kind of a fun game’
Cottager Rachelle Kelln doesn’t mind the sneaky visitors.
“It's kind of a fun game,” she said.
Her cottage is in the Carwin Park subdivision near Emma Lake. It’s also a favourite dumping ground for the shoe-swiping foxes.
“We just started noticing more and more shoes,” Kelln said.
She’s found at least six on her property since July 10, and even more left on the side of the road — all types of shoes, including flip flops, Birkenstocks, even Adidas Sambas.
“Those are expensive shoes and there's a bit of panic around those ones,” Kelln said.
She’s had a few people stop by to pick up their shoes, and they’ve all been excited to get back on the right foot.
McGuire said visitors to the park are advised to keep their kicks inside, as the foxy thieves will remain at large.
With files from Aishah Ashraf

These bookshops let Chinese readers question their country - now the doors are closing
- Published
When Chen Zhu heads to Hong Kong from mainland China every month, there's one place she always goes: Hunter Bookstore.
Founded four years ago by a former councillor, the independent bookshop has earned a reputation for stocking what authorities would consider sensitive books - accounts of Hong Kong's pro-democracy campaigners to famous allegories on authoritarianism, such as George Orwell's Animal Farm or Hajime Isayama's Manga series Attack on Titan.
It's a short journey from Zhu's home in Guangzhou on China's southern coast to the crowded street in Hong Kong's Sham Shui Po district, where Hunter is sandwiched between fabric sellers, garages and trendy cafes.
But, for the 23-year-old, it is also a passage into a different, freer world - where she can find answers to forbidden questions.
When she learned the bookshop had been raided by police in late June, Zhu broke into tears: "I was devastated."
Hong Kong saw a boom in independent bookshops after huge pro-democracy protests rocked the city in 2019. But it has been increasingly difficult for them to survive as China's control over the city has grown.
While Beijing defends its far-reaching National Security Law (NSL) as essential for stability, many Hong Kongers and rights groups argue it has crushed free speech. Thousands of locals, including activists and former lawmakers, have left in recent years, as tough new security laws have led to a slew of arrests and convictions.
When police searched Hunter Bookstore on 24 June, they accused owner Letitia Wong, 33, and a 32-year-old man, of violating those laws and arrested them for sedition and money laundering. They deny the charges and have since been released on bail.
In March, they arrested the owner of Book Punch, along with three employees on the same charges, and reportedly seized copies of a biography on Jimmy Lai, the jailed democracy campaigner.
On 15 July, when the annual Hong Kong Book Fair opened, national security police searched two more independent bookshops, Greenfield Bookstore and Have a Nice Stay, arresting five people for sedition. They, too, have been released on bail.
At the end of the month Greenfield posted on social media, saying: "Our store will be closing after our lease expires. Thank you for walking with us, through wind and rain, for 50 years since our opening." It was the third independent bookshop to shut within a month.
These bookshops have long had a loyal following not just in Hong Kong, but also among many mainland Chinese readers. Some like Zhu travel to the city in search of a single book.
For 19-year-old Li from Shanghai, who didn't give her first name, these are places where she "can see so many possibilities, and where existing ideas can be challenged". Others treasure them as spaces that offer a sense of freedom and community they feel is missing on the mainland.
Now they fear China is eroding that spirit in Hong Kong too.
When Zhu began university in 2021, she became increasingly curious about lesser-discussed chapters of Chinese history - such as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre, a taboo topic that has been scrubbed off the country's tightly controlled internet.
The massive student-led protests ended in a bloody army crackdown whose toll is still contested. Beijing said at the time that 200 civilians died, but according to de-classified UK diplomatic cables, at least 10,000 people were killed.
Zhu sought out films which touch on the era-defining event, but neither epic romance Summer Palace nor the secretly filmed gay drama Lan Yu could satisfy her curiosity.
She became set on tracking down The Unburned Book by Taiwanese poet Yang Du, a bittersweet reflection on protesters who later went into exile.
In 2023, as soon as the China-Hong Kong border reopened after the pandemic she made her way to Hong Kong to find it.
This was when the city's independent bookshops were taking off. People were sharing walking routes online, complete with neighbourhood guides and curated recommendations.
In bustling Mong Kok there was Luck Win, known for its generous discounts, and Greenfield, with its packed floor-to-ceiling shelves. A short walk away were the cosy Have a Nice Stay, founded by former journalists, which held popular late-night reading sessions, and Elmbook, whose cramped but beloved shelves made regulars feel like they were on a treasure hunt.
Then there was Book Punch on trendy Tai Nan Street, with a collection as defiant as its motto, "one punch to wake the reader", and the food lovers' favourite, Word by Word in historic Wan Chai, and, of course, Hunter, with a sofa outside where passers-by can take a break.
That's where Zhu found The Unburned Book. She had tried - and failed - in other stores, so she was surprised when she finally spotted it.
Hong Kong, once a refuge for those fleeing China post 1989, commemorated the killings every year with a vigil. They gradually disappeared as the new laws targeted political gatherings.
Still, when Chris, 20, whose name we have changed, travelled to Hong Kong in early June, he found that one bookstore was displaying relevant books, white candles and rolls of masking tape printed with the Roman numerals "VI-IV" - 6-4, a coded way of representing the 4 June anniversary.
These young people may not be from Hong Kong, but they describe feeling a deep sense of belonging in these bookshops: politically vibrant spaces that engage with the history their governments would rather they forget.
But it's more than just about the books.
Li visited Hong Kong during the Lunar New Year earlier this year, months after a massive apartment blaze in the north-eastern Tai Po district claimed 168 lives.
At Hunter Bookstore, she discovered a wall covered in black sticky notes, where visitors had left messages of encouragement for those affected by the tragedy.
Li says this sense of community is difficult to find in mainland China. She says while they have message boards there too, they wouldn't be focused on solidarity with victims of one particular incident, perhaps because authorities are wary of any outpouring of public sentiment. "People can only express themselves indirectly," Li says.
She was equally struck by another small detail: handwritten notes left by staff alongside the books. Using sticky notes, booksellers had shared reflections on books they had read or highlighted passages they found particularly meaningful. It's not something she had ever seen back home.
Zhu experiences something similar. "We all love books. We all value independent bookshops. That's why we choose to buy books here."
She rarely speaks to strangers while browsing, but she never feels like an outsider. The books and events the shops host give her the feeling she's escaped to somewhere with "at least a little freedom of expression".
"You've left mainland China behind. Of course, you know [this] freedom has its limits. But it's still better than not being able to say anything at all."
But now Zhu can sense this freedom being curtailed.
She says she finds herself encountering authorities more often in Hong Kong than in mainland China. At one bookshop event, she recalls government officials entering the premises. "They just sat there listening alongside us."
Increasing raids have not only targeted explicitly political shops, according to a bookseller who asked not to be identified because of possible repercussions.
"Luck Win Bookstore and Elmbook have always kept a very low profile," the bookseller says.
"They rarely make public statements or organise events. I genuinely can't think of anything they could have done to offend the government."
In the weeks leading up to this year's book fair, both shops were criticised in Wen Wei Po, a newspaper controlled by Beijing's liaison authorities in Hong Kong.
The paper accused them of selling books promoting "soft resistance". This included The Hong Kong Diaries by the last governor of Hong Kong, Chris Patten, before the city returned to Chinese rule, and 300 Short Essays by late Apple Daily columnist Lee Yee. The newspaper was shuttered and several senior staff, including its owner Jimmy Lai, were jailed for violating the new security laws.
"The authorities don't want people to know exactly where the boundaries are," says Tong Kin-long of University College London. "They want people to work out the red lines for themselves, or to censor themselves before crossing them."
Watching these changes unfold in Hong Kong has felt strangely familiar to a man we are calling K, in his 30s from Sichuan.
He remembers a time when mainland China's bookshops were also vibrant spaces for public discussion. Liberal books and magazines would be prominently displayed. Bookshops regularly hosted talks and discussions. But around 2015, he began to notice a gradual tightening.
At first it was books about the country's leaders. But then less obviously sensitive books started disappearing. Public events became less frequent, and the atmosphere changed.
Zhu has a friend who currently runs a bookshop in Guangzhou. She says police occasionally visit the shop to harass the bookseller. During film screenings organised by the bookshop, the electricity has even been cut off.
"Hong Kong," she says, "should be a freer place".
Still, mainland Chinese readers are keen on bringing books home from Hong Kong, even though customs authorities can confiscate those they deem harmful to national sovereignty, security or unity.
K feels anxious every time he returns from Hong Kong. He chooses busier border crossings, avoids books prominently featuring politically sensitive figures and has hidden books inside his clothes, or deep in his luggage.
But that is no longer his only worry. "In the past, people would simply think, 'If I can't buy a book in mainland China, I'll go to Hong Kong'. Now the feeling is different. You don't even know which bookshops will still be here the next time you come."
A week after learning it had been excluded from the Hong Kong Book Fair, Elmbook announced it would close its physical shop in April next year. Soon afterwards, Have A Nice Stay said it would close at the end of August, citing economic difficulties and unpredictable "red lines" over what material was considered problematic.
Many within Hong Kong's bookselling industry have grown pessimistic. Some believe things will only get worse before they get better.
But readers are not powerless, an industry insider says. "We can still buy books. We can still read. And we can still read a great many books."
Chris was frightened after hearing about the arrests at Hunter Bookstore, but he says he will keep going.
"Buying a book has become a quiet way of showing support, and a quiet form of resistance."

Guilt, grief and strength: Gaza’s ‘sole survivor’ children face life alone
Every morning, 13-year-old Jana al-Motouq wakes up alone.
The Palestinian girl prepares her own breakfast, washes her clothes and gets ready for school.
Not long ago, those small tasks were done by her mother.
“She used to wake us up, make breakfast, brush our hair,” al-Motouq said. “Now I do everything by myself.”
That is because al-Motouq was the sole survivor of her family after an Israeli strike killed them on 17 November 2023 in the Gaza Strip.

The attack on a residential building in Jabalia killed her parents, Ahmed and Heba; her twin sister Saja; and her younger brothers, Hossam, eight, and Mohammed, four.
She is among thousands of children left without parents, siblings or extended family after Israeli bombardment killed more than 73,000 people over two years.
Most of Gaza’s 2.2 million people have also been displaced repeatedly, stripped of their homes, schools and the routines that once gave their lives structure.
The result is a generation being forced to grow up amid grief, displacement and profound uncertainty.
Another 35 members of al-Motouq’s extended family, including uncles and cousins, were also killed in the strike.
Al-Motouq survived because she had slept at her grandmother’s house across the street that night after falling ill.
When the explosion shook the neighbourhood shortly before dawn, she rushed outside.
“Our house wasn’t there anymore,” she recalled.
“I kept calling for my mum and dad. I sat on the rubble calling them. Nobody answered.”
Survivor guilt
For days afterwards, al-Motouq returned to the ruins each morning, searching for traces of the family she had lost.
She picked up bloodstained blankets from the debris, hugging and kissing them, before relatives pulled her away from the danger.
“I wished I had been with them,” she told Middle East Eye. “I thought, if I had died with them, maybe I could rest.”
'I thought, if I had died with them, maybe I could rest'
- Jana al-Motouq, Palestinian girl
That guilt is common among people like al-Motouq in Gaza, according to Sereen al-Absi, a psychologist who has worked with survivors like her.
“They always feel that they are guilty: Why did I survive while they are gone? I didn’t protect them,” al-Absi, 29, told MEE.
“Even though logically they know they had nothing to do with what happened, their feelings cannot control the amount of pain they have experienced.”
Al-Motouq now lives with her maternal grandparents in a tent, after displacement destroyed the life she once knew.
Before the war, she and her twin sister were inseparable.
“We wore the same clothes,” she remembered with a faint smile. “If one of us wore something different, we’d get upset.
“She wasn’t just my twin, she was my life partner.”
‘I wasn’t even able to cry’
According to Riad al-Bitar, undersecretary at the Palestinian Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, the war has left more than 68,000 children and adults as sole survivors of their families, as well as more than 75,000 orphans who have lost one or both parents.
The scale of the phenomenon is such that medical personnel in Gaza have adopted the acronym WCNSF - “Wounded Child, No Surviving Family” - to describe patients who arrive at hospitals wounded and alone.
Eighteen-year-old Dima Junina, who lives in Gaza City, was one of them.
An Israeli bombing on 30 October 2023 caused a building next door to collapse onto their house.
Her father, Ahmed, her mother, Noor, and her three younger brothers - Anas, Baraa and six-year-old Mufeed - were all killed.
Junina survived because a door shielded her beneath the rubble. For hours, she believed the rest of her family were still alive.
'I don’t want people treating me differently because I’m an orphan'
- Dima Junina, Palestinian girl
Doctors treated a wound to her head as she begged rescuers for news.
“I kept saying, ‘Please bring my parents and my brothers out.’”
Only at dawn did relatives tell her they had all been killed.
“I wasn’t even able to cry,” she said. “It still feels like they’re going to walk through the door.”
Unlike many people around her, Junina rarely describes herself as a sole survivor. She dislikes being pitied.
“I don’t want people treating me differently because I’m an orphan.”
Sympathy can also bring painful reminders. Classmates sometimes mention her mother without thinking. Teachers occasionally ask students to bring a parent to school.
One English teacher, despite knowing her circumstances, told her to return with her mother after she missed class because she was ill.
“He remembered halfway through the sentence,” she said.
She never returned to his classroom.
Instead, she found teachers who quietly made space for her grief without turning it into a spectacle.
Strength and grief
Both teenagers are now being forced to learn to carry responsibilities their parents once shouldered.
Al-Motouq talks about making tea before school, studying alone, and trying to remain strong because her parents always encouraged her education.
Junina describes becoming “five people in one” - taking on everything her father once handled and everything her mother once managed.
“The war made my personality stronger,” she said. “It had to.”
But strength does not erase grief.
Al-Motouq still accidentally calls classmates by her twin sister’s name. Sometimes she reaches for a pencil expecting Saja to hand it to her.
The trauma she and Junina experience can cause them to withdraw from others or become intensely attached to people who remind them of those they have lost, according to al-Absi.
“It doesn’t necessarily have to be their face; it could be a feeling. So they become attached to that person,” she explained.
The opposite can also happen.
“It can also cause isolation, where you want to isolate yourself.”
Al-Absi said the trauma is compounded because sole survivors carry the grief of every person they have lost.
“It’s caused by losing one, two, three or more people, and it can create a complex form of trauma,” she said.
Wishes
But despite everything, both teenagers insist on completing their education.
Before the war, al-Motouq’s school average was 96 percent. She dreamed of memorising the Quran alongside her twin sister.
Today, she has memorised nine of its 30 parts and hopes to continue.
Junina recently finished high school and is considering studying psychology at university.
People often ask what she wants to become, but she no longer has a clear answer.
“I just want to finish school,” she said, before a brief pause.
“I want to build a water well as an ongoing charity for my family’s souls.”
Asked what they wished for, both said they just want what children elsewhere take for granted.
“A home, a school, a place where we can live without fear,” al-Motouq said.
“We have the right to learn. We have the right to play. We have the right to have dreams.”
Junina asks for something simpler.
“Treat me like a person,” she said. “Not just as the girl whose family was killed.”

The inside story of how Trabzonspor pulled off Salah deal
- Published
As Mohamed Salah signed his two-year deal in front of tens of thousands of fans inside Trabzonspor's Papara Park stadium, the man putting his signature to the contract next to the Egyptian was struggling to keep the smile off his face.
The reaction of supporters over the previous few days had already convinced club president Ertugrul Dogan he had pulled off a transfer coup.
"He's the biggest Muslim footballer in the world. He's an influential role model," he told BBC Sport Africa and BBC Turkish.
"We held Salah's signing ceremony in front of 35,000 people.
"It was clear from everything he did that he felt that love, and he told us as much too. He thanked us."
So how did Dogan persuade one of football's megastars to join a club without Champions League football and which has won the Turkish title only once since its heyday in the 1970s and early 1980s?
'Why should I choose Trabzonspor?'
Located on the Black Sea coast, the city of Trabzon sits near the border with Georgia in the north-east corner of Turkey.
With a population of around 800,000 people, it is not even in the top 20 when it comes to the country's largest urban centres.
But Dogan claims it has something special.
"I always say this about Trabzonspor and the city - we're the biggest one-club city in the world.
"Salah asked us something like, 'Why should I choose Trabzonspor now?'
"We told him about the city and said: 'You can be sure you will meet a group of supporters unlike any you have experienced before. You'll feel the genuine love those people have inside them'."
Born in January 1977, Dogan is himself a son of Trabzon.
The businessman made his money through a series of different ventures, including real estate and hazelnuts, before moving into the energy sector and specialising in biofuels.
He became Trabzonspor president in 2023, shortly after the club's most successful season in recent memory - having won the league title in 2021-22.
Under Dogan's watch, the Black Sea Storm, as the club is known, have finished third, seventh and third in the Super Lig.
Last season they won the Turkish Cup under coach Fatih Tekke, who is now looking to guide his team into the Europa League, despite a 1-0 home defeat in the first leg of their play-off tie against Hungary's Ferencvaros.
"We are working to make Trabzonspor and Trabzon itself a destination for talented young players from all over the world," said Dogan.
"We want to take them to the next level, to move on to bigger European clubs. Those young players… [combined with] star players… a star in every way, with their lifestyle, their professionalism, their smile, their positive energy.
"Mohamed Salah is a really great example in this respect."

Attention 'cannot be given financial value'
During the off-season, Trabzonspor sold 20-year-old Ivorian midfielder Christ Inao Oulai to Fiorentina and Brazilian forward Felipe Augusto, 22, to Zenit St Petersburg - both for large profits after only one season at the club.
Young players from Albania, Belgium, Cape Verde and Portugal have arrived to replace them, but Dogan wants to continue balancing those talents with experienced names.
Cameroon goalkeeper Andre Onana has returned for a second season on loan from Manchester United, but the deal for Salah is the potential gamechanger.
"The attention it has generated and the level of engagement it has created around the world cannot easily be given a direct financial value," explained Dogan, who has openly admitted that Salah will be earning €17m per year (£14.6m, $19.9m), as well as 20% of any merchandise with his name on.
"Purely from a financial perspective, this transfer has no direct return as such.
"We put up our season tickets this year. We had to make another increase. I told our fans, 'Look, I'm bringing you Salah, one of the biggest stars in the world'."
Dogan says nearly 70% of Salah's salary this year was covered by season ticket sales made within the first four or five days after the announcement of his arrival.
The initial target was 25,000 season ticket sales, but the club now expects to exceed 30,000, while major companies have been calling the president, looking to get involved in Salah-mania.
"We're having important discussions in Turkey, Europe and the Arab world as well."
'The whole city lives for football'
The news that Trabzonspor had won the race for Salah's signature after nine stellar seasons at Liverpool raised a few eyebrows.
Many had expected the man who sits fourth on the all-time list of Premier League goalscorers to sign a huge contract with a club in the Saudi Pro League like Cristiano Ronaldo or join Lionel Messi in the United States.
But while there was competition, Dogan says the deal happened quickly once negotiations really got going.
"Once we started talking, both sides genuinely approached each other very sincerely," he said.
"We'd actually been pursuing him since the World Cup, but we knew at the start he was also talking to other clubs."
This meant Trabzonspor initially had to bide their time, given Dogan says there is an unwritten rule in Turkey that if one club is holding talks then the others will wait.
"Yes, there were clubs in Turkey who were interested," he confirmed.
"After they said, 'We've pulled out of this transfer', we started talks. I think it took about five or six days to conclude.
"We had the first meeting over Zoom. At that point it was really just the two sides getting to know each other. Then Salah was on holiday - he was in Mykonos - and after that the talks continued again via Zoom."
Trabzonspor finally brought Salah to Turkey for his medical in Istanbul.
Dogan says they decided to hold it there to show the 34-year-old the kind of reception he would get across Turkey, not just in Trabzon.
Thousands of fans were at the airport to greet Salah when he arrived, even though it was in the middle of a working day.
Trabzonspor's new star also made his debut in Istanbul, entering the fray as a second-half substitute in a 1-1 draw against Kasimpasa on the opening day of the new league season last weekend.
He is expected to make his home league debut in Trabzon on Sunday.
"The whole city lives for football," said Dogan.
"Everywhere you go, on every corner, the city gives that player that energy and that happiness."
Thanks to Mohamed Salah, Trabzonspor's president could be smiling for a while yet.

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan was transferred back to jail early on Friday (August 21, 2026), hours after being taken to a hospital for court-ordered medical checks, the government said.
Also Read | Pakistan government to challenge court on moving Imran Khan to private hospital
The Supreme Court ordered on Tuesday (August 18) that Mr. Khan, Pakistan’s most popular politician, be taken to the private Shifa International Hospital in the capital Islamabad within 48 hours for treatment, after his lawyers petitioned the court over concerns that his health was poor.
The ex-cricket captain and his wife Bushra Bibi, who is also his spiritual guide, were both sentenced late last year to 17 years in prison.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar wrote on X that Mr. Khan was instead taken to the public hospital Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad, blaming the “security situation” caused by Mr. Khan’s supporters at the private clinic.
“A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist, and a physician, conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit,” Mr. Tarar said.
“After the completion of this entire process, he was transferred back to Adiala Jail,” he said.
Mr. Tarar also said that Mr. Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, who is a medical doctor, was present during the examination
Hundreds of police, some wielding sticks, were deployed near Shifa International Hospital late on Thursday (August 20), with roads leading to the clinic cordoned off ahead of the transfer.
Dozens of the 73-year-old’s supporters had waited outside the hospital.
The former prime minister received eye treatment at PIMS earlier this year, with his family and lawyer saying at the time that he had lost most of the vision in his right eye.
The court had warned against public gatherings on the hospital grounds or the use of information about Mr. Khan’s health for political gain, cautioning that any breaches could lead to the order being reversed.
The next court hearing was set for September 16.
Mr. Khan was prime minister from 2018 to 2022 before being removed in a no-confidence vote during a political crisis over tensions between his government and the powerful military establishment
He has since faced multiple legal cases on corruption and other charges, which Mr. Khan and his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party maintain are politically motivated.
His arrest triggered nationwide protests in May 2023, some of which turned violent and led to hundreds of arrests.
Ending decades of political dominance by dynastic parties, Mr. Khan was voted in by millions of Pakistanis who grew up watching him play cricket, where he excelled as an all-rounder and led the nation to a World Cup victory in 1992.
But PTI made little headway improving the country’s finances, with galloping inflation, crippling debt and a feeble rupee undermining economic reform.

Man Utd lack guts and fight, Leeds have a right to dream and Arsenal have rejuvenated attack - Premier League hits and misses

A familiar Spurs issue makes for a nightmare start
Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi spoke about creating a "team I have in my dream" after securing Premier League survival at the end of last season. Well, the new season has started in nightmare fashion.
In their 3-0 defeat at Brentford, Spurs were as bad as they were during that relegation dogfight last year.
After spending over £230m in the transfer window and fielding five debutants at the Gtech, that's hard to fathom. They should have been transformed. That was the expectation.
But it was not the quality of the players on the pitch that was the issue - it was, once again, the mentality.
"We were not ready to fight," admitted De Zerbi. "The first XI was able to compete."
New faces but a familiar problem after Spurs' application was repeatedly criticised last season.
The stats reflected it on Saturday. In that shocking first half, Spurs striker Richarlison managed to win just two of his eight duels. At the other end of the pitch, new centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke won just two of his seven.
Spurs were repeatedly second to the ball, outmuscled in challenges and run over by an incredibly intense Brentford side. The second goal was the perfect illustration of that.
More signings look certain before the transfer window closes. But unless De Zerbi can shift the mentality of this group his ambitions at Spurs will remain an elusive dream.

Encouraging signs at Everton
Everton's performance in victory over Crystal Palace was symptomatic of a team maturing under the influence of wily David Moyes. He fielded the second-youngest XI of his second stint at the club, inviting questions over the suitability of his inexperienced midfield.
But young Harrison Armstrong and new signing Hayden Hackney dovetailed perfectly, unafraid of their elevated Premier League stage. And others shone, too.
Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall delivered a masterful display, scoring a wonderful opener to set the tone. Under-the-radar Iliman Ndiaye was equally impactful. He has more Premier League goal involvements for Everton than any other player since his debut in 2024-25 (15G, 4A).
Everton made big strides following the return of Moyes last term and now have the potential to double down on that progress. No doubt Moyes needs a bit of help from the decision-makers at the club to climb higher in the table. He wants a right-back before the transfer window closes. And talk of a reunion with Jack Grealish offers more hope of investment and improvement.
With a few more signings, there are plenty of reasons for optimism in the blue corner of Merseyside.
Laura Hunter
Can Leeds dare to dream?
Daniel Farke is keen to quash any prospect that anything but survival is possible this season, but Leeds have started the new campaign in the same way they ended the last one.
Only reigning champions Arsenal have picked up more points since the start of April than the Whites - who have lost just once in their last ten games. Leeds are still very hard to beat.
This win over Forest was about defensive solidity. The back five that transformed the last campaign is still going strong. The back three of Jaka Bijol, Joe Rodon and Tarik Muharemovic make 18 clearances between them, while James Justin and Anton Stach won a combined 21 duels on their own.
That solidity earned them a first win - and first clean sheet of the season. Last season, they had to wait until New Year's Day for their first shutout on the road. Advances are already being made on last season - how far above last season's 14th spot could this team go?
Sam Blitz
Tzolis and Odegaard rejuvenate Arsenal attack
Vinicius Jr this, Morgan Rogers that... Arsenal have shown that their transfer window was better than many made out.
Christos Tzolis looks like a gem, a real livewire down the left wing. After a stale opening five minutes on the pitch, he set it alight with two shots and two chances created in the space of four minutes.
It was no surprise to see him strongly involved in the two goals that put this game to bed, winning the ball high up for the first, then crossing for Bukayo Saka for the second.
But Martin Odegaard's start to the season cannot be overlooked either. He backed up the stunning Community Shield display with a first goal of the season here, equalling his league tally last season that saw him miss 30 matches in all competitions.
"When he plays better, the team's a lot better. So we're happy to have him in this level," said Saka about Odegaard after the game.
In fact, this was just the second time since December 2024 that Saka, Odegaard and Kai Havertz started together. All three scored against Coventry.
That trio are like new signings. And with three open-play goals, Arsenal look like a new team.
Sam Blitz
O'Neil lays down his marker at Ipswich
Gary O'Neil needed a fast start as Ipswich boss - to give everyone the chance to move on from Kieran McKenna and turn the next page.
McKenna had taken the club from League One to the Premier League, created an identity and, ultimately, made Ipswich believe they belonged at this level.
That is a difficult act to follow.
O'Neil, though, has now got his first significant result to put his name on.
There was an authority in flashes about Ipswich's performance that suggested they aren't simply going to be making up the numbers this season. They were aggressive without the ball, willing to commit bodies forward and, crucially, showed the character to respond when Sunderland threatened to wrestle control away from them.
There will inevitably be comparisons with McKenna for a while. That's natural. But the quickest way to silence those is to win football matches.
Ipswich have done exactly that.
Lewis Jones
Don't sleep on Igor Jesus just yet
Igor Jesus could have won the game for Nottingham Forest against Leeds. He had two golden chance to score from two Ola Aina balls in - one was saved by James Trafford, the other header bounced over.
But despite the misses, there was a lot to like about the Brazilian forward. He was at the heart of everything good for Forest - especially in terms of shrugging players off. He won 11 duels - seven more than his opposite man Dominic Calvert-Lewin, and four more than the other two Forest starting forwards.
Oliver Glasner took Jean-Philippe Mateta to a different level at Crystal Palace and looking at the early signs of Jesus, there is no reason why the Brazilian cannot become a big player for both club and country.
Strikers will be judged on goals, but Jesus is showing a lot of potential and desire to make his own chances and get into the right areas. Don't sleep on him just yet.
Sam Blitz

A post by an X user named Sonali (@Sonalimumbai1), who describes herself as a BJP leader and is followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the platform, went viral last week. The post carries a somewhat blurred black and white image of a group of women dancing atop a table in what seems to be hotel. Sonali implied that one of these women is Congress leader Sonia Gandhi.
The image, posted on August 14, has more than 353,800 views till date. (Archive)
बारबाले चे मूत्र पिणारे असंच बोलणार. pic.twitter.com/C0jpHXHXMa
— 🚩 सोनाली 🚩🇮🇳 (@Sonalimumbai1) August 14, 2026
The post came shortly after Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi on August 14 mocked at the BJP government’s foreign policy and took a jibe at PM Modi’s customary hugs with international leaders.
The remarks triggered immediate backlash from the BJP and its supporters. As a part of that, X user Sonali, posted a video of Indira Gandhi hugging former President of Cuba Fidel Castro. The caption read, (translated from Marathi), “Whenever Rahul talks nonsense, all the misdeeds of his family come out in the open. Now watch this video. In this, Indira Gandhi is hugging Fidel Castro of Cuba. I don’t think anything there is wrong with it. What will the son of a bar dancer say about this? Now what do the sycophants of Congress have to say about this?”
राहुल्या जेव्हा कधी तोंडाने हागतो त्याच्या खानदानाची सगळी कर्म रस्त्यावर येतात.
आता हा व्हिडिओ बघा.
याच्यामध्ये इंदिरा गांधी Cuba च्या Fidel Castro यांच्याशी गळाभेट घेत आहेत.
I don’t think anything wrong with it.
बारबालेचा पुत्र याच्यावर काय बोलणार…??
आता यावर… pic.twitter.com/FVz3c1USL6
— 🚩 सोनाली 🚩🇮🇳 (@Sonalimumbai1) August 14, 2026
After an X user responded to Sonali’s post with derogatory comments, she countered it with the aforementioned image with the caption: “That’s what people who drink bar dancer’s urine would say.”
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the image, which was bearing the watermark of Getty Images, we ran a reverse image search on Google. This search led us to the archive of Getty Images, where a clearer version of the same image is available. The caption of this image reads: “Go Go dancing girls help break the beer drought on Rawson Hotel in Auburn on 21 November 1967.”
The image comprises three dancing women. If one zooms in on the image, it becomes clear that none of these women is Sonia Gandhi.
Upon further investigation, we came across a Facebook page named ‘I Grew Up in Mortdale 2223’. On November 17, 2025, the page posted the same image with the caption: “#OnThisDay 17 November 1967, a strike by more than 2000 brewery workers in Sydney led to what was to be known as the “Draught Beer Drought”. When, after 14 days of negotiations, the workers voted to return to work, a group of go-go dancers helped patrons to celebrate at the Rawson Hotel in Auburn. [Photo by Vic Sumner » Fairfax Archives]
This news was also featured on the November 15, 1967, edition of The Canberra Times of Australia.
According to publicly available information, Sonia Gandhi studied at Bell Education Trust, Cambridge, United Kingdom in 1964, where she met and married Rajiv Gandhi in 1968. During her studies, she worked as a part time server at a local restaurant in Cambridge. There is no official record mentioning that she moved to Australia in that time period.
Thus, it can be conclusively stated that an image from 1967 of go-go dancers in Australia was shared by X user Sonali to falsely claim that one of those women was Sonia Gandhi.
Sharing unrelated images to attack the Congress leader is not a new trend. Alt News published a fact-check on March 25, 2019, debunking a similar claim. At the time, BJP supporters circulated an image of actress Ursula Andress from the James Bond film Dr No, falsely claiming that it showed Sonia Gandhi in an “inappropriate” dress.

If there’s one thing young moviegoers seem to fear these days, it’s the idea of the in-between. The term liminal horror has gone from niche internet speak to Hollywood trend, thanks to the acclaimed TV show Severance and the recent smash-hit movie Backrooms. Stories like these mine the unsettling feeling of nondescript office corridors and basement halls that seem to self-replicate into infinity; this spring also saw the U.S. release of the excellent Japanese film Exit 8, a video-game adaptation about someone getting trapped in a subway station with seemingly no way out. Now there’s It Ends, a low-budget bit of creepy cleverness with a punchy pitch: What if you got lost driving down a road that never ends?
That this type of premise has grown more commonplace makes sense. Such a film typically needs only one set (for example, a long, lonely road, flanked by trees), a small cast of characters, and a spare, intentionally circular script. It Ends uses that scrappy charm to its advantage, the lack of frills dialing up a sense of realism. The film, written and directed by the newcomer Alexander Ullom, follows James (played by Phinehas Yoon), Day (Akira Jackson), Fisher (Noah Toth), and Tyler (Mitchell Cole), four friends who are headed on a celebratory graduation road trip. Their drive is occupied by the sort of nonsensical, wandering conversations young people love to have; there’s no real sign of anything being wrong until Tyler notices that he’s missed his turn.
The horror builds gradually, spikes, then slows to an existentially brutal crawl. The group realizes that there’s no way off the road, but when they get out of the car to look around, swarms of people emerge from the woods and fight to enter their vehicle. As the friends continue on in search of safety, they notice that the gas tank never goes empty, they never feel hungry, and nobody needs to sleep. They’re in a sort of limbo, condemned to keep moving despite having no destination. It’s essentially a Gen Z take on Sartre’s No Exit, a gentle riff on hell being other people, with a few jump scares tossed in for fun.
But while prior small-scale horror movies such as The Blair Witch Project and Paranormal Activity had an unseen villain guiding the scares, It Ends thrives on an utter lack of information about what is happening and why. The terror of liminality is how effortlessly it evokes the creepiness of a bad dream, the kind that begins in the middle of the story and seems just off. There’s no monster around the corner, no demonic puzzle to be solved. The characters of It Ends initially debate what’s going on, keeping track of patterns occurring around them in search of some explanation. While James keeps doing so as a way of staying sane, the others start to accept their frozen existence; the strangers in the woods, it seems, are also confined to the road’s environs.
That Ullom manages to squeeze a feature-length movie out of such a mundane premise is impressive; it helps that his cast is charming enough to carry it off. As the film plods on, it starts to skip further and further ahead in time, warping the viewer’s sense of chronology. It Ends is more aggressively aimless than other recent entries in the genre: Exit 8 sees its heroes try to figure a way out of their infinite subway station (it was based on a video game, so some resolution is built into the plot); the protagonists of Backrooms discovered a world of non-Euclidean corridors and lobbies in a basement, then found out that opportunistic corporate villains were plundering it; such a revelation hints at sequels that could expand its lore.
The simplicity of It Ends, by comparison, is wonderful and jarring, as is the total inability for future properties to spill out of it. Part of the dread that liminal horror mines is the drudgery of the never-ending scroll, a familiar feeling for anyone who’s been on social media; no matter how much you look, you’ll never hit bottom, only summon more of whatever the algorithm wants to serve you. It Ends is set entirely outdoors but captures that same fear of being stuck without any touchstones to distinguish simulation from reality.

When someone uploads a photo to the people-search tool ClarityCheck, the website has a clear message: “Your reverse image search is private and secure.” New research, though, shows that the website left more than 9 million image files, including photographs of people’s faces, publicly exposed. And a second misconfiguration publicly exposed people’s email addresses and phone numbers.
Overall, according to findings from independent security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, the exposed ClarityCheck database contained roughly 450 GB of images, including what appeared to be profile images, screenshots, and other photographs of adults, teenagers, and children. All of the images were stored in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket, with files in folders named “faces” and “profiles,” which could be accessed by anyone online through a URL included in the company’s publicly available website code.
ClarityCheck is one of a number of so-called people-finder tools that have appeared online in recent years. These websites broadly claim to be able to search the web, public records, and other databases to identify individuals. ClarityCheck’s website says it can run searches on phone numbers, email addresses, vehicle identification numbers, and names. Its photo-search page says it can help “identify anyone in a photo” and find social media profiles “in seconds.”
While ClarityCheck secured the giant image database after WIRED contacted the company in July, Fowler warns that it was seemingly exposed for months, and his initial efforts to flag the problem to the company were unsuccessful. Accidental data exposures create risk for any personal information, but particularly for sensitive and unchangeable biometric data like face images.
And while ClarityCheck’s website requires people to attest that they have permission to upload photos to its site, Fowler points out that in practice, people whose faces were exposed may have had no idea that ClarityCheck held their image. After all, he notes, the service is explicitly designed for identification, and people don’t typically seek to identify themselves or people they know.

A post is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and that the US was in talks to adopt India’s EVM system for the 2028 election. It further claims that Trump praised India’s EVMs as secure and called for an end to mail-in voting. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
Fact: The viral post is fabricated. In his original post, Trump mentioned CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s interaction with the US administration and praised India’s voter ID system while urging Congress to pass the SAVE America Act. However, he did not say that the US was in talks to bring India’s EVM system to America for the 2028 election. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports or official information confirming that US President Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
We then reviewed the social media accounts (here, here, and here) of US President Donald Trump to check whether he had made the statement mentioned in the viral post. However, we found no post from Trump stating that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
During this process, we found a Truth Social post (archived) by Trump dated 18 August 2026. In the post, Trump stated that earlier that month, India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had asked his administration how the US could conduct elections without valid photo ID. Trump also referred to India’s last election, which had 646 million voters, noting that less than 1% voted by mail and that every voter had to provide a valid photo identity document. He concluded by calling for the passage of the SAVE America Act.
The post was also reposted (archived) by US Ambassador to India and Special Envoy to South and Central Asia Sergio Gor on the same day, stating, “President Donald J. Trump is absolutely correct! 646 MILLION voters, every single one, required an ID in India’s last election. Congress should pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT.” This further confirms that the viral post claiming Trump discussed bringing India’s EVMs to the US is fabricated.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) about Trump’s post, in which the US President praised India’s election system and called for the passage of the SAVE America Act, referring to the conversation with CEC Gyanesh Kumar. However, none of these reports mentioned that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
The SAVE America Act (H.R. 7296), or the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, is a proposed US federal law that would require people registering to vote in federal elections to provide documentary proof of US citizenship and require voters to present an eligible photo ID when voting. The bill was introduced in the US House of Representatives on 30 January 2026 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration. As of 20 August 2026, it has not (here, here) become law. The legislation concerns voter eligibility and identification and has no provisions related to adopting or importing India’s EVM system.
To sum up, this viral post alleging that President Donald Trump said the US plans to bring India’s EVMs for the 2028 election is fabricated.

Srinagar, Aug 22: Electricity consumers across Jammu and Kashmir will face higher power bills from September 1 after the Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission (JERC) approved an average 6.83 per cent increase in the retail supply tariff for 2026-27.
The revised tariff has been approved through JERC Order No. 06 of 2026 dated August 20 and will remain applicable to electricity consumption from September 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027.
For metered domestic consumers, the energy charge has been fixed at Rs 2.45 per unit for consumption up to 200 units per month, Rs 4.20 per unit for 201-400 units and Rs 4.60 per unit for consumption above 400 units. The fixed charge has also been increased to Rs 10 per kW per month.
Under the previous tariff, domestic rates were Rs 2.30, Rs 4 and Rs 4.35 per unit respectively. This means the energy component has increased by around 5 to 6.5 per cent depending on the consumption slab, while the fixed charge has risen by 25 per cent.
BPL consumers have been protected from the revision. Those consuming up to 30 units per month will continue to pay Rs 1.40 per unit with a fixed charge of Rs 5.
Agricultural consumers will continue to receive subsidised rates. Metered connections up to 20 HP will be charged Rs 1.05 per unit, while connections above 20 HP will attract Rs 6.30 per unit.
Commercial consumers will also face higher rates, with single-phase consumers paying Rs 3.75 per unit up to 200 units and Rs 5.70 above 200 units, while three-phase consumers will pay Rs 6.15 per kVAh.
JERC has approved an Aggregate Revenue Requirement of Rs 5,095.82 crore for JPDCL and Rs 5,179.90 crore for KPDCL. The Commission has also factored in Rs 2,420.78 crore in tariff-related subsidy support committed by the J&K Government.
The revised tariff will come into force from September 1, with the actual impact on individual bills depending on consumption, consumer category and sanctioned load.

Aston Villa have agreed a deal sign West Ham defender Aaron Wan-Bissaka.
The DR Congo right-back will join on an initial loan deal with an obligation to buy at the end of the season.
Wan-Bissaka has been given permission to travel for a medical in the Midlands but the exact terms are not known, with the Hammers having previously asked interested clubs to pay a £25m fee.
The 28-year-old has missed Championship club West Ham's first two matches of the season during negotiations.
West Ham have sold Mateus Fernandes to Tottenham for £85m and Crysencio Summerville for £60m this summer, but captain Jarrod Bowen has signed a new contract.
Villa, meanwhile, have also had a busy summer in the transfer market, most notably selling Morgan Rogers to Chelsea for £117m.
They currently have the lowest net spend in the Premier League, at about £110m after sales are taken into account.
Despite that, Villa have signed midfielders Johan Manzambi and Joao Gomes, as well as Chelsea winger Alejandro Garnacho on a loan deal with an obligation to buy. They have also added highly rated young centre-back Modou Keba Cisse.
Villa begin their Premier League campaign at Brighton on Sunday (14:00 BST) and will also compete in the Champions League after finishing fourth and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery last season.

Ebola vaccine trial to start in DR Congo as warning issued over speed of infections
- Published
The Democratic Republic of the Congo is gearing up to roll out an Ebola vaccine with some doses being used as part of a trial to see if it is effective against the Bundibugyo species of the virus that is currently circulating in the country.
The Ervebo vaccine does help protect against the Zaïre species of Ebola but currently there are no proven vaccines or treatments for Bundibugyo.
The rollout comes as the World Health Organization (WHO) issued a new warning that Ebola was "growing exponentially" in the north and east of DR Congo and the spread of infections now covered an area bigger than France.
Close to 2,500 people have now died in this outbreak, which was declared three months ago.
Julien Harneis, the WHO's Ebola co-ordinator, told reporters that half of the deaths happened in the last 20 days.
"It is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response," he is quoted by the AFP news agency as saying.
A new report by Save the Children suggests that at least 180 Congolese children have lost both parents or caregivers since the outbreak began.
This outbreak is now the deadliest in DR Congo's history and the second-worst ever - only surpassed by the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak when more than 11,000 people died.
Experts say that it may have been spreading in DR Congo since as early as February but the infections of the Bundibugyo species were initially misdiagnosed as typhoid and malaria.
This, along with the difficulties health teams have in working in conflict-hit areas, local suspicions of health authorities and some traditional practices around burial, have hampered the response.
It is hoped that the Ervebo vaccine may be able to help.
The WHO confirmed that 20,000 doses would be used in a clinical trial to assess the vaccine's effectiveness against Bundibugyo, while 50,000 doses will be administered to front-line health workers.
The WHO and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention welcomed the allocation, describing it as a vital reinforcement of the response.
Meanwhile, the M23 rebel group that controls parts of the east of DR Congo has announced new restrictions on movement between government-held and rebel-held areas of North Kivu province.
Shared taxis and passenger boats between the areas will be suspended for one month starting on Saturday.
Other transport will continue to operate under strict health controls.
The measures follow reports that two travellers tested positive for Ebola in a village under M23 control. The rebel authorities said the restrictions were necessary to prevent further spread.
The move highlights the complexity of tackling Ebola amid ongoing hostilities between the Congolese government and the rebels.
The M23 alliance, which captured Goma and Bukavu in early 2025, has sought to demonstrate its administrative capacity by mounting a parallel Ebola response in territories under its control.
In late June, the rebel authorities declared their zones Ebola-free.
Ebola is a rare but deadly viral disease and the Bundibugyo species is even rarer, with only two known prior outbreaks.
Symptoms of Ebola, which are similar to the flu or malaria, include fever, headache and tiredness, and can begin suddenly within two to 21 days of infection.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea can develop, leading to organ failure. Contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit causes the virus to spread.

The lack of a final agreement means that new 50% duties, set to impact some $20 billion of Canadian exports to the United States, took effect on Saturday.

Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.
Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.
The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.
Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.
In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”
The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.
“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.
The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.
Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.
Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.
The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.
Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.
In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”
Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.
Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.
In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

Dozens die as dengue surges in Malaysia while vaccine uptake stalls
With 55 dead, medical experts warn that high costs, rather than vaccine hesitancy, are keeping uptake low amid the outbreak
Dr Shanmuganathan TV Ganeson, president of the Federation of Private Medical Practitioners’ Associations, Malaysia, said cost was one factor behind the low vaccine uptake.
A two-dose regime could cost between 420 and 500 ringgit (US$104 to US$124), depending on the facility, and was generally cheaper in general practitioner clinics, he said, adding that GPs also lag larger facilities in terms of publicity.
The dengue vaccine also had to compete with other vaccines that were more affordable, he said, especially the flu vaccine.
“People here tend to opt for flu protection, especially travellers, which costs less than 100 ringgit, rather than an expensive dengue vaccine,” Shanmuganathan said.
He explained that the dengue vaccine could not be given to pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers or immunocompromised patients and was recommended only for those aged between four and 60.

The weather conditions in Kochi city were not adverse and didn't warrant disruptions to SpiceJet services, the Cochin International Airport Limited (CIAL) said on Saturday, accusing the airline of spreading misinformation.
On Saturday, the airline alleged that, due to “bad weather in Kochi,” flight operations may be affected.
“Due to bad weather in Kochi, all departures/arrivals and their consequential flights might be affected. Passengers are requested to check their flight status via httpspicejet.com/#status,” SpiceJet said in a social media post.
The airport, in a passenger advisory, said it had noted ongoing operational issues with SpiceJet affecting its international services, including those from Kochi, causing considerable inconvenience and uncertainty for passengers.
“SpiceJet has issued a social media communication spreading misinformation by attributing the disruption to bad weather at Kochi,” CIAL said.
It said there were no adverse weather conditions at Kochi warranting the disruption cited by the airline. “No other airline operating from Kochi has reported such disruptions on account of weather conditions during the same period,” CIAL said.
The airport operator said that, despite ongoing passenger grievances, the airline had not adequately addressed the issues, which had worsened over the past few days.
CIAL said it had made every effort, as a responsible airport operator, to assist affected passengers and provide them with necessary support. Passengers who have booked SpiceJet flights have been advised to recheck their flight status with the airline before proceeding to the airport.
In a statement, SpiceJet Spokesperson clarified that the advisory issued by the airline on social media “was a precautionary measure intended to help passengers plan their journeys and make necessary arrangements in advance, in view of the prevailing weather conditions.”
The airline said its advisory clearly stated that flights might be affected and that it “was not an announcement of any cancellation or suspension of operations.”
The spokesperson said that there were no cancellations of SpiceJet flights from Kochi, and the airline operated both its scheduled daily departures to Fujairah and Dubai yesterday, Friday.
Reiterating its commitment, SpiceJet said it keeps its passengers and travel partners informed of any developments that may potentially affect their travel.
“Our advisories are issued with the safety and convenience of our passengers in mind, so that they have adequate information and time to plan accordingly,” it added.
SpiceJet also said it regrets any misunderstanding that may have arisen from the advisory and reassured that the airline continues to operate its scheduled services normally, subject to prevailing operational conditions.
SpiceJet was fined ₹7.5 lakh by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for informing the tribunal about their settlement at the last minute, after orders had been reserved in eight insolvency petitions against the airline.
The tribunal directed SpiceJet and Aviator ML to pay ₹7.5 lakh each to the Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund.
“Payment of cost of ₹15 lakh payable equally by the operational creditor (Aviator ML) and corporate debtor (SpiceJet), that is ₹7.5 lakh each, to be deposited in the Prime Minister National Relief Fund, within a period of 7 days from today,” the bench said, passing the oral order.
Taking cognisance of the manner in which SpiceJet informed the tribunal about the settlement on the day the order was due to be pronounced, the bench expressed its displeasure, saying, “It is a fraud played with the bench.”

Shigellosis has surfaced again in Keralam, with a three-year-old child from Kottukal in Thiruvananthapuram district admitted to SAT Hospital with the infection.
Following this, health officials have renewed public health warnings, urging people to be cautious about the food and beverages they consume outside their homes, especially during the festival season.
According to reports, the child had travelled with her family to Nagercoil on August 12. On the way, they reportedly consumed cold drinks from a wayside vendor. The child developed diarrhoea and vomiting the following day and was later admitted to SAT hospital, where she is now recuperating in one of the paediatric wards. The case was confirmed on Tuesday (August 18, 2026).
One more case of shigellosis was also reported from Vizhinjam in Thiruvananthapuram on Tuesday; and three scattered cases from Pazhayannur in Thrissur; Kattipara in Kozhikode and Noolpuzha in Wayanad.
Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) is a highly contagious bacterial diarrhoeal infection caused by shigella, which is contracted through contaminated food or water. The disease can present with mild symptoms or as severe cases of diarrhoea.
Health officials point out that cases of shigellosis are reported sporadically throughout the year from all districts in Keralam, with some cases triggering small local outbreaks.
The infection spreads through contaminated water, food and contact from infected surfaces.
While shigellosis is self-limiting in healthy adults, it can be fatal for children under five years, in whom the highest mortality is reported. The elderly and immunocompromised individuals are also highly vulnerable.
Symptoms usually appear within one to two days of infection and include fever, diarrhoea, vomiting, nausea, blood in stools, and painful, frequent urges to use the washroom.
The Health department has advised that affected persons use solutions of oral rehydration salts so that dehydration is avoided and that they seek treatment if there is no respite in diarrhoea.
It was in June this year (2026) that Keralam reported major Shigellosis outbreaks, with over 225 cases and six deaths reported from Kozhikode, Malappuram, and Wayanad districts. Outbreaks were officially declared in Kozhikode (77 cases), Wayanad (27), Malappuram (37), Thrissur (15), and Alappuzha (5). Cases were also reported from Thiruvananthapuram (20), Kollam (15), Kannur (14), Palakkad (6), Ernakulam (4), Idukki (3), and Pathanamthitta (1) during June and July.
As of August 18 this year, as many as 441 confirmed cases, 106 probable cases and eight deaths due to Shigellosis have been reported in the State. Last year, a total of 133 cases were reported, with zero deaths.

Break-up of Villa's Europa heroes leaves cracks for Emery to fill
- Published
Aston Villa's European heroes are already part of history.
They ended a 30-year wait for a trophy by lifting the Europa League in May against Freiburg but the club could have sold six of the starting XI by the end of the transfer window.
Ezri Konsa's imminent £51m departure to Arsenal is the latest high-profile exit at Villa Park this summer as Unai Emery's squad undergoes drastic change.
Istanbul goalscorers Youri Tielemans and Morgan Rogers left last month, Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea a record for an English player.
Lucas Digne was sold to Paris St-Germain and Villa must also find a solution for goalkeeper Emi Martinez after his failed move to Juventus and the signing of his replacement - Zion Suzuki.
Al-Hilal may also test Villa's resolve again before the 1 September transfer deadline for Ollie Watkins, with the Premier League club reportedly tabling a new contract to try to keep the striker.
That would leave Matty Cash, Pau Torres, Victor Lindelof, John McGinn and Emi Buendia as those who remain from the 11 that started in Istanbul.

Why are Villa a selling club?
Like many, Villa are a selling club, mainly due to necessity, and have been for a number of years.
They must comply with Uefa's squad cost ratio (SCR) which restricts them to spending 70% of their football related revenue on player and staff wages, transfer fees and agent fees.
They have already been fined twice by Uefa for breaches, being hit with a £9.5m sanction last year and a £19.4m fine in June, although £12.9m was suspended after Villa came to a settlement agreement with Europe's governing body. But it has meant the club's hands are tied in the transfer window.
The Premier League's Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) also limited financial losses to a maximum of £105 million over a rolling three-year period.
In their latest accounts, ending 30 June 2025, Villa had a post-tax profit of £17m but their two previous years showed losses of £119.6m (2023) and £85.4m (2024).
The regulations have now been replaced by SCR, which sees the Premier League fall in line with Uefa's model
"It's necessity because of the rules," one former Villa executive told BBC Sport, when asked about the sales. "The PSR, the SCR, issues are well documented.
"It does seem slightly unfair they're having their ambition capped at this level. But it has forced this very big churn of players, which is unfortunate.
"Some will be forced due to PSR, some will be player demand. Combined it makes a big problem for Emery and certainly it is a lot to swallow in one go and to try and replace. "
This summer has crystalised their situation further because of the high profile nature of the departures.
Villa had raised just over £200m with the sales of Jhon Duran (£71m), Douglas Luiz (£42.5m), Jacob Ramsey (£40m) and Moussa Diaby (£50m) over the past two years.
This window will see them bank, once the Konsa deal goes through, around £212m, including £9m for Lewis Dobbin who never played a senior game for Villa before leaving for Southampton.
The academy has also paid its way comfortably with Jaden Philogene and Cameron Archer being bought back to be sold again, while Burnley spent £12m on Aaron Ramsey in 2023.
Internally, when Villa first returned to the Champions League in 2024, it was recognised it would be harder for academy prospects to break into the squad which left Villa more open to selling them.
Last summer their gross transfer spend was £71m which was dwarfed by Manchester, City, Chelsea and Arsenal who were all over £200m while Wolves, who finished bottom last season, were £109m.
It justifies Emery's argument Villa are not part of the elite, especially when they spent months working on a deal for Conor Gallagher only for Tottenham to be the ones to step in and buy him in January.
Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea this summer was the easiest way for Villa to comply with Uefa's financial rules.
The plan came after their first fine last year and under it they must break even in 2026-27.
Their run to the Champions League quarter-finals in 2024-25 banked them close to £70m and the main reason they managed to turn a profit in the latest accounts.
Winning the Europa League means Villa guaranteed themselves around £45.6m, which includes the minimum earned for qualifying for next season's Champions League.
Despite the departures optimism remains. Last week's battling Super Cup defeat in Salzbug to Paris St-Germain still showed Villa's competitiveness and Emery's powers of adaptability.
Emery has constantly needed to roll with the punches during his three-and-a-half years in charge but he has consistently improved Villa, having taken over when they were 14th following Steven Gerrard's reign.
In Austria, skipper John McGinn pointed to the fact they still have Emery while others - Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea - have new managers and that Villa's structure remains intact.
"We have a structure in place, standards and rules which have made us a success. I am really excited about the new Aston Villa," said McGinn.
That includes Brian Madjo after Villa won their battle with Fifa to register the 17-year-old earlier this month.
The striker scored on his debut against PSG, eight months after initially signing from Metz for £10m, and could prove one of the surprises of the season.
The drive towards younger players comes after Roberto Olabe replaced Monchi last September as president of football operations with a long-to-mid term directive on transfers.
Midfielder Joao Gomes, 25, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, 23 and defender Matteo Ruggeri, 24, have joined this summer after 20-year-old Johan Manzambi became the club's record buy in July.
They have also had an £18m bid rejected for 24-year-old Southampton defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis.
The loan signing, with an obligation to buy, of Alejandro Garnacho from Chelsea allows Villa to spread the cost while Aaron Wan-Bissaka is due to move from West Ham on a similar deal.
"The problem is they may now be at the end of a chain of transfer deals, with the players involved and their transfer targets dependent on other moves happening first," said the former Villa decision-maker.
Above all, though, Emery remains Villa's biggest asset and he has overhauled them before. This time it would be one of his biggest achievements.
"There's a lot of hope and ambition resting with the manager," said the ex-Villa Park executive.
"He's the ace card they've got left and everybody's hoping with his experience and knowledge they can pull through.
"It's a lot of pressure on him and you've got to wonder if he's trying to think 'maybe I need to go somewhere else with more resources?'
"I don't think it'll be this season but, at some stage as a manager, you get fed up juggling all those demands."

Prince Harry, Elton John and others slapped with millions in legal fees after court loss to Daily Mail
Judgment is only for an initial payment, with potential for bigger sum
Prince Harry and other high-profile claimants must make an interim payment of £9.54 million ($17.9 million Cdn) toward the legal costs of the Daily Mail's publisher after losing their privacy lawsuits, London's High Court ruled on Friday.
Last month, judge Matthew Nicklin comprehensively rejected the case brought by King Charles's younger son and several others, rejecting allegations that the Mail titles had engaged in widespread unlawful activities, such as phone hacking.
Singer Elton John and his Canadian husband, David Furnish, as well as actors Sadie Frost and Elizabeth Hurley were among the other high-profile names suing Associated Newspapers. Other claimants included former Liberal Democratic MP Simon Hughes and Doreen Lawrence, who became an anti-racism activist after the killing of her son, Stephen, in 1993.
Explaining his decision on legal fees, Nicklin was highly critical of the way the claimants' case had been made, including that serious allegations had rested on "speculative and inferential" foundations.
"In my judgment, the cumulative effect of these matters takes the case well outside the norm. The conduct was unreasonable to a high degree," Nicklin said.

A spokesman for Associated Newspapers called the ruling "another overwhelming victory for the Mail and its journalism."
The outstanding amount should be paid on an "indemnity basis," Friday's ruling said. This means that as the losing party, the prince and the others must pay toward Associated's legal costs without the publisher needing to show these were reasonable and proportionate.
The court was told at a hearing in July that Associated had incurred a legal bill of £34.5 million ($64.7 million Cdn), while Harry and other claimants only had an insurance policy that covered £16 million ($30 million Cdn).
A spokesperson for Harry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The prince described the court loss earlier this summer as a "complete and obvious whitewash."
Harry and his wife, Meghan, announced this week their imminent return to Britain, where they will send their son and daughter to school. After briefly decamping in British Columbia, in a decision to leave the U.K. that stunned the British press, they have spent the past six years in southern California.
Previous case brought apology
The case is the final outstanding litigation in a series of lawsuits Harry had filed accusing tabloid publishers of using unlawful tactics.
Harry was previously awarded £140,600 (about $240,430 Cdn) after the High Court ruled he had been a victim of "modest" phone-hacking and other unlawful information gathering by journalists at Britain's Mirror Group Newspapers (MGN), publisher of the Daily Mirror, Sunday Mirror and Sunday People.
In 2023, Harry became the first British royal to give evidence at a trial in 130 years, when he testified as part of the case.
In the other major case, the Rupert Murdoch-led News Group in the U.K. offered a "full and unequivocal apology to the Duke of Sussex" for "the phone hacking, surveillance and misuse of private information by journalists and private investigators instructed by them."
But the court rejected an allegation made in a court filing that Murdoch's newspaper group had a secret deal with Buckingham Palace to block royals from filing such lawsuits.
