Push in Alberta to break away from Canada and form a new country
As he walks around his cafe refilling coffee and delivering baskets of gravy-laden poutine, Christopher Scott wears his politics on his T-shirt.
"Free Alberta!" the shirt declares.
The Whistle Stop Cafe's signature dish is the "heart attack burger", which boasts eight beef patties and various other meats. A MAGA baseball cap rests on the cafe's jukebox, but on this side of the US-Canada border, the acronym stands for Make Alberta Great Again.
The cafe has become a meeting point for Alberta's separatists, who are pushing for the province to break away from Canada and form a new country.
The movement is exposing deep fractures inside one of the world's most stable federations and shares striking similarities with Western Australia's historical secession attempts.
Cafe patrons stop Scott to shake his hand. "Nice to meet you. We're fans," one says.
Scott, who founded the pro-separatist group Let's Talk Alberta, hopes enough of those fans will vote in an upcoming referendum that could set Alberta on the path to independence.
"The facts point to an independent Alberta being far superior to what we're experiencing right now," Scott told the ABC.
"So I don't have a crystal ball, but I have hope."
Alberta is a province of vast skies, endless prairies, towering mountains and abundant oil and gas fields that have made it one of Canada's economic powerhouses.
Those natural resources provide for high employment and high incomes. They also generate a lot of money for Canada's federal budget, a factor that is fuelling the separatist movement.
Scott feels like the province is being forced to subsidise a country that neither respects nor represents them.
Like Australia, Canada has a federal system where funds from wealthier provinces are redistributed to other regions. The idea is to spread the country's wealth and enable each province to provide similar public services.
According to the conservative Fraser Institute, Alberta contributed over $CA300 billion ($304 billion) more to the federal government than it got back between 2007/08 and 2026/27.
"Albertans aren't exercising their sovereignty and it's costing them billions of dollars," he says.
The business owner has become a prominent voice in the movement.
He spent two decades working in the oil industry before buying the cafe in 2019, only to be ordered to close the following year due to the COVID pandemic.
He kept the cafe open despite public health orders, and it became a rallying point for Albertans opposed to pandemic restrictions.
It led to his arrest and a short stint in jail.
"As I was laying in a jail cell for three days for the crime of protesting government policy and doing so on my own property legally, that kind of changed things for me," he says.
"I came to the conclusion that Alberta independence is necessary and inevitable.
"Not just for economic reasons or policy and things like that, but because it's an opportunity to rewrite the rules from the people's perspective instead of the governing party's perspective."
Echoes of Brexit
Support for the movement has gone from a small fringe minority to up to 30 per cent of the population, according to some polls.
On October 19, Canada will learn whether those polls reflect reality.
The vote is technically a referendum on whether to hold a referendum.
Albertans will be asked whether the province should remain in Canada or whether the government should begin the legal process required to hold a binding vote on separation.
Alberta's Premier Danielle Smith says she personally opposes separation but she believes Albertans should have a democratic opportunity to express their views.
"Those who are unhappy with confederation are not fringe extremists and must be listened to," she said in May.
Separatists say the premier could also be in for a shock result akin to Brexit in 2016, when British voters defied the polls to break away from the EU.
Scott says many separatism supporters are too nervous to declare how they'll vote publicly.
"Many people find it difficult to talk about this because it's like, 'What's my boss going to think?' or 'What are my customers going to think?'" he says.
It's not just the pro-separatists who are invoking Brexit.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was governor of the Bank of England during the Brexit vote, has reminded Albertans of the turmoil that followed.
"They're still, 10 years later, trying to undo what people didn't think they were voting for but what they ended up having," Carney has said.
The province's former deputy premier, Thomas Lukaszuk, says that argument should be a powerful motivator.
"When you think you're going to win, a lot of people tend to be passive and not vote, so I'm reminding them of what happened in the UK with Brexit," he told the ABC.
"They woke up the next day and said, 'What have we done?' … and now their economy is in shambles and they're on their seventh prime minister in 10 years."
'Opening the gate for Donald Trump'
Lukaszuk has been driving an old motorhome, decked out in maple leaf decal, around Alberta on a "unity tour".
The former politician grew up in communist Poland. Now he heads up the Forever Canadian group and says spreading the message is his way of "giving back" to Canada.
For him, the most troubling aspect of Alberta's separatist debate is not the prospect of Alberta leaving Canada, but the growing interest in the idea from south of the border.
Alberta separatists sparked controversy this year by meeting with US State Department officials three times, in a move strongly criticised by the premier of neighbouring British Columbia.
"To go to a foreign country and to ask for assistance in breaking up Canada — there's an old-fashioned word for that, and that word is 'treason'," David Eby told reporters earlier this year.
The US's interest could run deeper than Donald Trump's trolling of Canada as the "51st state".
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told a conservative news network in January: "I think we should let them come down into the US, and Alberta's a natural partner for the US."
And in June, the Trump-aligned Heritage Foundation think tank published an article provocatively declaring "Canada's Texas is threatening divorce, and it could eventually become the 51st state".
More than 240,000 people have now put their name to a petition calling for the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, to be declared "persona non grata".
The petition accuses Hoekstra of undermining US-Canada relations and normalising Trump's "51st state" taunts.
At a Forever Canadian event in the town of Diamond Valley, long-time Albertan Mary Papais echoed the fear on many people's minds.
"I believe that they are opening the gate for Donald Trump," she told the ABC.
"Donald Trump wants into this province, he wants the resources that are here, and he will take them and he could [not] care less what any Albertan felt or thought."
The separatist movement is also facing strong opposition from Indigenous leaders, who say separation would affect their treaty rights, which were signed with the Crown, not the province.
They also fear the debate will fuel racism and deepen divisions in Alberta.
"[This] is really another step to try and eliminate First Nations," Piikani Nation chief Troy Knowlton told the ABC.
Earlier this year, First Nations groups took the issue to court, successfully arguing that Alberta had a duty to consult them before allowing the separatist petition to proceed.
The premier pushed ahead with the non-binding referendum anyway, but cited the court ruling for preventing a direct vote on separation.
"I told her this to her face: where you're going to fail in separatism, you're going to succeed in division," Chief Knowlton says.
"First Nations are under attack right now because of what they opened the door for."
Parallels with Western Australia
The debate in Alberta has drawn comparisons to Western Australia.
In 1933, angry over the perceived unfairness of the federal system and the distribution of the state's vast natural resource wealth, WA voted overwhelmingly to secede.
Its petition was ultimately rejected by the British parliament.
Tanya Clemens, a fourth-generation Albertan farmer who supports separatism, sees clear parallels.
"Western Australia voted yes to secede from Australia, but the difference is that they didn't have a legal pathway," she says.
"They had the democratic mandate, but they didn't have the legislative mandate to be able to do that.
"Canada has a legal pathway."
Like Scott, the cafe owner, Clemens was also motivated to get involved in the separatist movement during the COVID pandemic and what she saw as government overreach.
The mother-of-two says the biggest hurdle for many Albertans is that they still have a deep love of Canada, even while being critical of the way the country is run.
"I have [the] Canada maple leaf tattooed on my shoulder and grew up with an ideal of what Canada was and loving it and singing the anthem and having a very deep patriotic spirit to it," she says.
"It's tough for people to move past that and realise that you can still love Canada and want better for Alberta."
When asked what she would do about her maple leaf tattoo if the referendum was successful, Clemens says she would probably add an Alberta flag beside it.
"People have asked me if I would remove it. Heck no. I do love Canada and I love the people of Canada."

It would be 'nice to have choice' over Ashes venues - Root
- Published
Joe Root said "it would be nice to have a choice" over the venues where his England team play as they leave Headingley until 2029.
England's crushing victory over Pakistan is their seventh consecutive win in Leeds, their longest current winning streak at any ground in the world.
But they do not return for a Test at Headingley for three years, meaning they will not have the advantage of playing on this ground in next summer's home Ashes series.
It was put to Root that Australia would be unlikely to give up the advantage of hosting England at their most successful venues when the urn is contested down under.
Australia have not lost an Ashes Test at the Gabba in Brisbane since 1986, or been beaten by England in Perth since 1978.
"Obviously this is a slightly different system here and a different way that things are done," said Yorkshire batter Root.
"I think I should probably stay in my lane and understand that it's someone else's job to sort out. As a player, you want to play at the grounds you have most success at as a team, clearly.
"It's one that we generally do well at and I love playing here - as the Yorkshireman I have to say that from birth, so I'm glad it's the case."
For Root, the innings victory sealed inside three days against Pakistan was the ideal start to his second spell as captain.
It also extended England's run of wins at Headingley, which began in 2018. Their longest winning streak at another ground is six at Chester-le-Street.
The decision for Headingley and Old Trafford to miss out on the 2027 Ashes roster was announced in 2023.
But the match allocation has once again come into focus after the schedule for next year's series was confirmed in July.
Nottingham's Trent Bridge will be the most northerly ground to host a men's Ashes Test, with Southampton given an England-Australia Test for the first time. Headingley will instead play host to a women's Ashes Test.
Headingley staged a men's Ashes Test in 2019 and 2023, both matches England won. The 2019 win, inspired by Ben Stokes, was one of the most legendary contests in Ashes history, ranking alongside Ian Botham's heroics of 1981 on the same ground.
Overall, England's record of nine home Ashes wins in Leeds is bettered only by their 17 at The Oval, and The Oval has hosted 36 Ashes Tests compared to Headingley's 26.
"I would love to play as many games as possible here," said Root. "It's a great Test-match venue, a surface that provides brilliant Test cricket, and one we've had quite a lot of success on recently.
"It's a shame we don't get to play here next year, but I'm sure we will see many, many more brilliant Test matches here."
Headingley will next host a men's Ashes Test in 2031, from when the England and Wales Cricket has said it will keep at least one Test in Leeds or Manchester in the allocation for every home Ashes series. Southampton will get a Test in alternate men's home Ashes.
Root looks set to lead England into next year's Ashes after returning to the captaincy.
The 35-year-old resumed a job he gave up four years ago following the retirement of Ben Stokes.
Root will form a new-look leadership team with Stephen Fleming, who has replaced Brendon McCullum as Test coach.
However, Fleming is not yet in post, with Marcus Trescothick acting as interim coach for the Pakistan series.
Fleming is due to arrive in the UK in September, possibly not before the Pakistan series is over, but Root revealed the pair had been in contact throughout the win at Headingley.
"Every day. I think he's kept tabs on things," said Root. "It's just been great to have him on the end of the phone.
"I can speak to him as much or as little as I like, and it's great that he's very invested already in what we're trying to achieve. There's been constant communication with me and Marcus as well."
Former England opener Trescothick was an assistant to McCullum when the New Zealander was in charge of both the Test and white-ball teams.
England are yet to confirm the make-up of their backroom team now Fleming and McCullum are sharing head coach responsibilities.
And Trescothick said he would "love" to continue working with the Test team.
"I've a huge amount of respect for Stephen and what he's done in the game," Trescothick told Test Match Special.
"He was a fantastic captain and leader and has done a brilliant job doing what he's done as a coach. I'd love to carry on."

Your shots of Fireball could soon get pricier.
The Trump administration's threatened 50% tariffs on some popular Canadian goods went into effect Saturday morning after trade talks with its northern ally fell apart the night before.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney later announced a series of dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on imported US goods.
Those tariffs will apply to industries including dairy, steel, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, Carney said at a press conference in Ottawa.
"We take this step reluctantly," Carney said. "We recognize that it will raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians."
President Donald Trump first announced the new round of tariffs last month to "offset Canadian discrimination."
US and Canadian officials had been working on a deal to avoid the tariffs all week. Trump said in a Truth Social post earlier in the week that the deal was close.
Carney, however, announced in a statement released just before midnight on Friday that he was suspending trade negotiations after he said the United States proposed "last-minute changes" that were "unfair."
"We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship," Carney wrote.
The new tariffs are the latest in the ongoing trade dispute between Canada and the United States. Trump first ordered new tariffs on Canadian goods in early 2025, to which Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs of its own.
The latest tariffs, which took effect at 12:01 a.m. on Saturday, would apply to a wide range of goods, from beer, wine, and spirits to milk products and hockey equipment.
Here are the popular Canadian goods that could be affected.
Canadian whiskies and other alcohol
The list of affected items like beer, wine, and spirits, including the most popular alcohol Americans consume from north of the border: Canadian whisky.
Some of the most popular Canadian whisky brands that could be affected by the new tariffs include Crown Royal, Canadian Club, and Black Velvet.
Crystal Head Vodka, which comes in the signature skull bottle, is also made in Canada and could be affected.
While Fireball Cinnamon Whisky is a product of the United States, it is made from Canadian whisky, which means it could be indirectly impacted by the tariffs.
The trade battle over booze between the two allies heated up last year after Trump's initial tariffs. Most Canadian provinces pulled American-made alcohol from their shelves.
Hockey sticks and gloves
Hockey equipment, such as sticks and gloves, is on the list of affected products.
While several popular hockey equipment brands are based in Canada — including Bauer Hockey, CCM Hockey, and Sherwood — that does not mean their products will be affected.
Some Canada-based hockey brands make their products overseas, like in China and Vietnam, and therefore may not be subject to the new tariffs.
Some wooden hockey sticks from Sherwood are made in Canada, according to the brand, so it's possible those products could be affected.
Dairy products
Various dairy products, such as milk, cream, and powdered dairy, are on the list of affected products.
Notably, cheese was not on the list. However, in announcing the tariffs, Trump said he was responding in part to Canada's treatment of US-made cheese.
Motorcycles, honey, clothing, and much more
The long list of products affected by the new tariffs also includes motorcycles, honey, clothing, plants, essential oils, dog leashes, construction materials, paper, smartphones, and much more.

The DMK on Saturday approved a major organisational overhaul, introducing age caps and two-term limits for party posts and expanding its organisational districts from 78 to 110 following its electoral setback in the April 2026 Tamil Nadu Assembly elections, PTI reported. The party's executive committee, chaired by DMK president M K Stalin at the party headquarters Anna Arivalayam, passed nine resolutions aimed at restructuring the organisation. Under the new structure, each of the 110 organisational districts will broadly cover two assembly constituencies. The move is aimed at creating more localised administration, according to the report. The party will also abolish the standalone "city secretary" post in major urban centres such as Coimbatore and Tambaram. Urban areas will instead be reorganised based on voter density. Chennai Corporation Area Committees will have an average of 40,000 voters, while committees in other corporations will have around 30,000 voters. Once Stalin formally releases the boundary maps for the revamped districts, district executive committees will have to meet within 15 days under the supervision of the party headquarters to implement the changes. The restructuring introduces age limits for several organisational positions. The maximum age for a branch secretary has been fixed at 45 years, while ward committee secretaries in municipalities, corporations and town panchayats will have an upper age limit of 50 years. The maximum age for town panchayat committee secretaries has been fixed at 60 years, while the cap for district secretaries will be 70 years. All these posts will be limited to two terms. According to party sources cited by PTI, the changes are expected to reduce the territorial powers of the existing 77 district secretaries and shorten their tenure. Nearly 10 to 13 district secretaries could be affected by the age cap, with the party likely to move some of them to non-administrative state-level or zonal-level roles, the sources said. Addressing party functionaries, Stalin said the DMK had lost an election but had not suffered a permanent defeat. "Let us consider this as an opportunity we have been given to plan the future of the party," Stalin said, according to ANI. He acknowledged that the functioning of party office-bearers was among the factors behind the electoral defeat and said the party needed to accept its mistakes. Rather than examining individual constituencies and simply replacing party functionaries, Stalin said he had opted for a comprehensive self-assessment. "Even if the mistake is committed by an individual, it is the 75-year-old party that suffers because of it," he said. The party has also formed a 38-member committee to collect feedback from grassroots workers and launched a dedicated website to allow the public to submit their views, PTI reported. Stalin also took aim at Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and TVK leader C Joseph Vijay while addressing party workers. He alleged that Vijay was "busy changing the names of all the projects" introduced by the DMK and said the chief minister treated the Legislative Assembly like a "movie set". Stalin also called on DMK workers to strengthen grassroots mobilisation and focus on enrolling new members who were willing to work according to the party's principles and ideology. He said the party's objective was to remain connected with people regardless of electoral victories or defeats and to work towards making a political comeback. "We are specialists in making a comeback, and we will do it well," he added while appealing the party members to focus on grassroots mobilisation. Victim of sword attack at Swedish school was a 17-year-old girl
Police in Sweden say the victim of a deadly sword attack at a school was a 17-year-old girl
STOCKHOLM -- The victim of a deadly sword attack at a school in central Sweden was a 17-year-old girl, police said Saturday.
An 18-year-old man armed with a sword carried out the attack at the Brinell School in Fagersta, northwest of Stockholm, while classes were in session on Friday. One person was killed and three others were wounded, two of them severely.
Police said the suspect had been arrested and that the case was being investigated as murder and attempted murder. The police said they have no reason to believe there were more perpetrators.
Vastmanland County, where the town is located, said that the two seriously injured boys were ages 12 and 17. A third person, also under 18, was slightly injured and has been discharged from a hospital, Swedish news agency TT reported.
On Saturday morning, around 70 people gathered at the memorial site that the municipality prepared, carrying flowers and lighting candles, TT reported.
There was no official information on the attacker’s possible motive.
Sweden’s national police said that investigators have already carried out two house searches in connection with the suspect. Many witnesses were expected to be interviewed as part of the investigation.
The region went into a state of emergency on Friday, but it had ended by Saturday.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, in an earlier X post, lamented the violence in Fagersta “right after the summer break.”
“We do not yet know what lies behind the act, but we know that the police are working very intensively,” he said. “Our thoughts are with all those affected.”
Sweden has seen a series of violent school attacks over the years.
Last year, 11 people, including the gunman, died after an attack at an education center in Örebro in central Sweden, leading the government to propose tougher gun laws. It's considered to be the worst mass shooting in the country's history.
In 2022, an 18-year-old man attacked two female teachers with a knife and an ax in a school in Malmo, killing them.
In 2015, a 21-year-old local man rampaged through a school in the southern industrial city of Trollhattan, stabbing three people to death before being fatally shot by police. Authorities called it a racist hate crime, saying he methodically selected dark-skinned victims at Trollhattan’s Kronan school, where most students are foreign-born.

I left my wife and twins behind - why this Nigerian man fled South Africa
- Published
Nigerian Richard Itoro is not sure when he will see his twin children again.
Fearing for his safety as the anti-migrant protests cranked up in South Africa this year, the 47-year-old left his family and business behind in Johannesburg and boarded one of the voluntary repatriation flights to Nigeria in June.
His is just one of many experiences that is fuelling diplomatic tension and threatening to rupture relations between South Africa and other countries on the continent.
Tens of thousands of foreigners have left the country over the past two months.
"It was painful for me to leave [the] person who's my best friend," Itoro tells the BBC, with tears welling up, as he reflects on saying goodbye to his South African wife.
Over 15 years, he had built up a car-dealership business, bought a home and created a family. That is now all gone for him.
Itoro became the target of harassment but his wife was not spared the intimidation.
He says his neighbours told her: "You're married to a Nigerian. Those of you who are married to Nigerians we are supposed to arrest you people.
"You guys betrayed us. Go and leave the country with your husband and don't be here."
Itoro was baffled.
"My family was just a small family, which was beautiful and peaceful. I had no issues with anybody."
The pressure became too much.
"If I go home and start all over again, it's better than being here, being harassed, being scared for my life," Itoro says.
But, the businessman says, the Nigerian high commission would not let his wife and children travel with him.
He describes how leaving felt like a movie where someone boards the last helicopter flight out of a besieged city.
"I wish I could have just begged the people from the embassy and said: 'This is my wife, I can't leave her behind and my kids,' but I couldn't.
"So my car started departing and I wished I had told her not to cry."
The anti-migrant groups in South Africa said their protests were aimed at undocumented foreigners. The country's outspoken Culture Minister, Gayton McKenzie, who leads one of the parties in the coalition government, also emphasised this point.
"We say South Africa is open to our brothers on the continent but come here legitimately. Come with your papers," he told the BBC's Interview programme.
But Itoro says his legal status did not protect him from hostility as he shows the BBC a copy of the document that he says proves he had the right to stay in the country.
He was not alone, according to the Nigerian authorities.
"We have records of Nigerians who have legitimate papers to remain in South Africa, yet they have been attacked," Nigeria's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Sola Enikanolaiye said during a recent meeting with South Africa's Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.
The temperature was raised last week following the death of a Nigerian who was killed as police were arresting him over suspected drug offences. An independent body is now investigating.
Lamola maintained that South Africa deals with those who take the law into their own hands, but added that President Cyril Ramaphosa was also "very firm on South Africa's sovereign right to enforce its immigration laws".
Despite the diplomatic efforts, South Africa's reputation has been severely damaged.
Not least because of images and videos circulating on social media. Not all of them were what they were purported to be, but one, involving a Ghanaian, was genuine and it sparked huge concern once it started being shared in April.
When Emmanuel Asamoah left Ghana in 2023 for South Africa, he was chasing the kind of opportunity many migrants dream about.
The 37-year-old hairstylist settled in Soweto, on the outskirts of Johannesburg, found work, built a life and believed he had a future in one of Africa's biggest economies.
But three months ago that future suddenly felt uncertain when he was surrounded by a group of South Africans who demanded that he leave. The confrontation was captured on video.
"This thing of you guys moving from one country to another… is no longer working," one woman can be seen telling Asamoah.
"Now, we are making it very clear to you guys, we don't want you here. We want you to fix your countries."
Having returned to Ghana's capital, Accra, in May, Asamoah tells the BBC that the encounter left him terrified.
"They came to me and started pushing me... So, they started asking questions and harassing me… they said that I should go home, that we are spoiling their country, because of us, they don't eat, we are taking their girlfriends," he says.
South Africa's high jobless rate - standing at more than 30% - is seen as one of the factors fuelling the tension. It was a sentiment echoed by McKenzie.
"No man can feed another man's children while his children are starving. Our people are starving of jobs," he said backing calls for those who came to the country without papers to leave.
But Asamoah insists he had a stamp in his passport giving him permission to stay.
"I was not illegal. I was legal in South Africa. That's why I told them that, they can take me to the police station so that we can go to Home Affairs and verify," he says.
For Asamoah, returning home has brought an unexpected fresh start.
With support from a Ghanaian businessman, he has opened a cement business and is determined to build his future.
"My brothers and sisters in South Africa. I'm in Ghana now. I'm fixing my country," he says.
But Ghana's government remains angry at the way it sees its citizens are being viewed in South Africa.
In an interview with the BBC, Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa spoke about how he saw it as going against the spirit of continental solidarity and a failure to recognise how African countries helped in the struggle against apartheid, which ended in 1994.
South Africa "should be the epitome of Pan-Africanism. We talk about African integration. We talk about free movement… even if you have issues with high immigration, is this how you resolve it?", the minister asked.
In Lagos, Itoro is still pining for his family.
"It's not easy. But we talk every day, and I'm broken. There is hope, because... my wife is going to join me very soon, as soon as God lifts me up. But it was heartbreaking, and that's how I felt: like I lost everything," he says.

BEIJING – China is poised to launch Chang’e-7, its most technologically complex lunar mission to date, in its search for frozen stores of water in permanently shadowed craters near the moon’s south pole.
The uncrewed mission, named after a mythical Chinese goddess of the moon, will feature the deployment of a robotic lander, rover, and “hopping” probe to one of the coldest places in the solar system. It will represent a major step toward Beijing’s long-term goal of building a permanent human presence on the moon, with plans under way for a crewed lunar landing before 2030 and the setting up of a joint research station with Russia by 2035.
Next week, the Chang’e-7 spacecraft will lift off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in the southern island province of Hainan atop a Long March 5 rocket with payloads that also include an array of scientific instruments such as water analyzers, cameras and radars.

September 11, 2001, will be remembered as one of the darkest days in American history. As the 25th anniversary approaches, National Geographic, in collaboration with the 9/11 Memorial and Museum, is marking the occasion with a new documentary miniseries: 9/11: Reunited. The three-episode series revisits the personal stories of several survivors of the terrorist attacks, with a twist: It reunites people whose paths crossed at that time to celebrate the bonds they formed 25 years ago.
Director Julian Jones was a producer on NatGeo’s Emmy-winning 2021 documentary miniseries 9/11: One Day in America. The experience inspired him to return to direct 9/11: Reunited. “What emerged for me [while making the 2021 documentary] was a sense of people showing up for each other, a selflessness and everyday heroism,” Jones told Ars. As the 25th anniversary of the attacks approached, he and National Geographic decided to commemorate the milestone with a documentary series focused on that aspect.
“We wanted to bring people together to offer gratitude to each other, to answer unanswered questions, to talk about things that maybe they weren’t ready to talk about until now, and also to remember their fallen comrades or friends,” said Jones. “After 25 years, who do they want to meet? What questions have they got? I think we also wanted to tell the story of what many in the 9/11 community call 9/12, that’s the rest of your lives—the journey, and in many cases, the psychological and physical struggles.”
“The challenge was not to impose a story onto anything,” said Jones. “It was to let the story emerge organically in a way that would feel meaningful to our participants. Our job was to really listen to our participants and be guided by what they wanted.”
Jones and his team had vast amounts of archival footage at their disposal, and selecting which footage to use—and how much of the often gruesome details to include—proved to be a delicate balance. There is no footage of the desperate people jumping to their deaths from the burning North Tower, for instance.
“You can’t sanitize history,” said Jones. “You can’t sanitize what happened. But at the same time, you have to be sensitive. The horrible images we all remember of people falling or jumping—those people are someone’s husband, wife, child, or parent, and we have a duty to be sensitive to that. We tried to choose archival material that reflected the experiences our participants were having at that moment.”

Among those featured in 9/11: Reunited are John Paczkowski, George Phoenix, and Jan Demczur. Paczkowski worked on the 67th floor of the North Tower; Phoenix worked on the 74th floor. They had just entered the elevator to get to work that morning when Demczur, a janitor, jumped in at the last minute with his gear. The first plane hit the North Tower as the elevator approached the 65th floor; the car plummeted 15 floors before the emergency brake kicked in.
Trapped in the elevator with smoke pouring in, they managed to pry open the doors only to be faced with a wall. Undaunted, Demczur used his squeegee blade to carve a hole in the plaster so the men could kick through the wall to escape—a process Demczur re-enacts for the series. They ended up in the 50th-floor men’s room and managed to evacuate down the stairwell with other survivors before the North Tower collapsed.
Debbie St. John was taking the subway to work that morning, unaware that the North Tower had been hit. She disembarked to find police officers directing passengers to the street exits. She was walking down the street when the second plane hit the South Tower. So was Stefan Herlacher, a bond trader who worked nearby. He spotted a large piece of wreckage falling toward him and thought he would be hit; the wreckage hit St. John instead.
Herlacher braved the falling debris and panicked people running through the streets to help her and was horrified to find the fragment had cut through her back. He waved down a passing ambulance driver who transported St. John to a hospital. She was the first 9/11 patient admitted and the last to be discharged 18 months later after 50 surgeries. St. John spent years working on her rehabilitation, marrying her fiancé, and having children, but she never forgot the man who saved her life.
“I remember speaking to Debbie on the phone and she said, ‘I’d love to meet Stefan,’” Jones recalled. “I asked, ‘Well, what would you like to do?’ And she said, ‘I want to take him horseback riding.’ Because she had such terrible injuries and couldn’t walk. She just said, ‘I want to show him how far I’ve come thanks to him.’ So we did that.”
Cmdr. Craig Powell was working at the Pentagon when the third plane hit, as was Lt. Col. Marilyn Wills. Wills had been in a meeting and recalled a fireball flying past and singeing her bangs. Trapped in the burning wreckage, Wills led a group of survivors down the corridor, crawling, because she knew there was a window there. The window was bomb-proof and initially wouldn’t open, but Wills and her commanding officer kicked until it popped open. They were on the second floor, so Powell and others on the ground below formed a fireman’s catch as people jumped, one by one.
“You get a second chance, live life.”

It was Powell who caught Wills, one of the last to jump to safety. He initially thought Wills was dead when he passed her off to a teammate for CPR. “In that situation, giving a person CPR [on site], I didn’t hold out much hope,” Powell told Ars, although he later learned she had lived. As for her second-story jump, “That takes a lot of courage,” he added, since it was the equivalent of a fourth-story jump from a regular building. He remembers being in considerable pain the following day—“catching all those people is not easy on your body, and I was inside the room when the ceiling came down”—as well as needing a shower. “I stunk, and it wasn’t BO,” he said. “When the shit hits the fan, so to speak, your body dumps all these endorphins; it’s literally the smell of fear.”
Powell admitted to some apprehension about reuniting with Wills, mostly because of the cameras, but Wills took control of the situation and helped him through it. “I wanted to participate to close the loop,” said Powell. Despite his experiences with active combat, the events of 9/11 hit differently. “It was an attack on American soil,” he said. “It really hit close to home and made me very concerned about the safety of my family.” He was diagnosed with leukemia in 2015, related to his rescue work at the Pentagon that day, but the treatment worked, and he was able to walk his daughter down the aisle for her wedding. “My greatest appreciation is that my kids are alive and I got to watch them grow up,” he said.
Kevin Shea had just joined the FDNY’s Ladder 35 unit, and his shift was ending when the first tower was hit. He volunteered to stay on, and his supervisor agreed, but there was no room for him on the trucks. Shea planned to find his own way to the site and meet up with the team there. But when he reached the staging area, he couldn’t find Ladder 35. His crewmates were filmed walking into the South Tower several minutes before it collapsed—the last time any were seen alive. Shea was standing just outside when the tower collapsed. It’s the last thing he remembers.
Paramedic Al Kim was working triage in the South Tower Marriott lobby and survived the collapse. He recalled hearing beeping alarms sounding in the wreckage—motion sensors worn by all the firefighters that trigger alarms when the wearer stops moving for a prolonged time. Kim started combing through the wreckage looking for survivors when he came across an unconscious and badly injured Shea, and he salvaged medical supplies from one of the burning ambulances to stabilize the firefighter.
When the North Tower started to buckle, he moved Shea to the safety of an underground parking garage nearby, leaving him in the care of another physician who had taken shelter there. Kim never saw Shea after that—until they were reunited for the documentary—and found no other survivors. Shea spent several weeks in the hospital. He had broken his neck in three places and credits Kim’s on-site care not just with saving his life, but with preventing him from becoming quadriplegic.

Bill Spade of FDNY Rescue 5 on Staten Island was on site helping evacuate people from the North Tower when he met John D’Allara of NYPD’s Emergency Services Unit coming down the stairs. They ended up chatting for about 25 minutes about their respective wives and sons; Spade recalled that it was almost as if they were writing their own obituaries. Then everything went eerily quiet, and an evacuation order came through due to fears that the North Tower might collapse. D’Allara was hurrying others through the exit door when it fell. Spade curled up in a ball under falling debris, having lost sight of D’Allara, who was later confirmed dead.
Spade was only one of two Rescue 5 members to survive, but he never forgot D’Allara and contacted his widow, Carol D’Allara, a few years later. But D’Allara’s sons were still too young. Spade, who volunteers at the 9/11 museum in Manhattan, thought the 25th anniversary was the right time to reconnect with the family and let the sons know their father “was thinking of them right to the very end.” D’Allara saved 20 lives that day; his son Nicholas also joined the NYPD and even carries his father’s old badge.
Perhaps the most well-known story—depicted in Oliver Stone’s 2006 film, World Trade Center—is the rescue of Port Authority Police sergeant John McLoughlin. McLoughlin and colleagues William Jimeno and Dominick Pezzulo were on the main concourse between the two towers when the South Tower collapsed, trapping them in the rubble 30 feet underground. Pezzulo was attempting to lift debris off his comrades when the North Tower collapsed 30 minutes later and he was buried by falling debris. McLoughlin was buried up to his elbows, slowly being crushed under the weight, and recalled hearing Pezzulo take his last breath—but not before firing a single shot into the air to alert any rescuers to their location.
Meanwhile, above ground, Scott Fox had joined the rescue effort, despite having retired nine months earlier from Rescue 5, as the FDNY formed makeshift companies out of surviving firefighters. So did John Busching of the NYPD’s Emergency Services Unit. They risked their lives navigating increasingly unstable debris to help dig out first Jimeno (after 13 hours), then McLoughlin (after 22 hours)—a small victory in the midst of tragedy.
McLoughlin was gravely injured and spent six weeks in an induced coma, underwent 27 surgeries during his three weeks in the hospital, and then went through rehabilitation. He still walks with a slight limp. But thanks to Fox, Busching, and several others, “I got to see my kids grow up and meet my grandchildren. How do I thank you for that?”
These are harrowing stories, and it almost seems cruel to ask the survivors to relive that trauma yet again. Per Jones, it helped that there were pre-existing relationships with many of the survivors because of the earlier documentary, which helped establish trust.
“It’s a big deal to ask someone to share the story of the worst day of their lives,” said Jones. “It is emotional, and it is hard for them, but I was astonished by the bravery of the people who participated. They wanted so badly to meet the person who saved them, or the person they saved. In those fleeting moments, amidst all that chaos and horror, these incredible bonds were formed that can never be broken. Many survivors also have a real sense of gratitude and of a duty to keep telling their stories, to remember that day and all the people who didn’t survive.”
Fair warning: 9/11: Reunited is an undeniably powerful documentary series—how could it not be, given the subject matter?—and exquisitely well done. But it’s not an easy watch, and for many who lived through that day, even 25 years might feel a bit too soon to relive those painful memories. (As a former New Yorker who had just moved to DC four months before the attacks, I couldn’t bear to watch more than one episode at a time, and felt pretty wrecked by the end. But nonetheless, I’m glad I persevered.)
“It’s a tough watch, and it is emotional,” said Jones. “But I hope what comes out of the series is a sense that, out of all this tragedy, this was a day when people turned up for each other. There was a human instinct to help each other regardless of what you look like or believe in. People just wanted to help. Personally, I found that incredibly moving.”
9/11: Reunited premieres August 21 on National Geographic. It will be available for streaming on Disney+ and Hulu the following day.

Vieira named new Senegal head coach
- Published
Former Arsenal and France captain Patrick Vieira has been appointed as the new head coach of the Senegal men's national team.
The 50‑year‑old replaces Pape Thiaw, who was sacked in the wake of the country's last‑32 exit at the 2026 Fifa World Cup.
Born in Senegal's capital Dakar, Vieira will now manage the country of his birth, having moved to France aged eight before later winning over 100 caps for Les Bleus and lifting the World Cup in 1998 and the European Championship in 2000.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) said the appointment reflects its "desire to strengthen its high-level technical staff" and is "perfectly aligned" with the nation's sporting ambitions.
Details of Vieria's contract and his starting date in the role are still being discussed.
His first matches in charge of the Teranga Lions are expected to come next month in qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Vieira joins the West Africans after he left his role as Genoa head coach by mutual consent last November, with the team bottom of Serie A.
He won eight and drew nine of his 26 games during the 2024-25 season to guide the Italian club to safety and a 13th-place finish.
However, he left the club after managing just two wins in 25-26, with both of those victories coming in the Coppa Italia.
During his playing career, midfielder Vieira won three Premier League titles and four FA Cups at Arsenal, as well as silverware with AC Milan, Inter Milan and Manchester City.
He retired in 2011 and became the manager of New York City in 2016 before returning to Europe with Nice and leading them to seventh in Ligue 1 in his first season.
Vieira was sacked in December 2020 and became Crystal Palace manager the following year, guiding the Eagles to 12th in the Premier League and the FA Cup semi-finals in 2021-22.
He was dismissed in March 2023 after a 12-game winless run, before joining RC Strasbourg as their first appointment following a takeover by BlueCo, the company which owns Chelsea. He left Strasbourg by mutual consent in July 2024.
His predecessor Thiaw was at the centre of controversy in January when he ushered his Senegal team off the field when Morocco were awarded a stoppage-time penalty in the 2025 Afcon final.
The players eventually returned after a delay of about 17 minutes before Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved and Pape Gueye scored an extra-time winner.
However, Morocco were declared the winners of the tournament in March when the a Confederation of African Football appeals board overturned the result of the final following Senegal's walk-off.
Senegal have lodged an appeal against that decision with the Court of Arbitration for Sport - with the case due to be heard on 8 October.

The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing.
The killing of Hind and her family was one of the most high profile of a series of incidents involving civilian casualties during the first months of the Gaza conflict which prompted international outrage.
Hind died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.
Palestinian paramedics dispatched an ambulance to rescue Hind and stayed on the line until contact was lost, but the ambulance too came under fire, killing two medics. The bodies of the casualties were only retrieved 12 days later when Israeli troops withdrew. The IDF also admitted on Wednesday that troops had fired on the ambulance.
“Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by military police criminal investigation division,” the military said on Wednesday.
Criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.
The IDF published reviews on Wednesday into four other high-profile incidents in Gaza, saying it was launching a criminal investigation into the killing in near the southern city of Rafah of 15 Palestinian medics and humanitarian personnel in March 2025.
Troops lying in ambush for Hamas militants initially shot at an ambulance that was trying to retrieve casualties from an Israeli offensive, then fired on a series of emergency vehicles which approached their positions, according to phone footage and the sole survivor of the shootings.
The soldiers then bulldozed over the bodies and vehicles, burying them in a mass grave. UN and rescue workers were only able to reach the site a week later.
“They were killed in their uniforms. Driving their clearly marked vehicles. Wearing their gloves. On their way to save lives. This should never have happened,” said Jonathan Whittall, a UN official who helped recover the bodies.
The Israeli military initially said it had opened fire because the vehicles were “advancing suspiciously” without headlights or emergency signals. But it backtracked from that account after footage emerged showing the Red Crescent and civil defence teams driving slowly with their emergency vehicle lights flashing and logos visible.
Munther Abed, a Palestinian paramedic who was at the incident in which 15 of his colleagues were killed, said he hoped “those who killed my colleagues, who were like family to me, face justice, real justice”. “I want to say to the whole world, ambulances 101 is not a target and they must be protected,” he said referring to the speed dial number for the Red Crescent service in Gaza.
The IDF said it had decided not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of World Central Kitchen vehicles, killing seven humanitarian workers from the US-based aid group, which has distributed food in Gaza throughout the war.
The aid group said at the time it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars. The vehicles, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air, were left incinerated and mangled, indicating a series of targeted strikes.
The IDF said on Wednesday it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the convoy deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.
One of those killed in the strike was Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom. The Australian government has called the deaths a “tragedy and an outrage” and pressed for full accountability and “any appropriate criminal charges”. In February this year the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had made it clear to Israel and its president, Isaac Herzog, that there be transparency about Israel’s then-ongoing investigation into the incident.
  In April this year Australia’s foreign minister Penny Wong paid tribute to Frankcom on the second anniversary of her death, saying “people like Zomi are rare and their selflessness should not only be celebrated but protected”.
World Central Kitchen said it strongly disagreed with Israeli officials’ account of the airstrikes and their decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.
“At the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody. It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”
The UK Foreign Office issued a statement on Thursday, saying the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack.
The minister for the Middle East, Stephen Doughty, said: “For more than two years, we have pressed the government of Israel to deliver the justice and accountability that the families deserve. This is not good enough. We have raised this with the Israeli authorities today and will continue to push for urgent answers.”
The military also decided not to take criminal action over the killing of four humanitarian workers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. Israel later effectively barred the medical charity from operating in Gaza.
Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din, an Israeli rights organisation, said that over the last decade only a tiny proportion of investigations had led to indictments while growing political pressure “further deters Israeli law-enforcement authorities from holding those responsible accountable, even when clear evidence does exist”.
A UN report published in February described “a pervasive climate of impunity” by Israel in occupied Palestine “in relation to gross violations of international human rights law and serious violations of international humanitarian law … some constituting war crimes and possibly other international crimes”.
Israeli forces say they never deliberately target civilians in Gaza and accuse Hamas of using civilians to shield its militants.
The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law, it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”. “For more than a thousand days, the IDF has been conducting intensive combat across numerous fronts, carrying out a wide range of military missions in an exceptionally complex operational reality,” it said in a statement.
The war began in October 2023 when Hamas launched a surprise attack into southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and abducting 250. Israel’s ensuing offensives in Gaza have killed more than 73,000, mostly women and children, including more than 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October.
On Wednesday, Israeli airstrikes killed seven Palestinians. Israeli military officials told local media one strike that killed six had targeted a meeting of Hamas commanders in Gaza City.
Itamar Ben Gvir, Israel’s far right national security minister, said last weekend that “targeted assassinations should be carried out in Gaza, taking down 30 to 40 every night.”
“Not just those who pose an immediate threat … There are people there who are not worthy of life. They shouldn’t live. They’re not even people,” Ben Gvir told a podcast hosted by a former hostage held by Hamas in Gaza.

Omaha police recently agreed to stop carrying gloves that can deliver electric shocks to students in the halls of Nebraska’s largest public school district.
The decision affecting most Omaha middle and high schools came after the Associated Press first revealed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)’s plan to give officers the “Gloves” – or “generated low output voltage emitters”. The devices have also been used in recent years by some jails.
The superintendent of Omaha public schools, Matthew Ray, on 18 August requested that police working in the schools, known as school resource officers, stop using the gloves. Omaha police agreed two days later.
However, the suburban Bellevue police department that patrols two Omaha schools and the large Bellevue district said its officers will continue carrying the gloves. Three other large school districts in the metro area that have Omaha school resource officers assigned to their buildings have not taken action to stop police from using the devices.
The AP left messages seeking comment from the Millard, Elkhorn and Westside districts that are also patrolled by Omaha officers.
Bellevue schools spokesperson Amanda Oliver said the district has a great relationship with Bellevue police and doesn’t see a need to alter anything.
“We’ve got a great communication and dialogue that we have with them consistently. And so for us right now, no changes are being made,” Oliver said.
Ray said in a school board meeting on 17 August and in a letter to the public schools community that he’d only learned about the gloves the previous week. But local television station KETV found emails from 2023, when Omaha police notified the districts that the department planned to equip officers with the gloves, and an official with the Omaha district said they were already familiar with them because Bellevue police had them at two Omaha schools.
Students in all the Omaha area districts have gone back to class over the past two weeks.
Before halting the use of the gloves, the Omaha police department held a news conference in which an officer demonstrated how they can help an officer quickly get control of someone who is refusing commands.
Omaha police used the gloves twice during the 2025-26 school year. And Bellevue police have also used them twice in previous years.
At the school board meeting, about 30 people spoke out against police using the gloves. Residents and board members alike said they were appalled at the practice. No one spoke in favor of it.
“I can’t even imagine walking down the hallway and seeing a peer of mine being electrocuted in a place that is supposed to be a safe space for students,” said Nora Wessel, a senior at Omaha Central high school. “Yet, this is now a very real possibility. These are adults we are supposed to be able to trust, but these weapons create a barrier for our students to turn to resource officers when needed.”
Ken Trump, president of the consulting firm National School Safety and Security Services, said before schools allow police to bring in technology like shock gloves, there should be a careful discussion of questions like how school resource officers will respond to students with disabilities or special medical needs, how parents will be informed and under what circumstances the gloves can be used.
“Less than lethal doesn’t mean low risk,” Trump said.
Ray said the district recognized longstanding relationships with law enforcement partners and the important role school resource officers have in promoting school safety. Continued use of the gloves “would be counterproductive to our work together”, Ray said.
Omaha’s mayor, John Ewing Jr, who helped oversee creating the school resource officer program when he was on the police force, said the department has honored the school district’s decision to “opt out”. The Omaha police department said officers will continue to carry stun guns, batons, pepper spray and firearms.
Most of the Omaha police department’s 34 school resource officers had been trained and were allowed to use the gloves, the mayor and the police chief, Todd Schmaderer, said in a statement.
“We believe it is the safest use-of-force option in the rare times when it is used,” the statement said.
In 2025, Omaha police agreed to pay Compliant Technologies LLC, which manufactures the gloves, about $66,000 for 40 gloves, according to the contract.
Officers were expected to give warning before using the gloves and then touch the person for up to 15 seconds while the electric shock was delivered, the statement said.
Bellevue’s police chief, Ken Clary, said his officers will continue carrying the gloves, which they have had for more than three years.
“I am not comfortable having our officers give up a tool that has repeatedly proven to be safe, effective and less harmful than the alternatives,” Clary said in a statement.
The devices activate when an officer presses a button. The gloves must touch someone’s skin directly to produce voltage that causes pain, which is intended to make people stop resisting officers. Unlike stun guns, they do not leave burn or contact marks.
In the 2025-26 school year, an Omaha officer used the glove in one case to stop a high school student from another school from trying to escape after fighting with a security guard, according to the statement. In a second case, the glove was used on a student at the Omaha district’s integrated learning center for special education students. Police said that student made verbal threats and threw a chair at a school security guard, striking the guard in the head. The student also punched the guard in the head, according to the statement.
Bellevue police didn’t immediately have details about when its officers have used the gloves. Clary said the devices have been an extremely effective tool that sometimes make students cooperate on sight even without shocking a student.
Omaha public schools is Nebraska’s largest school district and serves more than 50,000 students, its website says. The metro area’s other districts are also among the biggest in the state.

Childcare centre threatened with closure in Sydney's east given lifeline of 12 months free rent
In short:
The City of Sydney has offered a childcare centre free rent for 12 months to prevent its closure.
The not-for-profit Goodstart East Sydney centre said it had been suffering significant losses despite high occupancy.
What's next?
The centre is yet to respond to the council's offer.
A not-for-profit early learning centre on the brink of closure has been handed a lifeline, with more than 60 families rallying in Sydney's eastern suburbs to keep the doors open.
The threatened closure of Goodstart East Sydney in Darlinghurst triggered a petition this week after the centre informed families that the site was shuttering from November 26.
Goodstart had been leasing the site from the City of Sydney but said the design and location of the building meant the centre was making a significant loss, despite high occupancy.
In response Lord Mayor Clover Moore offered the early learning centre 12 months free rent while its future is resolved.
"I hope this gives comfort and certainty to parents that we are committed to ensuring stability and the learning community they have built in Darlo [Darlinghurst]," Cr Moore wrote in a Facebook post.
It is unclear if the provider, which leases three other sites from the City of Sydney, has accepted the rent waiver.
The ABC has reached out for comment.
'There aren't many options in the area'
On Saturday, Tim Martin was among dozens of families at Potts Point who rallied in support of the centre.
"Losing the centre would be so devastating," the father-of-two said.
"What we really feel for is the staff of the centre too, they probably won't have jobs."
Mr Martin said he and his wife had already canvassed close to six centres nearby.
"They're all full, some have a day here or there, but it's just not doable."
Three centres in the local area have recently closed. Another not-for-profit in Paddington could also be lost as the site is earmarked to be sold.
Fiona Thatcher said her 11-month-old daughter Mave had been on the centre's waiting list since she was 12-weeks-old.
"I don't think many of us have much of a plan B because there aren't many options in the area at all,"
"It would certainly involve enrolling in multiple centres, driving quite a distance … it would also mean losing the educators, which was the primary motivators for getting together like this."
Ms Thatcher said she did not think the area could accommodate the 60 families enrolled at the childcare centre and the more than 100 on its waiting list.
Labor Councillor Zann Maxwell said the demand was there, but the provider had given "mixed messages" about the site's closure.
"The last thing we want to see is the loss of a childcare centre in the inner-city," he said.
"We want to be making sure that this is the kind of place where all sorts of people can live, including young families, and we're not serious about it if we let places like this close."

Fraying bond between Israel and young American Jews sparks deep concern
Within the Israeli Reform movement, which constitutes a minor segment of Judaism in the country, there is a distinct push to send more young Israelis overseas to work as camp counselors
Concerns are growing among Israelis across the political and religious spectrum over a fraying bond with younger Jewish Americans, who place less importance on supporting Israel as part of their identity compared to older generations, a recent AP-NORC survey reveals.
"It’s extremely important to us," stated Itai Nixon, the head of the diaspora department at Israel's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs. "We’re the state of the Jewish people, not just Israelis."
Lesley Sachs, chair of the Israel Movement for Reform and Progressive Judaism and a critic of the current Israeli administration, similarly views a close working relationship with diaspora Jews as a "strategic asset" for Israel and the global Jewish population.
Consequently, she expresses deep apprehension that Jewish people abroad are losing their feeling that Israel serves as a sanctuary, particularly at a time when growing antisemitism impacts them irrespective of their political or religious beliefs.
"That was always really, really important that everybody around the world, especially after the Holocaust, knows that there is a country that will always take them," Sachs remarked while at her Tel Aviv synagogue.
"This is already a few generations after, and this is less prominent in their DNA. And I think that this is really a failure on the part of both Israel and world Jewry, that we have not managed to keep that prominent."
Taglit-Birthright Israel has provided free 10-day "discovery" trips to Israel for one million young Jewish adults from the United States and other nations since 2000. According to the organization's chief executive, demonstrating how a personal bond with Israel transcends contentious political debates has become more necessary than ever.
"That really increases the importance of my job to expose people to what they give up on," explained Gidi Mark. "What we give them is a mirror."
Cracks appear in the long-standing Israel-US alliance
While Israel and the United States share a historical alliance, President Donald Trump met with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Washington earlier this week to confer on the conflict with Iran that both nations initiated five months prior.
"The United States is perceived as the best friend of Israel in the entire world, and that’s still the case," noted Tamar Hermann, director of the Viterbi Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at Jerusalem's Israel Democracy Institute.
However, disagreement surrounding a potential ceasefire in the conflict with Iran has eroded faith among Jewish Israelis that Trump places Israel's security first, falling sharply from 64% in March down to 26% by June, research from the institute indicates.
Against this backdrop of diplomatic strain, Israelis note that the influence of American Jews, who have traditionally advocated for military, financial, and political assistance to Israel, is becoming increasingly vital.
This amplifies anxiety that progressive youth in the U.S., including young Jews, view any allegiance to Israel as incompatible with their personal principles.
This drop in affinity has grown sharper following the October 7, 2023 attack, in which militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 individuals, predominantly civilians, in southern Israel and seized 251 hostages.
Israel's subsequent military campaign against Hamas in Gaza has resulted in over 73,000 deaths, based on figures from the Gaza Health Ministry.
Operating under the Hamas-administered government, the ministry keeps detailed logs that international entities and U.N. bodies generally consider dependable. Its tallies do not differentiate combatants from non-combatants, though it states that women and children constitute roughly half of those killed.
The war subsequently triggered widespread demonstrations throughout the U.S., particularly across university campuses.
"Holocaust, refugees, the importance of Israel in times of need abroad, and the fact that Israel is a small country fighting for its existence … that’s history they read in a book," Sachs observed regarding younger Jewish Americans. "They weren’t emotionally part of it in any way or any form. And so they look at their values and the things that they believe in. And they don’t see it in Israel."
Complex ties define the relationship between Jewish Americans and Israel
Data from the AP-NORC survey shows that roughly four out of ten religious Jewish adults under the age of 45 in the United States regard backing Israel as "extremely" or "very" central to their Jewish identity, compared to approximately half of older religious Jewish adults.
The poll of 1,022 Jewish adults—encompassing those identifying as Jewish by faith alongside culturally, ethnically, or secularly affiliated individuals—revealed that just around half of religious adults believe Israel's ongoing military operations in Gaza are justified. Among Jewish adults without a religious affiliation, that proportion drops to just two in ten.
Meanwhile, approximately six in ten Jewish adults view anti-Jewish bias as an "extremely" or "very" severe issue facing the United States today.
To many Israelis, growing safety threats faced by Jews make it all the more tragic that younger Jewish Americans no longer perceive the state of Israel as a refuge or even an ally.
"Antisemitism sadly helps us to explain why a Jewish homeland is not a bad idea," stated Asaf Zamir, a deputy mayor of Tel Aviv and former consul general in New York. "Opposing the government is fine, but you cannot understand your history as a Jew without understanding the part of Israel in it."
Israel seeks to engage secular and progressive North American Jews
To foster stronger bonds with diaspora communities, both Israeli state institutions and faith-based groups are expanding exchange initiatives. For decades, young Israelis have worked at North American Jewish summer camps, while Jewish individuals outside Israel receive complimentary visits to the country.
"To see Israel and meet Israelis is the gold standard," Nixon remarked regarding youth trips to the nation.
Gidi Mark of Taglit-Birthright noted that ongoing conflicts since 2023 have reduced trip attendance and altered how visitors experience the country. He described an instance where a visitor shouted "Israel! Israel!" outside a hotel simply because he felt secure enough to express his identity.
"These people don’t feel free to experience who they are in the places that they are coming from," Mark said.
These and other initiatives focus on non-religious Jews and members of Reform Judaism, which represents the largest Jewish branch in North America and emphasizes progressive values such as social justice.
Orthodox Jews living abroad tend to maintain stronger connections to Israel, while Orthodox Israelis typically report feeling closer to diaspora Jews than secular Israelis do, Hermann noted.
Within the Israeli Reform movement, which constitutes a minor segment of Judaism in the country, there is a distinct push to send more young Israelis overseas to work as camp counselors.
"That kind of action is important, that one-on-one connection saying, ‘You know what, we believe in the same things you do. Really, we have the same ideology in general, and we feel we need to change Israel together,'" Sachs said. "We need to be partners in making Israel the country that we all need."
Eighteen-year-old Alma Edry is spending two months serving as a counselor at a progressive Jewish summer camp in Ontario alongside teens and young adults from Canada and the United States. She noted her primary surprise was "that Israel is such a big deal for people outside the country."
"Most of their friends are anti-Israel," she observed concerning the campers. "This is their chance to celebrate their connection."
