Rejecting the idea of 'manusmriti', he asserted that a woman belongs to no one but herself.
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Friday described India’s 70 crore women as the country’s “biggest asset”, saying they are more forward-looking than men and have a crucial role in shaping the nation’s future. He also invoked the idea of women's autonomy and said that a woman should have the exclusive ownership of her own life.Speaking at the fourth event of 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' at the AISSMS College Ground in Pune, Maharashtra, he invoked a verse from the Manusmriti and contrasted it with his call for the empowerment and autonomy of women. Referring to the verse, he highlighted the notion that, “A woman in her childhood belongs to her father, after marriage belongs to her husband and in her old age belongs to her son.”Rejecting this idea, he asserted that a woman belongs to no one but herself. While acknowledging that the relationships in a woman’s life are important, he stressed that they do not determine her identity or ownership, which, he said, rests exclusively with her.Speaking on the central theme of the evening, “break the cage”, Rahul Gandhi called on the audience to recognise the individuality that sets each person apart and to resist the pressures that seek to confine them to predetermined identities or expectations.
He said the most important message he wanted people to take away from the evening was a simple but powerful one: “Every single one of you is unique in this universe.”Elaborating on the idea, Rahul Gandhi stressed that individuality is not merely about being different from others, but about recognising one’s own worth and identity. “You are unique. You are special. You are an individual,” he told the audience. He emphasised that every person has a distinct way of looking at the world, a different set of aspirations and the ability to imagine a life beyond the boundaries imposed on them.Rahul further connected this sense of individuality to the freedom to dream and choose one’s own path. “And you have your own dream, your own vision for your life,” he said. The emphasis, he suggested, was not simply on having dreams, but on having the freedom to define those dreams for oneself rather than allowing society, circumstances or established notions of what one ‘should’ be to determine them.Through the theme of “break the cage”, the LoP framed personal freedom as the ability to step outside these limitations and acknowledge that no individual should be reduced to a role, label or identity prescribed by others. His message was that recognising one’s uniqueness is the first step towards claiming the freedom to shape one’s own future, pursue one’s aspirations and live according to one’s own vision of life.
Rahul Gandhi attacks Manusmriti
Rahul Gandhi launched a sharp attack on the Manusmriti over its treatment of women, criticising the text’s prescription that women should remain under the authority of male relatives throughout their lives. He contrasted the idea with his call for women’s autonomy, arguing that a woman’s identity and freedom should not be defined by her relationship with her father, husband or sons.Quoting from the Manusmriti, Rahul Gandhi said, “I (would) like to quote here the Manusmriti, which says clearly that in childhood a female must be subject to her father, in youth she belongs to her husband and, when her lord is dead, she belongs to her sons. A woman must never be independent.”Calling the words unacceptable, Rahul Gandhi added, “These words are a shame. These words should not have been spoken.” He said the country should instead recognise women as individuals with their own aspirations and agency, describing India’s 70 crore women as its “biggest strength” because of their “70 crore unique journeys, unique imagination, unique dreams”.His remarks framed the debate around women’s independence as a broader question of individual freedom, with Rahul arguing that women should have the right to define their own identities and determine the course of their lives rather than be treated as belonging to male relatives.
Event follows political storm, clashes
The event follows a political storm and clashes between student organisations. The programme was preceded by a midnight clash between the NSUI and ABVP at the COEP Technological University hostel.It happened after ABVP claimed that female students were being forced to attend the event. Meanwhile, Congress leaders countered the claims, saying two female students, who had earlier expressed their support for the event, were threatened and confined inside the hostel.BJP has also accused Congress of paying influencers and manufacturing crowds for the event. Meanwhile, Congress has alleged that the ruling establishment was attempting to disrupt Rahul Gandhi’s student outreach.
NSUI-ABVP clash erupts at COEP hostel
Tensions escalated on Friday night when NSUI and ABVP members clashed at the COEP hostel campus ahead of the LoP’s interaction. Police resorted to a lathi charge to control the situation, while several injured activists were taken to Sancheti Hospital.According to police sources cited in the material, the Shivajinagar Police registered cases against 50 to 60 people, including six named NSUI and Youth Congress activists, following a complaint by an ABVP member.The confrontation reportedly centred on student participation in LoP Rahul Gandhi’s programme. NSUI activists said they were responding to distress calls from female students, while ABVP alleged that Congress-linked workers were forcibly encouraging hostellers to register for the event.
Congress alleges female students were intimidated
Congress leaders accused ABVP workers of entering the girls’ hostel and intimidating students who had expressed support for the event.Congress spokesperson Atul Londhe alleged that a female student was cornered and forced to apologise on camera. NSUI state president Sagar Salunke claimed that students had called the organisation for help and alleged that CCTV cameras had been switched off before NSUI members arrived.Salunke also alleged that students, including orphaned students, had been pressured to record videos praising the college administration. The case registered by police followed a complaint from 21-year-old student Malhar Nilesh Patil, who alleged that a student’s video statement had been recorded under pressure at the hostel.
Pawan Khera alleges conspiracy to disrupt event
Congress leader Pawan Khera alleged that there had been a conspiracy to disrupt LoP's Pune programme, claiming that the response among young people had rattled those in power.Khera linked the controversy to the issues female students were expected to raise with Rahul, including alleged diversion of scholarship funds. He accused ABVP workers of intimidating students and said the incident reflected an attempt to keep women away from public decision-making.He also invoked Pune’s history as the city where Savitribai Phule pioneered women’s education, arguing that the theme of the event was particularly relevant to the city.
BJP calls event ‘Paise Ki Goonj’
The BJP launched a separate attack on the programme, accusing the Congress of paying influencers to mobilise attendance and promote Rahul Gandhi’s event on social media.BJP Maharashtra spokesperson Navnath Ban alleged that influencers were being offered Rs 30,000 to Rs 35,000 each, along with travel expenses, and claimed that the overall expenditure could reach Rs 9 crore to Rs 10 crore if around 3,000 people were paid.Ban dubbed the programme ‘Paise Ki Goonj’ instead of ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ and demanded an investigation into the source of the alleged funds. BJP leader Keshav Upadhyay separately accused Rahul Gandhi of using student issues as a political platform.
Congress hits back, says BJP ‘rattled’ by youth response
The Congress rejected the BJP’s allegations and accused it of trying to create obstacles to LoP Rahul Gandhi’s programme because of his growing support among young people.Maharashtra Congress spokesperson Sachin Sawant claimed that the BJP was particularly apprehensive about Rahul's appeal among Gen Z and alleged that authorities and ABVP members had attempted to disrupt the programme.
NCP (SP) leader Mahesh Tapase also criticised the BJP, saying there was no reason to oppose a programme focused on issues affecting students and young people.
What is ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ about?
Rahul’s Pune interaction with female students is centred on student and youth concerns, with issues such as paper leaks, unemployment and the education system expected to feature in the programme.The Congress has sought to position the initiative as a platform for students to directly raise their concerns, while the BJP has characterised it as a political campaign by the Leader of the Opposition. The Pune event, therefore, has begun against the backdrop of an escalating political battle over who controls the narrative around student and youth concerns.

Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa named Sensi-Contugo director of the country's Centre of Strategic Intelligence (CIES) in January 2024.
The office of the president and Ecuador's National Assembly expressed their condolences over his death and that of Hollihan.
The Italian-Ecuadorean businessman had had close links to Noboa even before he was chosen to lead the intelligence service and was considered a close ally of the president.
Shortly before being named head of the CIES, he had served for four months as a minister in his cabinet.
Noboa has declared three days of national mourning starting on Thursday.
Newspapers in Ecuador have also run obituaries of Hollihan. The Guayaquil-based designer founded Sensi Studio, a brand praised for incorporating traditional Ecuadorean elements and materials in its designs.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The other victims have not yet been identified.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.

Great camera. Strong battery life. Solid performance. Qi2 25W support. Slick contextual AI features.
TIRED
Not much is new. eSIM only in the US. Secure face unlock still doesn’t work in the dark.
The hot pink Hibiscus color is dazzling, but is Google’s 11th-generation Pixel just another iterative upgrade, or does it dial things up to 11? Diving beneath the surface, we find a slightly better chipset and camera, faster wireless charging, a fresh batch of AI features, and not much else. Don’t get me wrong: This is a slick smartphone, perhaps the best Android phone for folks who are comfortable with Google and Gemini AI, but it’s only a very slight improvement over last year’s Pixel 10.
Although it lands alongside the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, the Pixel 11 shares more in common with the new Pro Fold (review coming soon). The Pro models' more powerful camera system, with the gimmicky, glowing HiLight LED, is what sets them apart. The base model storage has finally jumped up to a more practical 256 GB, but that means the starting price of the Pixel 11 is $100 more than the 10 at $899 (not technically a price bump since the 256 GB model of the Pixel 10 was the same price).
Refinement has been the pattern in smartphones for the last few years, and the Pixel 11 does nothing to buck that trend. If you’ve got a 3-year-old handset and you’re in the market for a new phone, the Pixel 11 should be in the conversation, but if you’re looking for a justification to upgrade from last year’s Pixel 10, you won’t find it here.
Minor Makeover
Photograph: Simon Hill
The instantly recognizable design has been slightly refined; most notably, the pill-shaped camera bump is thinner and all-glass. Stick a case on the Pixel 11, and it will lie flat on a desk. It sports the same satin finish on the recycled aluminum frame and gloss finish on the glass back as last year’s phone, but with some fun new colors.
I was delighted to get Hibiscus (otherwise known as hot pink), but there’s also a more subtle Pistachio (warm green), and the usual Frost (white) and Obsidian (black). I’m sad they cut Indigo (surely everyone’s favorite from last year). Like Apple, Google seems to save the fun colors for the regular Pixel, and the Pros look more muted.
Despite a 6.3-inch screen, this is what passes for a small phone nowadays. Switching from last year's Pixel 10 Pro XL, I really appreciated how easy it was to handle the Pixel 11 one-handed. It’s a little thick, but it feels good in hand and has almost the same profile as the Pro, so you can use cases interchangeably. And I do recommend snagging a Pixel 11 case; I already scuffed the paintwork when I dropped it on the beach.
The screen is the same as last year’s: an excellent 6.3-inch OLED display with a 1080 x 2424-pixel resolution and refresh rates of 60 or 120 Hz. It’s a shame Google didn’t upgrade to a variable refresh rate (1 to 120 Hz) since it can save battery life. It also defaults to 60 Hz, and you have to dip into the Display settings to toggle on the smoother 120 Hz. The display is plenty bright with a 3,000-nit peak brightness; I never found myself squinting. Side by side with the Pro, it’s not quite as bright or sharp, and it has larger bezels, but you have to look closely to see the difference.
The fingerprint unlock is as good as any, but Google’s Face Unlock still doesn't work in the dark, which will annoy any iPhone defectors. US buyers will also have to do without a SIM slot, as the Pixel 11 is eSIM-only stateside. Physical SIM cards make switching between phones more straightforward, but phone makers and carriers have made that process smoother with eSIMs than in the past. Sure, it’s much easier to pop a card in than to go through your carrier when traveling abroad, but setting up an international eSIM isn't that complex. Both have benefits, but with US phones and carriers embracing eSIM over the past couple of years, it's become a nonissue.
Power Up
The new chip, Google’s Tensor G6, is supposed to deliver 20 percent gains in power efficiency, 25 percent faster browsing, and 15 percent faster app loading. The Pixel 11 has 12 GB of RAM and 256 or 512 GB of storage. For everyday use, it feels fast and responsive. I had no issues with loading apps or scrolling web pages, and the camera app feels a bit faster. Compared with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, I also noticed the Pixel 11 notified and loaded video from my Nest video doorbell a second or two faster.
I put it through its paces with the challenging mobile game Wuthering Waves. It was playable, but the action stuttered, and even on the Balanced (graphics and performance) setting, there were dropped frames aplenty during combat. After an hour, the Pixel 11 was warm, and the battery went from 40 to 26 percent. Less demanding games, like Mini Metro and Alto’s Odyssey, were fine, but dedicated gamers should still look elsewhere.
The 4,985-mAh battery is a disappointing 15-mAh jump over the Pixel 10, but Google claims battery life has improved 25 percent from 24 hours to 30 hours. I’m not sure it’s quite that much based on my first week of testing, but the Pixel 11 has seen me through very busy days without hitting empty, though I still think daily charging will be the norm for most folks.
The Pixel 11 charges at 30 watts wired (cable but no charger included), but support for Qi2 25W enables faster wireless charging. I recommend buying a Qi2 wireless charger. The magnetic Pixelsnap (Google's version of Apple's MagSafe on iPhones) feels a touch stronger than the one in the 10-series, and it’s such a handy feature that saves you from fumbling with cables. Google has also expanded the screensaver so you can have a multiple swipe function on the nightstand, including clock, weather, photos, charging status, and smart home controls.
Google has also switched to a MediaTek modem in the Pixel 11. I wouldn’t normally mention a modem, but the Samsung variant Google used in last year’s 10 series was prone to draining the battery and not holding a signal terribly well. Anecdotally, the Pixel 11 does better in a few spots where I’ve traditionally had trouble with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, which is great news for when you want to use your phone for calls. Your mileage may vary.
AI Everywhere
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google’s phones have always been about software over hardware, but the real-world value of AI features comes down to context. If I have to go digging or remember that a feature exists, I probably won’t get much value from it. This is why Google weaves its AI into everything, rather than applying it as a layer on top. The latest Gemini Intelligence features extend Google’s lead in this space.
Rambler improves the Pixel’s voice-to-text, cutting ums and ahs and letting you draft messages conversationally. I didn’t like it as much as my colleague, but I’m not really a speech-to-text guy, and I have a Scottish accent that it sometimes picks up wrong. I use the Pixel’s Recorder app a lot and love it for instantly transcribing my interviews, but Rambler doesn’t show the text as you talk like Recorder does; everything pops up after you’re done, which I don’t like as much.
AI overviews pop up right there in the Messages app when someone texts with a meet-up request, and you can add it to your calendar, or if they have a restaurant suggestion, you can tap to open it directly in Maps. Gemini can also dig details like flight numbers out of your Gmail to share via Messages if you let it. This is quite handy.
Fans of Circle to Search will be glad to know you don’t even have to snap a photo anymore; you can open the camera app, hold down the nav bar, and circle anything in the viewfinder to get info on it. You can also get location-based suggestions on the lock and home screen, such as a shortcut to your loyalty card in Google Wallet when you’re in a relevant store or recommendations for what to order at a restaurant from Maps.
There’s nothing groundbreaking here, but features like Call Screen for screening spam calls and Now Playing for surfacing the name of the song you can hear are still there, and those are the kinds of things that I miss when I switch away from a Pixel phone.
AI is firmly embedded in Google’s apps, and there’s no switch to turn it off completely, but you can choose to turn off Gemini, cut its access to apps like Photos and Messages, and turn off features like Circle to Search. Most of the camera app AI options are exactly that: options. But if this all sounds gimmicky and the idea of an AI-infused phone gives you the creeps, the Pixel line is not for you.
Camera Magician
The triple-lens rear camera is one of the top reasons to buy the Pixel 11. The camera feels faster, with less processing delay than the Pixel 10, and you can snap a shot and instantly load it into the gallery. Spec-wise, it’s almost identical, with a 48-megapixel main camera, 13-megapixel ultrawide, and 10.8-megapixel telephoto for 5x optical zoom. The main camera sensor is larger, enabling slightly better low-light performance, and the digital zoom capability is up from 20x to 30x. The 10.5-megapixel front-facing camera is the same.
Screenshot: Simon Hill
Everything works beautifully. Most people probably only ever use the main camera and the selfie camera, and reviewers can get too far into the weeds, but the bottom line is that you don’t need a particularly skilled hand or eye to snap great photos with the Pixel 11. I really appreciate the telephoto lens. I rarely have a use for the ultrawide, but the telephoto is great for zooming in from a distance, and though the 30x zoom is digitally enhanced by combining multiple images, there’s no generative AI at work, so you get a real image.
The camera app is feature-packed if you want to dive in. The most notable new features are the Camera Looks, which are like filters you select before you snap a shot. Phone cameras are typically tuned a certain way—Google’s phones tend to be punchy and high-contrast with realistic colors, while Samsung saturates colors and Apple prefers brighter images—but Camera Looks lets you tweak that to opt for warmer colors or dial up the shadows.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google Pixel 11, main camera
Magic Capture is a clever new feature that lets you hold your phone up at a party or event and record video and select still shots simultaneously, without having to watch through the viewfinder. It’s a nice way to be more in the moment, and a safer way to hand your phone off to Mum and maybe get decent photos back.
No one really needs to upgrade their phone every year or two. It’s only by skipping a few releases that you’ll feel a real difference, and this is especially true for Google's phones because so much of what makes them special is on the software side, and many of those features will make it onto older phones too, though they might take a while.
For slick software features and a camera that’s easy to get great results from, the Pixel 11 is tough to beat in this bracket. If you want performance, both the Samsung Galaxy S26 and the Apple iPhone 17 are superior. Unless you’re a keen photographer, I don’t see a compelling case for paying more to get a Pro model. The Pixel 11 is the value sweet spot in Google’s new lineup, at least until the A-series next year.

RAIPUR: The ongoing probe into the BSc agriculture paper leak in Chhattisgarh’s Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya (IGKV) has opened a disturbing can of worms, pointing to a striking breach in exam security and integrity. The question paper was allegedly copied without even opening the sealed envelope, the police said, adding that an endoscopic camera, which could be extremely miniature in size, was inserted into the envelope after making an incision in it.
According to the FIR filed in the case, the miniature camera, which is typically used to see narrow and hard-to-reach places inside a human body, scanned the contents inside the sealed cover that were leaked thereafter.
The alleged method, which investigators believe allowed the question paper to be accessed without visibly tampering with the sealed packet, has emerged as the key modus operandi in the case.
Addressing the hurried media conference on Saturday, the police said the scanned paper was then converted into images or copies that were passed on to students and circulated on WhatsApp about two hours before the Entomology examination was scheduled to begin.
According to the FIR, Kawardha Agriculture College received an email about the leak at 8.41am, followed by similar information to university officials around 8.54 am. Students and their representatives also alerted the university about portions of the paper that were circulating on WhatsApp.
Raipur Crime DCP Smritik Rajnala said six people have, so far, been arrested in connection with the leak. The arrested suspects include Yogesh Sonkesariya, a professor of a private college in Durg, and five students who allegedly purchased the leaked paper for Rs 12,000 each.
The sleuths also suspect that Sonkesariya played a central role in the operation. Elaborating on the statement recorded from the alleged accused, police said Sonkesariya did not need to break open the packet. After taking the sealed Entomology question paper home, he allegedly pierced the envelope with a needle and another pointed tool, inserted a Rs 2,500 endoscopy camera through the tiny opening and recorded the paper inside. He then allegedly reconstructed the questions from the video, sold the paper and passed it to a student network from where it was circulated through social media handles.
The leak surfaced on Aug 20, when the question paper began circulating on WhatsApp shortly before the exam. As the paper distributed at examination centres was compared with the viral copy, the contents matched, triggering alarm in the university administration. The exam was subsequently cancelled and has been rescheduled in the first week of Sept.
About 1,200 students from 27 agriculture colleges were to take the exam, officials said.
Chief minister Vishnu Deo Sai directed a strict and impartial probe, while the university constituted a five-member committee to probe the leak. The govt also ordered a wider review of question-paper security — from printing and storage to transportation and custody at exam centres.
Vowing ‘zero tolerance’ towards any attempt to compromise the credibility of examinations, the CM said the probe must establish the entire chain — from the source of the question paper to those who circulated it and any others who may have been involved.
Raipur police commissioner Sanjeev Shukla constituted a force of more than 100 personnel after a complaint was lodged at Telibandha police station. Crime and cyber teams examined screenshots, WhatsApp messages, social-media posts, mobile numbers, digital contacts and location data in an attempt to trace the first point of circulation.
The police said they identified the alleged source of the leak within 36 hours and arrested the six suspects. An FIR was registered under Chhattisgarh Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2008 and BNS sections, the sleuths said, adding they were now on the lookout for two more absconding suspects.
The probe teams spread out across Raipur, Durg, Kawardha, Rajnandgaon and Bilaspur, while mobile phones, WhatsApp chats and other digital trails were used to identify the suspects. More than 16 people have been questioned so far in connection with the leak, the police said.
Investigators said they were in the process of reconstructing the distributionchain — from where the sealed paper was accessed, who first scanned it, how it was transmitted and who ultimately received it.
The leak, meanwhile, has brought the university’s paper-handling system under scrutiny. If the police version is established, the leak would point to a security gap not just at the stage of physically opening the packet, but also in assuming that a sealed envelope itself was sufficient protection.
The police said they were also probing whether the six arrested accused were part of a wider network and whether the leaked paper was sold or circulated to more students beyond those already identified. Digital evidence was being examined to trace the full distribution chain.
The sleuths said they were also looking beyond the August 20 Entomology examination, probing claims that another BSc Agriculture paper — first-year Plant Pathology exam, scheduled earlier in August, may also have been compromised.

Prime suspect Yogesh Sonkesariya, a professor of a private college in Durg, allegedly used a needle to make incisions in the sealed envelope
He then slipped in the camera, which scanned the contents inside the sealed cover and took pictures
He then allegedly reconstructed the questions from the video and sold the paper

New York City Mayor administration opted not to attend Tuesday’s (August 25) City Council hearing on the rollout of the pied‑à‑terre tax, submitting a written memo instead, according to a report by Business Insider. Finance Commissioner Richard Lee said ongoing litigation prevented him from appearing in person, though he pledged to testify after the lawsuit is resolved. The levy, passed in May, imposes a progressive surcharge on non‑primary residences valued at least $5 million, and condos or co‑ops worth $1 million or more. In late July, the Department of Finance (DOF) sent letters to 17,000 addresses and published valuations for nearly 960,000 properties, sparking confusion and privacy concerns. Some residents reported receiving letters for their primary homes, while others criticized the release of property records.
Why Zohran Mamdani's Office stayed away
As reported by Business Insider, in the memo Department of Finance Commissioner Richard Lee detailed that the pending and active litigation prevented him from appearing at the hearing directly. He further added that he would have welcomed the chance to filed council members’ questions in person. 
Lee also noted that the Administration had asked the Council to postpone the hearing until the litigation was resolved, a request the Council declined. He said he would be prepared and willing to testify in person after August 31.
Council members demand answers
Council Member Gale Brewer said her office has been “bombarded” with constituent complaints and compiled “pages and pages” of questions for the Mayor’s Office. The Council had requested an in‑person briefing, but the administration declined, citing the pending lawsuit.
Defending the release of property data
A central point of contention has been the DOF's release of home values and addresses ahead of the levy. In his written testimony, Lee maintained that this practice is standard, stating that the City's assessment roll is "highly accessible to the public, and it has been for many years," and pushing back directly on any suggestion otherwise. He pointed out that this property data has long been available as a searchable database on both the DOF website and NYC Open Data, with online archives dating back to fiscal year 2009, and that assessment rolls have been required to be published annually in New York for well over a century.
How the controversy started
The uproar began in late July, after the NYC Department of Finance sent letters to roughly 17,000 addresses identified as potential pied-à-terre properties based on property values and internal records. The DOF also published a broader list of more than 900,000 properties and their valuations across the city. Lee clarified in his testimony that this supplemental roll does not itself determine which properties are actually subject to the surcharge; rather, it exists to identify relevant properties and give owners a basis to challenge their valuations. Homeowners have until September 18, an extended deadline, to demonstrate that their property doesn't qualify for the tax before it could begin appearing on bills starting in 2027.
Residents report confusion and privacy concerns
Some New York residents said on social media that they mistakenly received letters intended for non-primary residences despite the property in question being their primary home, while others said they felt their privacy had been compromised by the DOF's broader records release. Council Member Gail Brewer, who represents Manhattan's Upper West Side, told Business Insider that her office has been inundated with concerned constituents in recent weeks, and that she and fellow council members had compiled extensive lists of questions about the rollout that they hoped the Mayor's Office would address.
A pending lawsuit
Separately, a lawsuit filed by three residents based in Manhattan and Staten Island is pending, with a court date scheduled for August 31. According to court documents, the plaintiffs are seeking emergency relief, arguing that the DOF's records release caused widespread confusion and invited unwanted scrutiny of homeowners' personal information. Their attorney, Randy Mastro, said hundreds of thousands of New York City homeowners had been drawn into a process they should never have been part of in the first place.
The city's response and next steps
The city has hired two dozen staffers specifically to field resident questions about the tax and assist with appeals. The policy itself, passed in May, imposes a progressive levy on non-primary homes valued by the DOF at $5 million or more, and on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. Deputy Press Secretary Matt Rauschenbach previously told Business Insider that the Law Department is prepared to vigorously defend the city against the lawsuit, and said the roughly $500 million a year the levy is expected to raise would help fund cleaner parks, safer streets, and other public investments across the city.
In his written testimony, Lee also detailed the broader implementation process, noting that the surcharge was authorized under state legislation passed as part of New York's 2026/2027 budget on May 28, 2026, with rules formally adopted by DOF on July 14 following a public comment period that included a hearing held July 9. He emphasized that the initial determination letters sent to around 17,000 property owners represent only a small subset of the roughly 960,000 properties listed on the supplemental roll, and stressed that receiving a letter does not constitute a tax bill, only a preliminary determination that owners can challenge by submitting proof of primary residency or by contesting their property's valuation directly with the Tax Commission.
Lee said DOF plans to continue outreach through senior centers, community meetings, its dedicated website, 311, and direct coordination with co-op and condo boards, property managers, and elected officials, describing these efforts as part of a broader commitment to ensuring homeowners have clear information and a fair opportunity to challenge determinations they believe are incorrect.

LUCKNOW: A Rs 1.5 crore financial settlement sought by Divya Mishra in her divorce could have been a likely motive behind her murder by her banker husband, Manas Bajpayi, police said as the investigation into the double murder-suicide continued.
Police are also examining strained relations between the couple over Manas’s younger sister, Sheeba, 28, with whom Divya reportedly did not want to live.
Police have based their premise on the divorce case hearing in a family court on August 18, where the demand for Rs 1.5 crore in alimony came up.
According to the preliminary probe, Manas became distressed after the court hearing and subsequently began preparing for the attack.
Police, however, have not officially concluded that the Rs 1.5 crore demand alone was the motive. The financial dispute is being examined alongside the couple’s troubled relationship, allegations of domestic discord and the disagreement over Sheeba.
Couple had been living separately
Manas and Divya had a court marriage in 2017 but had been living separately since November last year after years of marital discord.
Divya had filed for divorce in January this year. 
The couple had no children.
According to relatives, their relationship was initially stable, but disputes gradually emerged over domestic and family matters and Divya left home.
When Manas’s mother was diagnosed with cancer in 2018, Divya again came back to live with him. Disagreements over Sheeba subsequently intensified.
After the death of Manas’s mother in 2019, Divya again moved away. The couple later reconciled, but their relationship deteriorated again over the following years.
Three shootings in one day
Manas, a bank clerk, shot dead Divya, a relationship manager with a private bank, outside her workplace in Gomti Nagar on Thursday afternoon.
He then went to his residence near Husadiya Crossing, where he shot dead Sheeba and turned the gun on himself.
After reaching home, Manas allegedly locked himself inside the room and switched on the TV at high volume. Police suspect the loud audio may have been intended to mask the sound of gunfire.
WhatsApp status under scrutiny
After killing Divya and before taking his own life, Manas posted a WhatsApp status claiming that he had killed his wife because she had betrayed him.
The message also reportedly stated that he intended to kill himself and his sister and named Divya’s sister, YouTuber Pragya Mishra, and her husband, Bharat.
Divya’s cousin Mayank Dixit has denied that Pragya and Bharat had any knowledge of the matters referred to in the message.
Police are examining the WhatsApp status, digital records and other electronic evidence to determine whether the allegations made by Manas had any factual basis.
Police examine planned attack
With the recovery of three firearms, CCTV footage showing the attack and the reported two-day surveillance of Divya, police are examining the case as a pre-planned sequence of killings.
Police are questioning family members, bank employees, security guards and neighbours and analysing CCTV and digital evidence to establish the precise chain of events and determine what ultimately triggered the killings.

A burial row over Zambia's late president has turned its election into a hot contest
- Published
A spectre is hanging over the Zambian election campaign in the shape of former President Edgar Lungu.
Despite having died more than a year ago in South Africa, his body remains unburied amid a bitter dispute between President Hakainde Hichilema and the Lungu family that has sharpened political divisions.
This has had a role in energising support for the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), particularly in the northern half of the country, traditional strongholds of Lungu's Patriotic Front (PF), as people see it as offering the best chance to unseat the incumbent.
Meanwhile, it has complicated the second-term bid of Hichilema and his United Party for National Development (UPND), which draws its core support from the south, west and north-west while seeking to expand its reach nationwide.
The political battle is playing out on the streets of the capital, Lusaka.
As the afternoon heat blazes across the city, the familiar hum of commerce hanging over the busy markets is overlayed with the sound of campaign songs and jingles.
Election posters are everywhere: from lamp posts and shop fronts to massive billboards, with faces of presidential and parliamentary candidates looming over passers-by.
All this as Zambia prepares for one of its most unpredictable elections in years.
On 13 August, more than eight million registered voters will get the chance to choose a president and a new parliament. Hichilema wants five more years after his 2021 landslide win over Lungu on a platform of change.
Yet what many expected to be a relatively straightforward contest this time has been reshaped by Lungu's death, the late surge of opposition challenger Brian Mundubile, persistent cost of living pressures and questions about electoral credibility.
This is all against the backdrop of recent constitutional reforms aimed at boosting the voice of youth and women.
The dominant conversation on street corners and in minibus taxis is the cost of living.
Zambia has not been spared from the worldwide pressures of high food and energy prices that followed the pandemic and subsequent geopolitical shocks.
Annual inflation has cooled to around 6.6%, its lowest in eight years, and the currency, the kwacha, has strengthened, but for many households the relief remains theoretical.
"The cost of living, I cannot say is okay," says Given Kangwa, a 27-year-old flour-mill worker standing in Lusaka City Market.
"Where I work, for example, the money we are getting paid is not enough and we cannot sustain our lives."
Kangwa explains that he was paid about 3,000 kwacha ($157; £117) a month, which is barely enough to cover food, rent and other expenses.
Theresa Zulu, a street-food seller, puts it more starkly. "Money has become so hard to come by. We are trying to stay strong to survive, but things have become really hard for us."
Voters, as ever, are unforgiving.
Macroeconomic gains matter less than the cost of cooking oil, for example, which has risen by more than 70% over the past five years. Zambians have also been battling with an unreliable power supply.
A severe drought in 2024-2025 slashed hydropower generation, creating power outages of up to 20 hours a day in parts of the country.
The government has since ramped up costly electricity imports and accelerated solar projects, easing the blackouts in recent months.
Yet the memory of darkened homes and food spoiling in fridges lingers.
We inherited a broken-down country… the economy was declining"
But Hichilema defends his record, saying that when he came to office things were a mess and he has laid the foundations for success.
"We inherited a broken-down country… the economy was declining," Hichilema told the BBC in Lusaka.
When he took office in 2021, Zambia was in debt distress and had been failing to make its payments.
The subsequent restructuring of more than $13bn (£9.7bn) in external debt has, according to the president, produced annual savings of roughly $1.9bn.
"That's the money we're putting in the economy… into investment expenditure such as free education."
The free education policy - covering primary and secondary levels - has brought millions of children back into classrooms.
Thousands of teachers and health workers have been hired. Constituency development funds have been sharply increased.
Copper production, the backbone of the economy, has recovered strongly, foreign reserves have climbed to record levels and investor confidence has returned.
Supporters point to tangible openings.
"I think opportunities have been increased, looking at the number of people who have been employed - it has increased amongst civil servants. And, opportunities have just increased," one young woman, who is hoping to become a teacher, said.
The unemployment rate as measured by the statistics agency has registered a slight fall from 13% to 11% over the last four years.
Critics counter that the benefits have yet to reach enough families.
There are also concerns from civil society groups that despite Hichilema's promises of running a more open democracy, some opposition figures have been silenced after being convicted of hate speech.
The political landscape shifted dramatically with Lungu's death on 5 June last year.
The courts had ruled that he could not run again, after having won two elections, but his passing removed the opposition's most recognisable figure and initially appeared to create a smoother path to victory for the incumbent.
Lungu's PF party fractured, with some politicians and supporters shifting to other opposition groups.
This accelerated the consolidation of a split opposition around Mundubile, a 55-year-old lawyer, accountant and former government chief whip under Lungu.
In a matter of weeks from filing his nomination papers in May, Mundubile's popularity grew as the presidential candidate of an opposition grouping, the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, running under the previously unknown NRPUP banner.
Makebi Zulu - a lawyer closely associated with the Lungu family - is his running mate.
The alliance has capitalised on lingering loyalty in former PF strongholds and on public frustration with the cost of living.
We believe the youths have solutions to most of their challenges. What they don't have is a big brother, what they don't have is a caring government"
Mundubile's central pitch is generational and inclusive.
"We are moving the women and the youth from the margins to the centre of policy and economic transformation," he told the BBC.
"We believe the youths have solutions to most of their challenges. What they don't have is a big brother, what they don't have is a caring government to be able to assist them achieve their objectives and goals. So I'm positioning myself as president as big brother to the youth."
The Lungu legacy still hangs over the race in unexpected ways.
The row over the former president's burial - still unresolved as the family do not want Hichilema to have anything to do with it - has become a potent political symbol.
Mundubile has publicly pledged that he and Zulu would ensure a dignified burial if they win the election.
Second-hand clothes seller Enock Mabenga said he was backing Mundubile "because we want to improve our lives".
I wouldn’t love to see them come back... because we gave them chance to rule the country and we saw what they did"
But not everyone is persuaded by the opposition's return.
"I wouldn't love to see them come back in the first place because we gave them a chance to rule the country and we saw what they did," Edith Muntanga, in her late 30s said, referring to the previous government's record on corruption and governance.
This election is the first under significant constitutional changes enacted in late 2025.
The amendments introduced a mixed-member system for the National Assembly with most seats given on a constituency basis but some reflecting the proportion of votes each party gets.
The number of constituency seats has expanded from 156 to 226, and 40 additional seats will be awarded through proportional representation: 20 for women, 15 for youth (counted as under 35) and five for persons with disabilities.
The reforms aim to boost representation in a parliament where women have long been under-represented. Whether they will translate into meaningful influence remains to be seen.
On the presidential ballot itself, gender representivity is limited: of the 14 candidates cleared by the electoral commission, only one is a woman - independent Given Katuta.
To win in the first round, a presidential candidate needs to have more than 50% of the votes cast. A second round is triggered within 37 days if no-one reaches this threshold, which could happen with such a fragmented field.
Civil society voices have raised concerns about the integrity of the process.
Linda Kasonde, human rights activist and former president of the Law Association of Zambia, has questioned the composition of the electoral commission.
"In terms of the constitution of the electoral commission itself, a number of the members of the commission are actually politically aligned to the incumbent ruling party and are not seen to be independent," she said.
"And so we're yet to see how they'll manage the actual election, but in the run-up to the election, there is some disquiet as to whether or not they're acting in the interest of all Zambians."
The commission has consistently rejected accusations of political bias saying it operates strictly "within a constitutional mandate [and] adheres to principles of transparency and independence".
Zambia has a proud record of peaceful elections and democratic transfers of power.
That history is frequently invoked by all sides. Yet trust in institutions, the cost of living and the unfinished story of a former president's final resting place have combined to make this contest harder to predict.
As campaign rallies fill football grounds, Zambians are weighing the tangible gains of the past five years against the daily struggles that still define their lives.
On 13 August, they will deliver their verdict.

Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity
- Published
Warning: This story contains details some may find distressing
A 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belies her age and the concerns she has for his future.
"This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC.
Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan.
She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023.
El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October.
For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare – with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food.
In the end Amira and her family decided to flee early in 2025, desperate to find a safer area.
But as they snuck out on a road south-west of the city, she says she was abducted by three armed men from the RSF and held captive.
"They blindfolded me and took me to the Tabit area south of el-Fasher. I was locked in a room for two months, and every day one of them raped me in turn," she recounts in a low voice
After weeks in captivity, she discovered she was pregnant and became very sick.
Amira says when the men wanted to get rid of her, they dropped her near the area she had been captured.
It was with the help of other people fleeing el-Fasher that she was taken to receive medical help.
Months later, at a humanitarian hub that was not under RSF control, she gave birth at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps.
There she received some support from a Sudanese aid organisation - the Nada Al-Azhar Foundation for Disaster Prevention and Sustainable Development (Nada).
The group was also able to find her family, who had made it to a camp where hundreds of thousands of people from el-Fasher have sought refuge.
It was a huge relief for them all to be reunited, but the family still face challenges - one being that eight months after giving birth, Amira has been unable to register her son's birth.
"Even getting a birth notification from the hospital requires information that doesn't exist," says Amira, explaining that she is unable to provide any details about the child's father.
Without this she cannot organise any official recognition of the baby's legal identity.
"I can't get him vaccinated, or enrol him in nursery or school," she says.
"I'm afraid for his future because he isn't registered at all. My economic situation is very difficult, and I can't afford his treatment or care. I can't even go to work for fear of being exposed to violence again."
According to Nada, Amira's story is not an isolated case, but part of a reality repeated in areas experiencing conflict across Sudan.
This is because many children are being born in complex circumstances, often without the knowledge of the father - meaning their births cannot be registered, explains Abu Bakr Yousif Yaqoub, Nada's director of protection programmes.
"Registering a child requires identity information, a national number and a birth certificate. But when the father is absent or unknown, it becomes extremely difficult," he tells the BBC from el-Fasher.
"The mother is often alone, and sometimes she herself is still a child who needs care, which limits her ability to care for her baby.
"There are also health challenges related to the lack of follow-up on essential vaccinations, which begin at birth and continue through the child's early years."
He warns that this situation does not just affect a child's early years but extends to their future education and as an adult being able to travel or obtain official documents.
It is not easy to obtain data about the number of children that have been born as a result of rape in Sudan.
According to Nada's director general, Shaza Ahmed, this comes down to social stigma as the true numbers are not recorded.
"Women who experience such assaults do not feel comfortable reporting them," she tells the BBC, speaking from Port Sudan, an army-held city in the east of Sudan.
"Unfortunately, most of the mothers of these children are themselves children - girls under the age of 18. Therefore, they cannot make the decision to go officially to court or the police, as they need a guardian to accompany them."
She notes that 90% of the cases recorded by her organisation involve families refusing to allow official reporting of the sexual assaults that led to pregnancy.
"As a Sudanese woman, my greatest fear and concern for children born as a result of rape is that we are facing a whole generation that will live under stigma, danger and fear," Ahmed says.
"These children will not receive respect from society, their well-being will not be truly protected, and above all, they will not have access to services or their rights."
For Ahmed they are not being treated as if they are "fully human", even though Sudanese law does grant all children the right to obtain an identity.
Sudanese lawyer Majida Idris explains that the Child Act of 2010 allows for the registration of children born outside marriage.
But it relies on the mother being willing to file a report that she has been assaulted - because this kick starts the registration process.
Once reported, the case is then referred to social services for documentation, before being sent to the civil registry, where the child is registered under the mother's name and given a full legal name according to procedures.
However, Idris says that the reality during war is completely different, especially in Darfur, where the ongoing conflict has led to the collapse of civil services and the shutdown of civil registry offices, leaving thousands of children unregistered.
"The absence of documents does not just mean the absence of a piece of paper - it means denying the child access to education, healthcare and legal recognition," she tells the BBC.
The lawyer says it is imperative to reactivate civil registry offices in accessible areas and intensify legal efforts to ensure children obtain their right to identity and legal recognition.
Amira and her child remain in Darfur - and therefore in administrative limbo.
Her mother admits that the lack of paperwork for her grandson is a worry.
Yet for the moment the family is overwhelmed with gratitude to have found one another again.
Amira has also been offered emotional and psychological support sessions and other advice by Nada - which is a comfort to the family.
"I was so extremely worried until I found her. I hadn't been eating or drinking," Amira's mother told the BBC.
"The reunion was like a miracle from God. To see our daughter back sitting among us is a gift and blessing that could not be thanked enough for."

More than 20 years after stealing the Declaration of Independence, National Treasure 3 is in the works.
On Friday, National Treasure (2004) director Jon Turteltaub revealed that a third installment in the Nicolas Cage adventure franchise is in the works with a script that Disney has approved.
“I was thinking about mentioning this tonight, I’ll say it tonight,” he teased during a live recording of the National Treasure Hunt podcast in Philadelphia. “It’s happening. You’re the first people I have said this out loud to.”
Turteltaub continued, “It’s finally real. Now, it’s ‘Hollywood real,’ meaning things can happen. Nic gets hit by a bus, there’s no National Treasure. If I get hit by a bus, there’s probably a National Treasure. Welcome to Hollywood, that’s Hollywood.”
Watch on Deadline
The director, who also helmed the 2007 sequel National Treasure: Book of Secrets, noted that they “finally have a script that I like,” which Disney has also said “sounds like a movie we can make.”
In National Treasure, Cage stars as historian Ben Gates, who has to steal the Declaration of Independence in order to get the map to an ancient rumored treasure, before his shady colleague Ian (Sean Bean) has the chance to steal it for himself. The movies surpassed $800M at the global box office.
Following the 2007 sequel, Disney+ released the spin-off series National Treasure: Edge of History in 2022, starring Catherine Zeta-Jones.
YES. A sequel we actually want!! Just hope it follows the OG team and doesn’t try to incorporate a younger team for the sake of seating up future installments following them that will never happen (see: pirates of the Caribbean, etc)

Normal deliveries are declining and C-section deliveries remain high at the Government Hospital for Women and Children at Kottaparamba in Kozhikode City, Keralam.
According to the Health department, there were a total of 5,201 deliveries (2,729 normal and 2,472 C-section) in 2020-21. This number came down to 2,238 (1,387 normal and 851 C-section) in 2025-26. A large number of people from the urban areas of Kozhikode are dependant on this hospital.
The data also reveal that between 2020-21 and 2022-23, a high number of deliveries were in the C-section category. In 2020-21, of the 5,201 deliveries, 2,472 were C-section; in 2021-22, of the 3,552 deliveries, 1,841 were C-section; and in 2022-23, of the 2,205 deliveries, 1,148 were C-section.
Though there were fewer C-section deliveries between 2023-24 and 2025-26, the percentage remained higher than the ideal population-level rate, between 10% and 15%, as suggested by the World Health Organisation. It is even higher than the national average of 21.5%, claims Satheesh Parannur, chairman of the Kozhikode-based rights organisation, Pouravakasha Samrakshana Samithi, who gathered the data through a Right to Information Act (RTI) query.
Mr. Parannur says that between 2020-21 and 2023-24, the number of total deliveries came down by 61% from 5,201 to 2,019. Though this number slightly went up to 2,238 in 2025-26, it was fewer than what was reported in 2020.
The RTI data show that in-patient admission dropped from 8,315 to 4,683 between 2020-21 and 2023-24. The next year, 5,089 people were admitted. The number again dropped to 4,838 in 2025-26. Meanwhile, a high number of people are seeking outpatient (OP) treatment. In 2020-21, a total of 81,329 people sought OP treatment and in 2024-25, this went up to 1,55,257 and slightly declined to 1,50,305 in 2025-26.
Inquiry sought
Mr. Parannur claims that though a large number of people could be approaching the hospital for medical check-up and medicines, at least some are not willing to get admitted there for deliveries.
He says the Health department should conduct a detailed inquiry into the decline in the number of deliveries and IP admission.

The Los Angeles Dodgers expected Kyle Tucker to be one of the biggest offensive additions in baseball this season. Instead, the 29-year-old outfielder has endured the most difficult season of his career despite being surrounded by star hitters and rising expectations.
Tucker entered last offseason as the consensus top free agent after turning down a qualifying offer from the Chicago Cubs. The Dodgers ultimately committed $240 million over four years to land him, making his struggles particularly significant for a team built to contend for another World Series.
“Tucker, who has endured the worst season of his career in the first year of his four-year, $240 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers, had been in the midst of the longest hitless stretch as a big leaguer,” Fabian Ardaya wrote for The Athletic. “He’d gone 26 at-bats without a hit by the time he came up in the fourth inning Tuesday against the Colorado Rockies.”
The slump has created an uncomfortable situation for the team. Tucker is being counted on as a middle-of-the-order presence, but the enormous contract has made every prolonged downturn more difficult to ignore.
Los Angeles Dodgers Superstar Mookie Betts Sends Kyle Tucker Message After $240 Million Contract
One person who understands the pressure better than most is Dodgers star Mookie Betts, who has experienced the expectations that accompany playing with a massive contract in Los Angeles.
Betts recently sent a message about how Tucker’s contract is making things particularly uncomfortable for his teammate.
“We know Tuck is kind of going through it,” Betts said during an episode of his “On Base” podcast. “He came into a tough situation, you know, you give somebody that type of contract, there’s going to be external pressure and really internal pressure for himself because he knows he needs to play well.”
Betts acknowledged that Tucker has failed to meet expectations, though he might not find many sympathetic listeners outside of the Dodgers fanbase when pointing to the pressure added by such a lucrative contract.
However, after committing so much to the new player, the Dodgers have little choice but to continue publicly supporting him throughout his slump. Manager Dave Roberts took a similar approach when deciding how to handle Tucker during his slump.
“I think the easy thing for me to do is to not play him,” Roberts said on Wednesday, according to Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times. “But for me, what I can do, a way of showing support, is by playing him. ... I think he gives us the best chance to win.”
Los Angeles Dodgers Need Kyle Tucker Turnaround
The stakes extend beyond Tucker's individual production. Los Angeles already surrendered significant draft capital and international bonus-pool money earlier this offseason as a penalty for signing closer Edwin Díaz, while the Tucker deal represented another enormous investment.
That makes the Dodgers' decision to continue giving Tucker opportunities understandable. His track record suggests the current production is not representative of the player they signed.
For now, Betts’ message reflects the Dodgers' position: Tucker may be struggling under immense pressure, but the organization believes the best path forward is to keep putting him in position to succeed.

In his prime as an opener, Gautam Gambhir loved the scent of a battle and drew inspiration from it. The same combative streak lingers in his second avatar as the coach.
Speaking to the media at the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground here on Saturday, there was a point in which he was asked about criticism. The former India star was quick with his riposte: “I am here to win trophies!” Later he added: “People in the press box and commentators know that we are going through transition.”
Looking ahead to the second Test commencing on Sunday, Gambhir said: “Even if you score 1000 runs, you still got to get 20 wickets, that’s how you win matches. So be it three left-arm spinners or an off-spinner or three seamers, we will take a call on what is the best team suited for this surface, it is about the team and the results.”
Praising Devdutt Padikkal and Manav Suthar for their success in the first Test, Gambhir said: “It is encouraging to see them step up and perform straight away but then again we should not judge on just one or two performances. There will be ups and downs and we all know cricket is tough.”
The coach did not reveal if there would be a swap between Kuldeep Yadav and Saransh Jain, but he did tell about his chats with the former: “I want Kuldeep to just try and bowl good spells rather than looking desperate to take a wicket.”

Refusing to be drawn into a discussion over India’s chances in the ICC World Test Championship, Gambhir said the immediate focus is on the second Test. And as for players breaking down with injuries, he said: “We had a discussion; we want our best players to play as much cricket as possible.”
Gambhir also backed the three-Test series format, terming it ideal. “A three-Test series gives a chance to a team that has lost the first Test to make a comeback and win the series,” he said.
“You cannot do that in a two-Test series, as the team that lost the first Test can, at best, only draw the series. Remember it happened with India once after losing the first Test against Australia, the team could still make a comeback.”

Within minutes of the BJP announcing its new social media team on Monday, August 17, a search on X revealed that the accounts of the four newly appointed social media co-convenors had either vanished or their posts had become inaccessible.
Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav were appointed as social media co-convenors by BJP national president Nitin Nabin. Gandhi’s profile initially remained accessible but her timeline showed no recent posts, suggesting that her tweets had been deleted. Soon after, her profile disappeared altogether, displaying X’s “account doesn’t exist” notice. The X profiles of the other three appointees are also currently inaccessible.
The X handles belonging to Shiwanand Dwivedi and Arun Yadav have been made private while Alok Bhatt’s X handle has been deactivated.
The appointments came as part of a rejig of the BJP’s national office bearers, with Amit Malviya, who had served as the party’s social media convenor since 2015, replaced by Deepak Mhaskey.
Deepak Mhaskey’s X account (@deepakmhaskey), which is not a verified handle as of August 18, offers a clear indication that posts were removed. At 5:19 pm on August 17, the account displayed 6,905 posts. The same account currently displays 5,563 posts — a reduction of 1,342 posts. (Screenshots below)
His timeline tells a more striking story: Only two original posts are currently visible, both posted on August 17, both concerning his appointment as the social media convenor of the party. The discrepancy is particularly noteworthy given Mhaskey’s new role.
At least three of the four newly appointed co-convenors have a documented history of amplifying communal rhetoric and spreading misinformation. Gandhi has been fact-checked by Alt News multiple times for disseminating communal misinformation. Her X activity shows repeated support for Nathuram Godse, including a tweet expressing her desire to have Godse as her last name instead of Gandhi.
In March 2014, Priti Gandhi was identified by WikiLeaks as the person responsible for amplifying a fabricated endorsement of Narendra Modi. Gandhi had promoted a fake quote falsely attributed to WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, claiming he said Modi was “incorruptible,” complete with Assange’s forged signature. Modi’s online supporters then seized upon the false endorsement as a high-profile international validation of the BJP Prime Ministerial candidate’s credentials.
Alok Bhatt, meanwhile, has a pattern of publicly posting sexist and anti-Muslim slurs. He has even targeted journalists like Barkha Dutt using vitriolic language.
Arun Yadav, who was the BJP Haryana IT cell in-charge, was removed by the party on July 7, 2022, amid calls for his arrest over his Islamophobic tweets, dating between May 2022 and 2017. #ArrestArunYadav was trending at the time with over 184,000 tweets. The state BJP president said Yadav was removed with immediate effect but gave no reason.
Malviya congratulated the new office-bearers in an X post and said they have been appointed at a “crucial juncture”. Speaking specifically about the social media co-convenors, he said he had the “privilege of working closely with each of them” and that he was confident that under their leadership, the party’s digital communication would “achieve newer milestones and continue to shape India’s public discourse with conviction, creativity and clarity.”
Just as this report was getting published, the X account of Shiwanand Dwidevi (@shiwadwivedi) became accessible again. Notably, the total post count came down from 10,800 (as shows in the screenshot used in this story) to 10,200. This indicates that roughly around 600 posts were removed.

Bangladesh’s ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence.
“They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government.
Hasina, 78, who has lived under tight security in India since fleeing Dhaka, said on Wednesday she would return in December – Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, marking the defeat of Pakistani forces in the 1971 war of independence.
“Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people,” the former Awami League leader told a news conference at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi, speaking via audio link.
Her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, told the news conference she was being treated well in exile.
“She is staying with the full services and security of a head of state,” he said. “Prime minister [Narendra] Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect, and for that I am eternally grateful.”
India officially distanced itself from the news conference, saying it had no role in organising it and did not endorse the political views expressed.
India has been walking a diplomatic tightrope over Hasina, who was one of its closest regional allies. Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since her downfall and India has been seeking to mend relations with Bangladesh while resisting demands for her extradition.
Hasina’s flight ended more than 15 years of increasingly authoritarian Awami League rule. The Bangladesh Nationalist party, led by Tarique Rahman, the son of the former prime minister Khaleda Zia, swept to power earlier this year in an election that barred the Awami League. The government has said Hasina would probably be arrested the moment she set foot in Bangladesh.
Last November, Bangladesh’s international crimes tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the violent suppression of the protests. The demonstrations began over government-job quotas and snowballed into a mass movement against Hasina’s government.
The UN estimates up to 1,400 people may have died. Hasina’s supporters say the death toll was about 800. She has rejected the court’s verdict as politically motivated and said the execution threat would not change her plans.
Hasina was imprisoned several times during her fierce rivalry with Zia, who died in 2025. The two women traded claims of using corruption cases and arrests against each other in a “Battle of the Begums”, an honorific title for a senior woman.
Bangladesh has prohibited domestic media from broadcasting or publishing Hasina’s statements. She has demanded that the ban on the Awami League be lifted, political prisoners be released and “false cases” against party activists be dropped.
Claiming Bangladesh is sinking into lawlessness and economic ruin, she accuses the new government of trying to erase the country’s secular character.
The government has been grappling with high inflation and sluggish economic growth while blaming many of the country’s problems on alleged corruption and mismanagement during Hasina’s years in power.

What Does a Trump Endorsement Actually Mean in 2026?
A few recent losses for Trump-endorsed politicians hardly mean a sea change in Trump’s power, but they do complicate his narrative.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Cory Mills’s reelection campaign was in trouble before it even began. Washington, D.C., police investigated the Florida representative early last year after a woman alleged that he’d assaulted her; later in 2025, a different woman was granted a restraining order against him. Neither woman was his wife. Mills, who has denied any wrongdoing, was never charged with anything, and the woman who alleged that he’d assaulted her walked back her claim after it became public. Still, questions lingered. Then, in February, Donald Trump endorsed him anyway, calling him an “America First Patriot and Tremendous Champion” of his district.
Not everyone in Florida’s Republican establishment felt the same. Governor Ron DeSantis declined to back him, and Representatives Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos threw their support behind his opponent. A House ethics probe is ongoing. On Tuesday, Mills lost his primary election—and despite never having rescinded his endorsement, Trump is now trying to back away from the congressman retroactively. “I told Congressman Cory Mills of Florida, a friend of mine, to get out of the Race, but he wouldn’t listen,” he posted on Truth Social yesterday morning. Mills’s opponent, Ryan Elijah—who already won the primary—now has Trump’s “Complete and Total Endorsement!”
What does a presidential endorsement mean for a Republican facing a primary election in 2026? If not enduring loyalty from the White House, then at least a reliable boost in the polls. The candidates that Trump supports still tend to win big; about 96 percent of the politicians he tapped this year (more than 300 of them) won their primary, according to Ballotpedia—an impressive ratio. Trump clearly enjoys the perception that his endorsement makes or breaks a candidate. “If they don’t get the endorsement, they don’t win,” he said in 2021.
For many voters, particularly in the MAGA camp, perceived loyalty to Trump remains a deciding factor. (Just ask Bill Cassidy.) But not every bet Trump makes pays off. An endorsement has never been an outright guarantee of victory, and the rare exceptions illuminate some truths about Trump and the GOP. Two of the president’s other picks lost their primary race on Tuesday: Megan Degenfelder, the head of Wyoming’s Department of Education, who was running for the state’s governorship, and the former Commerce Department adviser Catalina Lauf, who was up for an open House seat in southwest Florida. By CNN’s count, that makes 10 Trump-endorsed candidates who have so far lost their primary this year.
No single, unifying theory can explain these races. Sometimes, the timing makes a difference. When Trump endorsed Degenfelder as Wyoming’s best choice for the governorship, back in January, the state’s education chief hadn’t even entered the race. Once she did, the nod gave her campaign an early lead—an advantage she held on prediction markets for about seven months, despite being outraised and outspent by her main opponent in the GOP primary. In the end, she couldn’t sustain it. Lauf got her endorsement from Trump last week, almost a full year into her campaign, and well after mail-in voting had already begun. Her primary was always more of a toss-up than Degenfelder’s, but Trump’s endorsement may have arrived too late to make a difference.
 
 The president also cares more about some races than he does about others. In Indiana, he was able to use his endorsement power to punish those who had opposed his agenda. Trump vowed that Republican state senators who were up for reelection would lose their race if they rejected a gerrymandering plan he backed—and in May, after a concerted effort and successful fundraising from the MAGA base, most of those politicians did indeed lose their primary. Compare that with what he gave Lauf: not much more than a one-off Truth Social post.
Not every race is a blanket referendum on Trump’s endorsement power; the particulars always matter. The Republican strategist Doug Heye told me that “when the voters go in the voting booth, the word Trump doesn’t appear. It’s those candidates.” Mike Lindell, the Trump-endorsed MyPillow founder and MAGA stalwart, lost his bid for the Minnesota governorship earlier this month. He’d been leading in the polls, despite the fact that he was obviously unqualified—and that the state’s GOP leadership had declined to endorse him, suggesting that he’d be an “easy target” for Democrats. On Election Day, though, he lost to the experienced state House speaker Lisa Demuth. His adjacency to Trump couldn’t get him over the line.
As much as Trump likes the idea that he alone can propel a candidate to victory, he also seems to try to skew the odds in his favor. As NPR points out, the president has lately been backing more incumbents than he did during the 2018 midterms (75 percent of his choices this year have been sitting politicians), which suggests a greater aversion to risk. He also tends to make endorsements much earlier than he used to, getting involved from the outset and attempting to deter competition. Recent history is full of examples of races where Trump’s endorsement did make a big difference: The Ohio Senate seat that ultimately went to J. D. Vance in 2022 was fiercely contested until the president made his pick. Often, though, the president is simply playing the odds, betting on the candidate he thinks has the best chance.
That’s exactly what happened in Texas earlier this year. Ahead of the GOP primary for John Cornyn’s Senate seat, Trump was widely expected to endorse the incumbent. As my colleague Elaine Godfrey noted at the time, the senator tried to rename a highway after Trump in an effort to secure his support. But the president went with a competitor, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who’d been ahead in the polls despite being impeached a few years prior. Back in 2022, in the lead-up to Missouri’s Senate primary, Trump went with a more unusual strategy. He wrote on social media that he’d decided to endorse “ERIC”—but didn’t specify which of the three candidates named Eric he actually supported. Was it a gaffe, or a sly acknowledgment that he didn’t want to pick among them?
Trump has been more involved in primaries than his predecessors were, setting a new expectation for how active presidents should be in those races. Many of his endorsements have been a boon for his favored candidates. But not every election is about Donald Trump.
