Despite making changes last fall to help block adults from messaging unknown children, Roblox is still failing to stop adults from creeping on kids in other ways, Australia’s eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, said on Thursday.
Suspecting that Roblox may not be doing enough to stop child exploitation, eSafety conducted testing earlier this year that flagged alarming gaps in Roblox safeguards. The agency found that adult strangers could still send connection requests to kids, whose “profiles and biographies, including account names, number and names of connections, avatar images, and non-sensitive biographical information such as their interests were visible to anyone on the Roblox platform, with no option to restrict the visibility of this information.”
Such requests did not trigger parental alerts, eSafety found, and bad actors could also search kids’ visible-to-anyone contact lists for more targets.
Perhaps even more concerning, adults could also search for kids and comment on their posts “without parental or carer consent” in “forums outside game environments,” eSafety said.
Australia’s Online Safety Act requires that platforms prevent unwanted contact between adults and minors. It also mandates setting children’s accounts to private by default. Although Roblox “believes it is meeting its obligations,” the online gaming platform—which 1.7 million Australian kids use—has entered a court-enforceable agreement to make changes in the next three months.
Upcoming measures will prevent adults from contacting kids without parental consent across the platform, Roblox has promised. Providing better protections for kids starts with “strengthening the account settings of children’s accounts so they are private by default,” eSafety said, and ends with Roblox making it easy to report unwanted contact and notifying users of outcomes after reports are made. Those are critical protections for Australia’s second most popular online game for kids, Inman Grant said.

- Fortnite players can get the Crown Sprite by finding and using Cheat Codes, defeating opponents who have it, or trading it with friends.
- The Crown Sprite in Fortnite grants extra Crown Wins after getting a Victory Royale.
- Unlike other Fortnite Sprites, the Crown Sprite has to be leveled up by securing Victory Royales.
A king has arrived on the Fortnite island with the release of Chapter 7 Season 4 in the form of an adorable creature called the Crown Sprite. Unlike other Sprites that grant in-game buffs, this one only grants a very specific bonus at the end of each match. If you’re thinking about an XP boost, that’s not it. Nevertheless, if you’re wondering, here’s how to get the Crown Sprite in Fortnite.
Where to Find Crown Sprite in Fortnite: All Locations and Methods
To find the Crown Sprite in Fortnite, you’ll need to be familiar with all the new locations added to the Battle Royale island. The current Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 map is full of wonderful secrets and gaming-themed features that can lead you to a Victory Royale. That said, here are some methods you can use to find the Crown Sprite in Fortnite:
Using Cheat Codes
You can get the Crown Sprite in Fortnite by making use of the newly added Cheat Code mechanic. Do not confuse these with Fortnite Lobby Hack (Admin Panel) Codes, which are limited to the main Battle Royale lobby menu. Cheat Codes can be found all over the island; in fact, you could find multiple within a single POI. If you’re lucky, the Crown Sprite could be obtained from the very first attempt.
Just be careful while entering Cheat Codes, as you’ll not be able to see much around you. With limited vision, enemies may just get the upper hand in a Fortnite match. We recommend exploring the POI you land at the start of the match using the Sonic Power Sneakers in Fortnite to save some time.
Eliminating opponents
If you are good at combat and able to secure Victory Royales easily, this method is better suited to your needs. Instead of searching for the Crown Sprite in Fortnite, you can simply eliminate an opponent and claim it as yours.
Use the newly added 8-Bit Shotgun from the Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 loot pool to deliver devastating close-range blows. If you prefer fighting from afar, the Fortnite Mega Buster is a great tool for the job.
Trading with friends
Trading Sprites in Fortnite is your last option. If you have a friend who has a Crown Sprite, you can ask them to trade it with you. They’ll need to spend some Sprite Dust to summon it back, but it’s by far the easiest method.
If they are reluctant, try offering them a Klombo Sprite in Fortnite to add value to the trade. Given how rare it is, someone must surely need or want it. Once the Crown Sprite is added to your collection, you can share or exchange it with other players.
Furthermore, the Crown Sprite can be found in high-altitude areas on the Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 map. This means you will have to search for Cheat Codes in and around locations such as Lifty Lodge, Green Hill Zone, Golden Grove, and Stone Sanctum. We’ve added a Fortnite map below to help give you a better idea of where to begin your search for Crown Sprite:
That said, the Crown Sprite is one of the many new Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 Sprites that you will come across. If you’re looking for something stylish to pair it with, you could perhaps try donning the Mali skin from the Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 Battle Pass. Her attire is red and will match the Crown Sprite’s color scheme.
Fortnite Crown Sprite Powers Explained
The Crown Sprite in Fortnite grants you extra Crown Wins after getting a Victory Royale. If you want to show off your Victory Crown count, this Sprite will help you immensely, granted you win matches, that is.
However, you will not be able to level up the Crown Sprite that easily in Fortnite. Akin to the Klombo Sprite, it has its own leveling mechanics. Using Campfires in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 or opening chests and ammo boxes does nothing.
Here is how the Crown Sprite works as it levels up in Fortnite:
| Crown Sprite Level | Power Increase Per Level | 
|---|---|
| Level 1 | TBA | 
| Level 2 | TBA | 
| Level 3 | TBA | 
| Level 4 | TBA | 
| Level 5 | TBA | 
Based on its functionality, we’re going to say that the Crown Sprite doesn’t offer much in terms of buffs during the match. Unless you secure a Victory Royale, it’s not of much use. Consider using other Fortnite Sprites for a better competitive advantage.
How to Master Crown Sprite in Fortnite
To master the Crown Sprite in Fortnite, you will need to secure Victory Royales. As mentioned, it won’t level up like other Sprites. Unless you’re capable of winning every match, it’s going to be an uphill battle trying to upgrade the Sprite. Thankfully, there is a little ‘hack’ you can use to master the Crown Sprite in Fortnite without having to win matches.
You’ll need to own the Adventure Sprite and have it equipped, while keeping the Crown Sprite as the only item in your inventory. Next, you’ll need to search chests, open ammo and produce boxes, and light campfires; do just about anything that will level up your Adventure Sprite. You can also try your luck catching fish at Golden Fishing Spots in Fortnite to earn XP.
When your Adventure Sprite gains a level, one item in your inventory – in this case, your Crown Sprite will level up. This will allow you to bypass its upgrade level requirements. Once you master it, extract it, and give it a forever home in your Fortnite Sprite Garden.
Lastly, if you’re really great at Fortnite and manage to find a Victory Crown and secure a Victory Royale, you’ll be able to master your Crown Sprite immediately. You will also unlock the Cheat Master variant of the Crown Sprite once you get a dub in a Fortnite match.
All Crown Sprite Variants in Fortnite
As of the update v42.00, there are a total of three Crown Sprite variants that you can find in Fortnite. This includes the base variant in Chapter 7 Season 4. More could be added in future updates, but for the time being, here’s the list of all Crown Sprites in Fortnite and their variants:

That’s about everything we can tell you about the Crown Sprite. If you’re new to the season or just getting started, you can read our Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 patch notes to get a better understanding of things.

Student wellbeing in India declines sharply through the senior school years, the Student Well-Being Pulse Report by IC3 Institute has found. The report is a part of a wider study on student suicide aversion, which focuses on mental health and well-being. The proportion of students reporting high overall wellbeing fell from 62% in Grade 8 to 43% in Grade 12, the report has stated. The findings are based on the responses from 8,515 students across India, showing a consistent decline across wellbeing, happiness, confidence and motivation as students progress through school. The report was launched at the 10th Annual IC3 Conference and Expo in Mumbai on Thursday (August 20, 2026).
“The findings point to a widening gap between the pressures students experience and the support they seek. Happiness falls from 65% in Grade 8 to 48% in Grade 12, confidence from 64% to 47% and motivation from 64% to 49%. Negative emotions also intensify with age, with anxiety, low energy, frustration, loneliness and sadness all peaking among students in Grades 11 and 12. When students do seek help, they most commonly turn to friends and family, with 49% and 44% respectively. A smaller proportion also reach out to teachers (13%) and school counsellors (6%), while 2% report seeking support from therapists. Notably, 52% of students believe that therapy or counselling would be helpful, indicating openness to structured support when accessible,” a statement issued by IC3 stated.
Gender gap
As per the report, girls experience significantly higher levels of negative emotions than boys across every category. Across all five negative emotional states (anxiety, low energy, loneliness, frustration, and sadness), female students consistently report higher “Often/Always” levels than males. 33% girls experienced anxiety, while 23% boys reported experiencing it.
Also, negative emotions intensified steadily as students moved into higher grades. “Almost every emotion shows a clear upward trend from Grade 8 to Grade 12 in the “Often/Always” category. Seniors (Grade 11 and 12) show the worst overall emotional wellbeing profile. In every negative emotion category, Grades 11 and 12 have the highest, or among the highest, “Often/Always” responses. This reflects academic pressure, board exams, college planning, and burnout,” the report said.
High level of flourishing
Students generally reported high levels of flourishing, especially in social belonging and emotional connection. Across nearly all indicators, the majority of students fell in the ‘Strongly Agree/Agree’ category, often above 60–80%. Overall, 62% students felt happy at school while 78% have a close friend at school and 74% felt safe and included in school. Additionally, 64% said they took care of their physical and mental health, 78% said their friends and family support them and 70% said they feel hopeful of their future. Girls tend to flourish more socially and emotionally, while boys rate themselves higher on personal resilience measures.
Well-being declined steadily as students progressed to higher grades, with Grade 12 showing sharp drops. Across every indicator, Grade 8 students report the highest flourishing, and Grade 12 the lowest.
Sleep concern
According to the findings of the study, sleep declined steadily and sharply as students moved into higher grades. The grade-level trend showed a deterioration in sleep (recommended: 7-8 hours) as academic pressure increased.
“The senior grades (11 & 12) show the most worrying sleep patterns. Students in Grades 11 and 12 report that 19% slept for less than five hours, nearly half slept only 5–6 hours, while 22–23% got the recommended 7–8 hours of sleep. “These are the years where cognitive performance and emotional resilience are most needed and yet students appear to be the most sleep-deprived,” the report said.
The 2025 Student Well-being Pulse Report was conducted by the IC3 Institute in collaboration with the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations (CISCE). 8,515 students across India participated in the survey, with the majority of them being from Grades 8 through 12. The survey was developed using Google Forms and disseminated through email and WhatsApp.

Jaishankar said India’s ties with Bangladesh must be based on mutual interest, while stressing that stability with China and the fight against terrorism remain key to New Delhi’s foreign policy
NEW DELHI: For any relationship to work, it has to meet the test of mutual interest, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said Saturday on the current state of ties between India and Bangladesh, particularly in the context of uncertainty over PM Tarique Rahman's visit. "It has to work for them, it has to work for us. I'm not expecting neighbours to only do what is in my interest...when you get that common landing ground, relationships work smoothly," Jaishankar said.The external affairs ministry had earlier announced that India has invited Rahman for a bilateral visit.At ET World Leaders Forum, Jaishankar reaffirmed India's position on Pakistan that dialogue and terrorism cannot coexist, and said the govt cannot be impervious to public opinion in the country.Ahead of Modi’s meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the margins of SCO and Brics summits next month, Jaishankar said both Delhi and Beijing have an interest in maintaining stability in the relationship and India needs to do business with the entire world, including China. While an official announcement is awaited, Xi will be travelling to India for Brics summit on Sept 12-13 for his first visit to the country since 2019.
“But for us, the interaction... the purpose of it is finally to modernise our economy and to develop our capabilities, but even as we do so, obviously there will be trade, there will be other economic interactions with them,” said Jaishankar. He also said India remains in touch with China about business visa delays faced by Indian nationals.Recalling the 2020-24 difficult phase in the relationship, he iterated India’s position that the state of the border will determine the relationship. “Having said that, I think naturally, if assuming things are stable and the needle is more cooperative, obviously, I mean we are both very big economies in many ways, we are markets to each other.”

Toronto, Aug 22: Two men, including a priest, were injured after a 27-year-old man stabbed them with a screwdriver inside a gurdwara in Canada’s Edmonton, with police investigating whether the attack was hate-motivated, authorities said.
The incident took place at Nanaksar Sikh Gurdwara in northeast Edmonton around 5 am (local time) on Friday, police said, adding the suspect entered the gurdwara and attempted to access the prayer area before he was confronted by the staff.
The confrontation escalated and two men, aged 75 and 51, were stabbed, Edmonton Police Service (EPS) said in a statement on Friday.
Witnesses intervened and detained the suspect until police arrived and arrested him, it said.
The two injured men were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, while the suspect was also injured and taken to the hospital, CBC News reported.
Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with the Sikh community.
"The attack at the Nanaksar Gurdwara in Edmonton this morning is appalling. My thoughts are with the two people who were injured and the wider community that is shaken by this terrible event," Carney said in a post on X.
“No one should ever feel unsafe in their place of worship. I want to thank the Edmonton Police Service for their swift response,” he said.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith condemned Friday's act of violence against the Sikh community and called for reforms to federal bail and parole laws, CBC News reported.
“Everyone deserves to feel safe in their communities and places of worship, and we will continue to defend that right,” Smith said, adding that the attack underscored the need for the federal government to take bail and parole reform seriously.
Naheed Nenshi, leader of Alberta's official opposition, described the violence at the Edmonton temple as shocking and said crimes in places of worship were particularly disturbing and had left members of the community shaken, the report said.
Police said the suspect had been seen walking in traffic on Highway 15 shortly before the stabbing, Global News reported.
The suspect, who was known to police, has an extensive history of violent attacks dating back to 2015, police said. He had been released from a federal prison in Alberta the day before the attack, and failed to report to his designated halfway house in Edmonton, officials said.
A designated halfway house is a transitional residential facility designed to help individuals safely reintegrate into society.
The EPS Investigative Response Team has taken over the case and is working with the Hate Crimes Unit to determine whether the attack was motivated by hate. Police said charges are pending against the suspect.
Nanaksar Gurdwara Gursikh Temple vice-president Zora Grewal identified the injured men as a temple priest and a longtime volunteer, CBC News reported.
Grewal said the suspect allegedly used a screwdriver and stabbed the priest repeatedly before attacking the elderly volunteer. He said no Sikh scripture was damaged in the incident, the report added.
EPS Chief Warren Driechel said the incident had not resulted in more serious injuries or deaths but acknowledged the trauma caused to the victims and the Sikh community.
“This level of violence has no place in our city,” he said, adding that police were taking the incident and the safety of Edmonton's Sikh community seriously.
World Sikh Organisation of Canada president Danish Singh said, "We are asking gurdwaras across Canada to review and strengthen their security procedures and to remain vigilant," CBC News reported.
Friday’s stabbing comes days after two Sikh temples in Alberta received threatening phone calls. Calgary police said the two temples, both located in the city's northeast, received threatening calls from the same number on August 15, the report added.
Police said they were working closely with the temples as the investigation continued, but there was no indication of an active threat to the wider community.

For some prisoners with problematic sexual arousal (PSA), “images of sex flood their minds” all of their waking hours, according to Prof Belinda Winder, a leading forensic psychologist who has evaluated the use of drugs to control libidos.
“I remember talking to one guy a few weeks after he started taking the medication. He said: ‘It’s amazing. I followed a film plot. I wasn’t just looking for when I could see bra straps, when I could see nipples, when someone’s going to bend over so I could see their bum.”
“Without the drugs, these images were going around his head all the time. He did not want them any more,” she said.
Drugs used in the UK to treat PSA include antidepressants, which help control obsessive urges, and anti-androgens, which lower testosterone levels.
The treatments, typically taken as pills, are not suitable for some offenders such as those who are primarily motivated by anger, or who struggle to moderate their behaviour while using alcohol or drugs.
A similar approach has been used in some European countries. In Denmark and France, the use of chemical suppression has only been administered on a voluntary basis.
In Germany, the Dunkelfeld project provides free and confidential therapies including medical interventions to men with paedophilic or hebephilic obsessions.
An advert on YouTube urging men to contact the project shows unidentified men saying: “In therapy, I learned that no one is to blame for their sexual preference. But everyone is to blame for their behaviour. I don’t want to be an offender.”
But many other countries have taken a harder line. Poland introduced mandatory chemical suppression for some sex offenders.
South Korea became the first country in Asia to legalise chemical castration, passing a law in 2010. The law grants courts and a Ministry of Justice committee the authority to order involuntary hormone treatment for convicted sex offenders to suppress their testosterone.
In Australia, several states grant courts and parole boards the power to order anti-libidinal treatment for high-risk sex offenders which can then become a condition of release. Kazakhstan and a number of US states including California and Florida already have mandatory prescribing of anti-libidinal drugs to some sex offenders.
Officials in the UK have explored whether taking part in programmes such as these could be made a condition of a parole licence, similar to a scheme in California. However, ethical dilemmas remain over whether it would be right to give someone parole based on whether they take a drug that can be life-changing.
In the 50s, hormone treatments were given to men convicted of crimes related to their homosexuality with the promise that they could avoid jail. Alan Turing, the computer scientist and codebreaker, who was convicted of “gross indecency” in 1952, accepted chemical castration as a way of avoiding imprisonment. He took his own life two years later and received a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.
The side effects of anti-androgens in particular can be severe. Some men experience fatigue, hot flushes, muscle loss, mood changes, weight gain and a loss of bone density.
Experts acknowledge that problems remain. The medication is not a cure and does not change underlying behaviours. Some programmes have high drop-out rates.
Each offender would have to be assessed by the Parole Board on their merits, according to Winder. “It is never going to be so simple that a decision will be taken on whether to give someone parole based on whether they are taking their meds,” she said.
Winder added: “Parole Boards take such decisions by assessing many factors, including how receptive they are to staff and how they interact with their peers. It is really important that people are trained in understanding what it means if someone is taking this medication and how that might affect a person’s behaviour.”

The 4 Best Monitor Arms
Featured in this article
A monitor arm should be one of those simple products you buy once and never think about again. A good one lets you adjust your screen for more comfortable viewing and improved ergonomics while helping you save valuable space on your desk. But I've seen horror stories of cheap, knock-off models that collapse, damaging both the desk and the monitor. Anything that mounts a very heavy piece of expensive tech like a high-end monitor should be high-quality, which is true of all the options below.
We've personally tested each of the monitor arms on this list. In fact, most are currently clamped down to the desks of our product reviewers. For more home office gear recommendations, check out our Best Laptop Stands, Best Monitors, Best Laptop Docking Stations, Best Office Chairs, and our comprehensive Home Office Setup guide.
Updated August 2026: I've added the Flo and Jarvis monitor arms from Herman Miller. I've also included additional information on warranty lengths and how I test monitor arms.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Other Monitor Arms We’ve Tested
Wali Heavy-Duty Monitor Arm for $75: I made the brilliant decision to buy a 42-inch monitor without thinking about actually using a 42-inch monitor. Most monitor stands can’t support that kind of size, regardless of whether you’re using something like a 42-inch LG C4 or Samsung’s massive Odyssey OLED G9. This arm from Wali looks inconspicuous, but it’s kept my monitor—the KTC G42P5—stable for over a year without even a hint of droop. —Jacob Roach
Branch Monitor Arm for $129: As I've discovered while testing monitor arms, many of them use the same exact parts with only minor differences in branding. You likely wouldn't know that just by looking at the Amazon listing or even the company's photos. I tested the Branch Monitor Arm, for example, and discovered that it's nearly identical to the BenQ Ergo Arm. It's a solid option and slightly cheaper, but it doesn't come with the reinforcement plate to protect your desk, and the dual-arm version isn't as versatile.
Monoprice Workstream Single Monitor Arm for $83: I'm using this dual version of this monitor arm to hold a 32-inch ultrawide monitor and a wide vertical monitor, and it's been treating me wonderfully for several months. The arms move smoothly and don't sink under the weight of the screens. It's also one of the few monitor arms that has a clamp large enough for my thick 5-inch desktop. —Julian Chokkattu
Pout Eyes 12 Monitor Arm for $55: This was previously my pick as a solid budget monitor arm option. You have to be very careful with super cheap monitor arms on Amazon, but that's not to say there's nothing good out there. I tested this one out based on the clean look and cheap price, and although it's far from perfect, I found a lot to like about it. First, there's the design. It's a simple touch, but the dual-tone, gray-and-black aesthetic has a bit more flavor than your average all-black monitor arm. The mechanism in the arm is mechanical, or “spring-assisted,” as the company says, meaning the motion isn't as fluid as a gas spring. Unfortunately, it appears it's no longer being sold directly to consumers, and is primarily a business-only product
AmazonBasics Adjustable Desk Mount Arm for $29: I'll set aside the fact that the first version of this I received was beat up and busted, like it had been used (and even the replacement box had a big hole in it). But really, when it comes down to it, your monitor (and your neck) deserves something better than this. It might function better than some of the plastic, bottom-of-the-barrel stuff you'll find on Amazon, but this old-school pole design means adjustments are inconvenient to make. It's also pretty shaky, and I couldn't get it to be as stable as other monitor arms I tested.
Mount-It! Heavy Duty Dual Monitor Arm for $322: I used this mount to hold up my 34-inch ultrawide monitor for years, and it worked like a charm. It can hold screens between 15 and 34 inches (up to 20 pounds). It's adjustable, has built-in cable management, and doesn't look hideous. It uses the VESA mounting standard, so make sure the monitor you have supports that. —Julian Chokkattu
Why Buy a Monitor Arm?
Removing your monitor from its stand, buying a separate monitor arm, and clamping it down to your desk can be a frustrating experience. There are two main reasons why it's worth the trouble.
First, it's the ergonomic flexibility. Many monitors come with built-in stands, but they're limited in terms of height adjustment. Ideally, you want your monitor to be at eye level to avoid being hunched over. A good monitor arm gives you a dramatically wider range of motion, even allowing you to pull it forward when you want to lean in. This is all done with a level of ease that a built-in or external monitor stand cannot match.
The second reason to buy a monitor stand is the space savings. Ridding your desk of an unwieldy monitor base gives you a cleaner workspace and opens up more room for storage. This is particularly important with larger monitors, such as ones that use an ultrawide aspect ratio, which need infamously huge bases to hold up the extra weight.
What to Look For in a Monitor Arm
Once you’ve decided it's time to buy a monitor arm, there are still hundreds of options out there, especially if you're shopping on Amazon. Here are some of the most important factors to consider.
Type of Arm: These days, the most common kind of monitor arm is fully articulated. This is most likely what most people imagine when you say “monitor arm.” It resembles a robotic arm. However, there are some simpler pole designs that only let you adjust the height of the monitor. I don't usually recommend those, as the adjustments are very limited. The in-between option is a pole design with an articulated arm, which is how some multi-arm designs function.
Brand: Sticking with a well-known brand is a safe way to go, although Amazon also has some best-selling options from less-known names like Huanuo or Ergotron that offer great value. Monitor manufacturers also often make monitor arms and are a good place to look, whether that's Asus, MSI, BenQ, or Acer. Lastly, more high-end names in the home office game, like Herman Miller, also make arms with more panache.
Materials and Design: Monitor arms tend to be ugly contraptions, especially when they're overly chunky and made of cheap plastic. Look for aluminum or steel options for more robust, elegant arms.
Weight Limit: A monitor arm’s job is to keep your monitor in position without constantly sinking or damaging your desk. Make sure to look up the weight of your monitor and pay careful attention to the stated weight limit of the monitor arm you're considering. If your display is curved, give yourself a buffer of around 5 pounds, as the curve adds extra forward weight that puts more tension on the monitor arm. It's also not recommended to use a lightweight monitor on a heavy-duty monitor arm, as it can cause it to float up because the tension in the arm is too loose.
Clamps, Grommets, and Stands: When we say “monitor arms,” we usually mean ones that clamp to a desk. Some monitor arms take things a step further and come with an option for permanently installing the arm to your desk by drilling a hole and attaching it through a metal plate or grommet. Personally, I don't love the idea of drilling holes into my desk, but it's certainly the most stable method of securing the arm. Some are also designed for wall mounting if that's your only option.
What Is a Gas-Spring Monitor Arm?
If you start perusing the digital aisles of Amazon for monitor arms, you'll likely come across the term “gas spring.” This means that instead of using traditional springs, the internal cylinder in the arm is filled with nitrogen gas, which creates a more powerful counterbalance when making adjustments. Monitor arms using gas springs often cost more but feel smoother and less rigid when moving around. Mechanical springs, on the other hand, are much cheaper and feel more stiff. But they can be a decent option if you don't intend on making frequent adjustments.
Should I Buy a Dual-Monitor Arm or Two Single Monitor Arms?
If you're working with two monitors, I recommend a dual-monitor arm, which includes both arms in a single clamp. Not only is this a simpler setup with less mess, it's also easier to position them side-by-side without a gap.
However, if you're creating a PC gaming setup, you may prefer using two single monitor arms next to each other. This way, you have a primary display that can be centered more easily. Dual-monitor arms can be awkward if you're using one screen as your dominant source and want it to be centered in your view. This is also true if you plan to use a secondary monitor vertically.
Can Your Monitor and Desk Support a Monitor Arm?
Not all monitors and desks can safely use a monitor arm. For example, if your desk is overly thin or has rounded edges, it'll be difficult to install the clamp securely. Also, if you're using a glass table or a lightweight table with a hollow core, you're out of luck.
You'll also need to check that your monitor is VESA-compatible, meaning it has four screw holes on the back in a square. This is what allows you to attach the back of the screen to the monitor arm. The most common size is 100 mm by 100 mm, though some smaller or older monitors use the 75 mm by 75 mm size.
These days, the only monitors that lack VESA support are cheap monitors under $200, so it's something to keep in mind if you're shopping in that price range.
How I Test Monitor Arms
As the WIRED monitor reviewer, I've got plenty of external screens lying around to attach to monitor arms. To test an arm, I assemble it, mount it to a monitor, and clamp it down to my desk. For heavy-duty monitor arms, I test them with larger-format or ultrawide displays to make sure they can handle the weight they claim to. In terms of how I choose which monitor arms to review, my goal is to test ones from both established brands and smaller companies you find on Amazon.
Either way, because so many of these monitor arms are built using many of the same parts, I've been on the hunt for ones that really stand out from a design and functionality perspective.
Next, I'll be looking at the higher-end market, with monitor arms by boutique furniture office companies Humanscale and Herman Miller. On the opposite side of the spectrum, I'll also be diving more into the murky waters of Amazon to hopefully surface with some gems from the depths that balance quality with affordability.

The ‘Resistance’ Won
The much-derided movement was right about Trump’s nature, and how to defeat him.
Donald Trump celebrated the defeat of one of his first impeachment nemeses—retired Army Lieutenant Colonel Alex Vindman, who lost the Democratic Senate primary in Florida on Tuesday—in typical form. “SleazeBag Vindman loses tonight to a Radical Left Lunatic. How cool is that???” Trump exulted on Truth Social.
Vindman served as a witness in Trump’s first impeachment. Whatever currency this once gave him with Democratic voters has long since expired. In this, he is not unique. Democrats such as Dan Goldman, George Conway, and Tom Steyer, all of whom pushed for or played prominent roles in Trump’s first impeachment, have discovered in primaries this year that this credential means little to their party’s voters. Diana DeGette, a House manager during Trump’s second impeachment trial, and Harry Dunn, a Capitol Police officer who battled insurrectionists, have also lost primaries.
The rout of the Democratic Party’s impeachment stars has been interpreted, generally, as a sign of the end of resistance politics. “The string of losses for resistance candidates from the first Trump term illustrates a new era for the restive Democratic base, where vocal opposition to the president through official channels and public remonstrations no longer guarantees success,” Politico reports.
The “resistance,” once a dominant mode of Democratic politics during the first Trump administration, was never cool. But in the second term, the “resistance liberal” has fallen out of favor so completely that the phrase has become a derisive punch line across the political spectrum. Which is a shame, because the resistance was, broadly speaking, correct. It was right about Trump’s nature, and also right about how to defeat him.
Resistance politics depicted Trump as a crook and an aspiring authoritarian with a troubling fondness for dictators, especially Vladimir Putin. He was a con man, unfit for office, and had broken faith with the best traditions of American politics. The Robert Mueller investigation found, among other things, that Putin had dangled a lucrative no-risk deal to Trump during the 2016 campaign. The Senate Intelligence Committee, found, in a bipartisan report, that the campaign’s links to Russia posed a “grave counterintelligence threat.” The first impeachment charged Trump with having “placed his own personal and political interests above the national interests of the United States, sought to undermine the integrity of the U.S. presidential election process, and endangered U.S. national security.”
These much-derided processes turned out to supply an accurate, almost banal, description of how Trump has operated during his second term. His corruption and abuses of power have been let loose at a scale that was previously only imagined. Trump has all but severed America’s system of alliances, mocked and bullied Ukraine’s president, and showered praise upon Kim Jong Un.
What discredited resistance politics in liberal eyes is that it was closely associated with institutional procedures that were deemed to have ultimately failed to restrain Trump. Mueller’s investigation ended anticlimactically. Neither impeachment drew enough Republican support to remove Trump from office. Somewhat similarly, conservatives have sometimes claimed that the Russia investigation and first impeachment helped Trump politically by drawing to his side Republicans who resented the overreach.
One Republican who doesn’t seem to believe either of these arguments is Trump. The president has worked hard to ensure that no such humiliations recur during his second term, by stacking the Justice Department with loyalists, firing inspectors general en masse, purging the armed forces of “woke” officers, and generally eliminating any potential source of independence within the federal government.
Trump himself does not seem to think that the investigations that were avidly followed by resistance liberals did nothing to restrain his actions during his first term, or that they helped him shore up partisan support. And the absence of any such processes in his second term has not made Republicans in Congress feel freer to criticize the president. To the contrary, their fealty is more absolute than ever.
Even in the first term, resistance Democrats were dogged by their populist left-wing critics. This split first appeared in the spring of 2017, when Jon Ossoff ran to fill a special election for a House seat in Georgia, in a previously Republican district. Ossoff’s campaign, which attacked Trump’s corruption but declined to articulate a sharp progressive alternative, fell short.
Supporters of Bernie Sanders blamed Ossoff, and the party, for not taking up the Sanders message. “Ossoff’s campaign has failed to support or address any progressive issues. He embraces a centrist—not progressive—message, that both political parties waste taxpayer money, rather than politicians being corrupt by outside money,” the progressive writer Michael Sainato complained in the Observer. Winnie Wong, a co-founder of People for Bernie, told The Guardian of Ossoff, “He didn’t have a core progressive message and that ultimately is why he lost.” (Ossoff won a Senate race in 2020 and is leading the polls again this year, making slashing attacks on Trump’s personal corruption while steering clear of controversial left-wing policy stances.)
Like the Republican critics of resistance politics, progressive ones depicted it as substituting legal tactics for electoral victories. Yet the resistance was never limited to cheering on Mueller or hoping to persuade Republicans to convict the president of high crimes and misdemeanors. Resistance themes inspired the Democrats’ political message during Trump’s first term. And that message landed. Democrats retook the House in the 2018 midterms, despite a hot economy, and then defeated Trump’s reelection effort. Joe Biden, a link to a bygone era of civility and bipartisanship, ran in 2020 on a message of restoring the soul of America. He won.
Once in office, however, Biden ceded his domestic agenda to progressives who believed in Sanders’s vision of transformational change. They believed that only overturning the neoliberal order, handing control of domestic policy to neo-Brandeisians and climate hawks, and giving unions almost every policy they demanded would allow Democrats to regain the trust of working-class voters. This theory, not the resistance, failed. Biden’s support collapsed within his first year, and Kamala Harris’s half-hearted efforts to distance herself from her unpopular boss were too little, too late.
Trump’s return to office has left Democrats casting about for a stronger and more effective response. Perhaps the most obvious solution is the one they hit upon when Trump was first elected nearly a decade ago: Rather than promise to change everything about American politics, focus relentlessly on Trump’s unfitness. The crisis in the United States is not the general corruption of both parties; it is the specific corruption of Trump and his enablers. And the solution is simply to replace the corrupt, racist authoritarian with a governing party that respects the rule of law, equality, and basic decency.

Russian and Ukrainian attacks kill 5 a day after deadly shopping mall drone strike
Authorities say that Russian and Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have killed at least five people
KYIV, Ukraine -- Russian drone and missile strikes killed at least three people in Ukraine, officials said Saturday, while a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Krasnodar region killed two others, a day after a strike on a Ukrainian shopping center killed 16 people.
In the latest attacks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that one person was killed and another wounded when ballistic missiles hit railway infrastructure in the capital, Kyiv, overnight.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces had hit a locomotive depot.
In a separate attack, local authorities said one person was killed Saturday afternoon in a Russian ballistic missile strike on the Kyiv region, which surrounds the capital.
Moscow’s forces have recently intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine’s chronic shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down the missiles.
Russian drone strikes also killed one person overnight in a village in the Zaporizhzhia region, local officials said Saturday. Zelenskyy said that three people were wounded in an attack on a minibus in the regional capital, also called Zaporizhzhia.
In Russia's southern Krasnodar region, authorities said that two children were killed and two adults were wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike.
The latest attacks came a day after Russian drones struck a shopping center in the city of Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine on Friday.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said in the early hours of Saturday that the death toll had risen to 16 and nine people remain missing after the attack, which wounded another 130.
Kryvyi Rih is the hometown of Zelenskyy, who described the attack as a double-tap strike, in which an initial wave of drones hit the area followed by a second wave as rescue workers responded. The Ukrainian leader said the fire, which spread across 9,000 square meters (around 97,000 square feet), had been extinguished and rescue efforts were underway.
Kryvyi Rih has been hit multiple times during the 4½-year all-out war between Russia and Ukraine, with one of the deadliest occurring in April 2025, when 20 people were killed, including nine children.
Large-scale Russian strikes have become a regular occurrence this summer, with Friday’s attacks landing just 24 hours after Russia pounded Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime assault that killed 16 people.
The capital has been hit hard repeatedly in recent weeks: 17 people were killed in a strike on Kyiv and its surrounding region just over two weeks ago, and nine died in another attack on the city two days before that. The United Nations said last week that Kyiv was one of the hardest-hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 wounded.
At the same time, Ukraine has shifted the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities that have caused fuel shortages across Russia. It also has unsettled the Russian public by striking warehouses of Wildberries, the country’s biggest online retailer.
The Russian online news outlet Astra reported Saturday that a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil refinery in the Samara region. Local officials said that damage was recorded at an unidentified “industrial facility” and a logistics center for Ozon, a competitor to Wildberries.

The biggest talking point ahead of this year’s Duleep Trophy isn’t a batter who scored close to 950 runs in the Ranji Trophy or a fast bowler who picked 60 wickets over the last two domestic seasons.
It’s, instead, a 15-year-old vice-captain.
The East Zone selectors’ decision to appoint Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as deputy to Ishan Kishan has dominated the build-up to the tournament.
Not because the teenager isn’t good enough. In fact, few youngsters have captured the imagination quite like the Bihar batter has over the last year. If the selectors see him as a long-term India player, there is every reason to expose him to bigger stages early.
But even then, it has revived an old debate.
For decades, the Duleep Trophy represented the highest reward for sustained excellence in domestic cricket. Leadership roles, too, generally went to players who had spent years proving themselves in the Ranji Trophy. Sooryavanshi’s elevation doesn’t diminish his credentials, but it does reflect how the conversation around selection has evolved.
There is plenty to look forward to on the field as well.
Rajat Patidar leads Central Zone after another productive domestic season. Ruturaj Gaikwad captains a formidable West Zone side. Ishan returns to red-ball cricket as East Zone skipper, while Karun Nair, fresh from a prolific domestic campaign and back in the national reckoning, headlines South Zone. Prithvi Shaw and Harsh Dubey are among several players with plenty to play for.
The tournament also comes at an important time for the selectors.
India has a packed Test calendar ahead, and several places below the established core remain open. Fringe internationals, India A regulars and domestic performers all have another opportunity to strengthen their case.
There are openings at No. 3, in the middle order and even for a fast-bowling back-up. Patidar, Karun and Gaikwad are among the contenders, while seasoned campaigners such as Shardul Thakur have an opportunity to push for a comeback. With the selectors also investing in youngsters such as Sooryavanshi, it is a chance for the experienced players to stamp their class across formats.
There was a time when the route to the Test team seemed almost predictable. A prolific Ranji Trophy season earned a place in the Duleep Trophy. Success there led to India A. A good India A tour often resulted in an India cap.
That isn’t quite how it works anymore.
These days, the selectors weigh domestic performances alongside India A tours, overseas assignments, fitness reports, workload management, technical assessments and long-term planning. The IPL has also become an important scouting platform, particularly for identifying players with exceptional upside. It is also worth remembering that the Duleep Trophy squads are now selected by zonal selectors, who do not necessarily share the same priorities or assessments as the national selection panel.
The Duleep Trophy has also thrown up some interesting stories over the years. In 1991, two teenagers made their debuts against each other in Guwahati - Sachin Tendulkar, 17, scoring 159 for West Zone and Sourav Ganguly an unbeaten 124 for East Zone. Both would go on to become India greats.
Irfan Pathan’s breakthrough came through the tournament too. He took 22 wickets in the 2002 edition and 19 the following year before making his India debut on the 2003-04 Australia tour. Yuvraj Singh’s 208 in the 2003 final was another statement, followed by his Test debut weeks later.
VVS Laxman’s 121 in the 1995-96 semifinal was an important step towards his India call-up, while Jasprit Bumrah’s 2014 performances for West Zone showed that his white-ball skills could translate into First-Class cricket. Gautam Gambhir, meanwhile, used the tournament as both a launchpad early in his career and a route back into India’s Test side in 2016.
The list is long and revealing. The Duleep Trophy has often been where future India players first made a serious case for themselves.
Nobody is saying domestic cricket doesn’t matter. It clearly does. But it has left many in the circuit wondering where sustained First-Class performances fit into the equation. Last season’s Ranji Trophy offered enough evidence to keep the debate going.
Karnataka’s Smaran Ravichandran finished with 950 runs. Delhi’s Ayush Doseja scored 949. Mumbai’s Siddhesh Lad averaged over 77, while Bengal’s Sudip Kumar Gharami produced another prolific campaign, amassing 797 runs. Harsh Dubey continued his remarkable consistency with the ball. Auqib Nabi, after another outstanding season, finally earned his maiden India call-up.
For Rajasthan fast bowler Aniket Choudhary, the priorities have changed over the last decade.
“Back in 2011-12, making the India A team was the biggest motivation for a domestic cricketer. Tours to New Zealand or the West Indies taught you a lot. They prepared you for international cricket,” Choudhary says.
“Now, the IPL has become the biggest focus. Even state associations seem to be following that mindset. Players with strong T20 records often get the first opportunity, but four-day cricket is a completely different format. You can’t judge a player’s red-ball ability on what he does in T20 cricket…”
Choudhary insists the distinction between formats should remain clear.
“Four-day cricket tests your patience, temperament and skill over long spells. It deserves to be viewed separately from T20 cricket. The two formats require different skill sets,” he says, pointing to Nabi’s journey as an example.
“It isn’t easy to be as consistent as he has been over the last couple of seasons. He was always in the mix, but perhaps never the first choice. As a domestic player, that makes you wonder what more you need to do. The BCCI should reward sustained performances in red-ball cricket.
“There are so many fast bowlers in the domestic circuit consistently bowling at 140 kmph. The talent is there. Players need to know that if they perform in four-day cricket, those performances will be recognised.”
That perception isn’t confined to one dressing room.
Several former domestic cricketers believe the selection ecosystem has become far more layered than it was a decade ago, with Ranji Trophy and Duleep Trophy performances now competing for attention alongside India A tours and the IPL.
Paras Dogra has seen that change from close quarters. After nearly two decades in domestic cricket, the Jammu and Kashmir captain believes the route has become far less straightforward.
Dogra, who still missed out on a North Zone berth for the Duleep Trophy despite leading J&K to its maiden Ranji Trophy title, says, “There are only one or two players who get picked purely on the back of domestic cricket now. The IPL seems to get preference.”
“Earlier, IPL squads were bigger and there were more opportunities, even for rookies. Now, only one or two new players make it into the playing XI because most franchises stick with their core. That has reduced opportunities for domestic players,” he adds.
He also believes team performances increasingly shape individual opportunities.
“Look at Nabi. He took around 60 wickets, and Jammu & Kashmir also had an excellent Ranji Trophy season. It’s a similar case with Saransh (Jain). He’s getting opportunities because he has been consistently performing and, at the same time, his team (Madhya Pradesh) has been doing well. We have also seen players miss out on the Duleep Trophy or India A despite scoring heavily because the team they represented didn’t have a successful season.”
There is another side to it: money.
“The opportunities are becoming narrower with the IPL’s growing dominance. Most domestic cricketers come from humble backgrounds, and this is their only pathway. Those who make it to the IPL earn financial security. Those who don’t continue to struggle,” Dogra points out.
Lad agrees with parts of that argument, but also sees encouraging signs.
While he lauds the selectors for picking a 33-year-old Jain, sending the message that age is not a deterrent to making it to the Indian team, Lad also believes such instances can’t be one-offs.
“There are encouraging signs that domestic cricket is getting its due. Take Saransh, for example. He’s 33 and has finally earned recognition after years of consistent performances. It’s well deserved. Every now and then, selectors do reward domestic cricketers, and that’s a positive sign,” Lad says.
“At the same time, it can feel unfair when a player goes straight from a handful of good IPL performances to the India team. The IPL is a fantastic tournament, but the grind of a full First-Class season is very different.”
Growing up, Lad saw his father, Dinesh Lad, groom several young cricketers, most notably Rohit Sharma, who went on to become stars.
That, Lad feels, happened because domestic performances were never neglected.
“A Ranji Trophy season lasts four to five months, and your preparation starts two or three months before that. You’re constantly in that red-ball mindset and rhythm. You play on different surfaces, in different conditions and against different bowling attacks. That prepares you for the highest level,” Lad says.
“Players who come through a full domestic season are match-ready. They understand how to build an innings, how to bowl long spells and how to adapt to changing conditions. Those are qualities that are difficult to replicate in a shorter format…”
With the focus shifting towards white-ball cricket, the idea of preparing sporting wickets at the domestic level has also changed, which invariably has an impact on the national team.
“If you look at India’s recent struggles on turning tracks at home, it’s not because our players don’t have the skill. We have plenty of quality. The issue is that we don’t play enough First-Class cricket in those conditions anymore. There is no substitute for that kind of experience,” Lad says.
As the players gear up for another gruelling season, the Sooryavanshi appointment sits at the heart of this discussion, not because he isn’t deserving, but because it represents a changing philosophy.
For years, leadership in the Duleep Trophy was almost an acknowledgement of years spent performing in First-Class cricket. Sooryavanshi’s appointment suggests Indian cricket is increasingly willing to reward potential as much as performance.
East Zone selector Pravanjan Mullick’s explanation is straightforward. “We want him to grow, and maybe one day he could even captain India,” he says. Many in the domestic circuit, however, aren’t convinced.
Their argument isn’t against Sooryavanshi. It is about the message such decisions send to players who have spent years grinding through First-Class cricket.
The Duleep Trophy has never been short of quality. This season, it also finds itself carrying an unusual burden of proving that it can still shape careers as much as it showcases them.

Bangladesh has lashed out at India for allowing the ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina to address journalists in New Delhi, plunging already strained bilateral relations to a fresh low.
Dhaka accused India of giving a platform to a fugitive it labelled a “convicted genocider” and of undermining efforts to repair ties, after Hasina vowed to return to Bangladesh in December despite facing a death sentence on charges of “crimes against humanity”.
The angry response late on Wednesday came hours after Hasina, speaking on the second anniversary of the massive student-led uprising that led to her flight to India, declared: “Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people.”
Bangladesh’s foreign ministry said it was “outraged” Hasina had been allowed to participate in the event, where it said she and her allies launched “venomous vitriol” against Bangladesh and its people.
“This interaction by Hasina on Indian soil stands as an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh,” the ministry said. Dhaka also renewed its demands for India to extradite Hasina.
India earlier distanced itself from the news conference – Hasina’s first since fleeing Bangladesh in 2024, saying it had no role in organising it and would not endorse any political views voiced.
Hasina said she was ready to face whatever fate awaited her in Bangladesh, where her Awami League party is now banned. “They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but I still have to go,” the 78-year-old said via audio link.
“My life moved beyond calculations of personal safety long ago.”
After 15 years in power, Hasina fled to India in 2024 following weeks of student-led protests. Her government was accused of misusing state institutions to entrench its hold on power and stamp out dissent, including through the killing of opposition activists.
In her speech, she dismissed criminal cases against her as politically motivated and accused Bangladesh’s new government, led by Tarique Rahman, of economic mismanagement, political repression and persecution of her supporters.
Hasina was sentenced in absentia to death by hanging over her government’s deadly crackdown on the uprising. She said she wanted to return in December because it marked Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, commemorating Pakistan’s defeat in the 1971 independence war.
She claimed thousands of Awami League activists had been killed or jailed since her downfall.
Her son Sajeeb Wazed Joy stoked the diplomatic row by extolling India’s hospitality. “She’s being treated very well and has been provided with the full services and security accorded to a head of state,” he said. “Prime Minister Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect.”
Hasina was joined at the event by Shakib Al Hasan, a former national cricket captain. Hours later unidentified attackers hurled petrol bombs and smashed windows at his home in Bangladesh, but no one was hurt, police said. Shakib, elected to parliament as an Awami League candidate, has remained outside Bangladesh since Hasina’s overthrow.

NHAI orders audits, inspections for new highways after Del-Dehradun Expressway defects
NHAI has issued new safety and quality guidelines for newly inaugurated highways, including independent audits and frequent inspections of major projects.
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has issued new quality, safety and event-management guidelines for newly inaugurated national highway projects, including provisions for independent audits of major projects and more intensive inspections after highways open to traffic.
The guidelines, issued on Friday, come after a review of existing protocols and incorporate “experience and lessons learnt” from recent inauguration and foundation-stone laying events.
The move comes weeks after the Delhi–Dehradun Expressway, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in April, developed potholes, cracks and a cave-in following intense rain.
Also Read: Centre considering 65-km expressway linking Delhi-Dehradun to Noida, Faridabad
NHAI has also directed its media teams to proactively monitor print and digital media reports after such events and, in coordination with regional offices, prepare ready responses or “counter narratives” to address reports it considers “factually incorrect or politically motivated”.
In its policy circular, NHAI said the addendum supersedes an earlier addendum issued in October 2025.
Greenfield expressways, high-speed corridors, specialised projects and projects with a total capital cost of more than ₹2,500 crore may undergo an independent audit by a reputed third-party entity or premier institutions such as Indian Institute of Technology (IITs) and National Institute of Technology (NITs). The audit may examine the anticipated impact of traffic after opening, drainage and related issues.
Also Read: 80 days of Delhi–Dehradun E-way: Light rain creates sinkholes in Shamli, videos viral
The NHAI has also prescribed joint inspections of newly opened highway stretches by the contractor or concessionaire’s project manager and the supervision consultant’s team leader. These are to be conducted weekly for the first three months and fortnightly for the next three months, covering pavement and riding quality, drainage, safety installations and embankment slopes.
Route patrol vehicles will also regularly cover the full length of highways after opening. Defects or anticipated deterioration are to be geo-tagged and immediately reported to the project director, contractor or concessionaire and supervision consultant for rectification.
The circular sets out arrangements for large Prime Ministerial events, noting that attendance can range from 25,000 to one lakh people. It calls for adequate venue capacity, parking, connectivity, security, crowd management and contingency measures for adverse weather.
It also says the number of officials at a function should preferably be restricted to 500 and that event preparations should be completed at least 24 hours before the programme.

On the court, the WNBA is thriving. After 30 years, its players are receiving a historic payout, along with a massive TV distribution deal that will mean more games, and hopefully even more fans. But off the court, all that attention has some downsides. Most recently, it means that the culture war has come for the WNBA.
Sophie Cunningham and the WNBA culture wars
How the league became embroiled in a fight over trans athletes.
Specifically, the league has found itself at the center of a debate over transgender athletes and women’s sports, one that Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham ignited last month.
Cunningham, 30, has gained a reputation as an “enforcer” for her All-Star teammate, Caitlin Clark. In July, she told ESPN that “I think that I am here to extend love, but I also think that with love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”
No known trans athletes have ever played in the WNBA, but that hasn’t much deterred pundits from weighing in. It’s the latest instance of the WNBA playing a central role in conversations about race and gender — even as most of the outrage is happening outside the court, while players and coaches would rather focus on basketball.
To get a better sense of what’s going on in the league — and why — Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Ringer staff writer Seerat Sohi, who covers the NBA, WNBA, and women’s college basketball, about why the WNBA can’t seem to escape the culture wars.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
What is it about the WNBA ?
The WNBA is a league that invites, frankly, a lot of distraction, both because of its own institutional failures — I do think the WNBA really struggles at telling its own story and has at times run away from its own story — but I think in general, the WNBA has become fertile ground for the culture wars, as we put them, because the league has exploded in popularity at the same moment in the country where we are embroiled in this cultural, political, legal fight over what the role of women is in society.
Let’s break this down to the two pieces you mentioned. You referenced institutional failures. What do you mean?
The WNBA, from the top down, has been understaffed, and it has historically been marketed in a way that is obsessed with trying to bring in some apocryphal average American, the nuclear family. And at the same time, this has been a league that has been defined by people who have historically existed on the margins. They are female athletes at a time when historically female athletes were not paid much attention to, and in fact were mocked.
It’s the league that is primarily Black, that is openly queer, that is politically outspoken. And the league has always tried to toe the line of marketing the faces that feel more like a girl-next-door type of vibe.
To the point that early on, we can look at, for example, Sue Bird, who, when she entered the league [in 2002], was encouraged to not come out.
And if you look back at pictures of her, she is dressed in a way that not only is it feminine, but it is also not the issue. The issue is that she’s very clearly uncomfortable in her own skin. Diana Taurasi, whose jersey was just retired — if you look back at her awards, it’s the same thing.
Fast-forward to 2026, these are queer icons who are highly marketable in the media environment that we are in right now, but the WNBA has always been behind the eight ball in that regard because it has run away from its identity.
So by institutional failures, what we mean is maybe a lack of bravery or a lack of spine. You also said this exploded because the WNBA is of great interest at this moment to right-wing figures. What do you mean by that?
The right cares about the WNBA in the same way that it cares about who becomes a Disney princess. It understands the power of a good story. It understands symbolism. To see women on that stage thriving, to see them sweaty, to see them wanting, to see them be the main character instead of the object of somebody else’s affection or interest, to see them be the subject and be the ones that are going for something as opposed to being on the sidelines.
That in and of itself alone is very, very powerful. And then you think about where the WNBA is politically. This has always been a league that has been very outspoken. This is a league that in 2020 helped flip a Georgia Senate election and actually ousted their then-owner of the Atlanta Dream who spoke out against the Black Lives Matter movement.
I always understood the WNBA to have a smaller fan base. But the situation with Sophie Cunningham has made me realize it is much larger and much more middle-of-the-road than I would have thought. Did something change recently? Did the fan base of the WNBA grow?
[Indiana Fever All-Star] Caitlin Clark was an explosive figure. Caitlin Clark was really a gateway drug for WNBA fans. The sheer amount of eyeballs that she has brought to the game, the attention, her logo threes. She is the type of player that makes children out of all of us. And then there’s also this right-wing movement that has latched onto her as a symbol.
Why is that? For someone who doesn’t watch many games, what’s going on?
Caitlin is white and straight. That is a demographic that I guess you could say is maybe underrepresented in the WNBA. And there was a feeling when she came into the league that she wasn’t welcomed in the same way that maybe other stars in the past have been. There was a sense that maybe there was some resentment.
Now, I don’t know if that’s true. I would imagine, look, these are human beings that we’re talking about. There was probably a spectrum of feelings when you think about it. This was a league that didn’t have charter flights. Caitlin Clark comes in, they get charter flights.
Now, obviously that’s great for the players, but I also think that there was a feeling of, “Oh wait, the WNBA could have done these things that we’ve been advocating for for a long time. Now they’re finally listening because Caitlin is here.”
She is, ironically, an organic phenomenon that is bringing to light the manufactured failures of the WNBA in the past.
Caitlin Clark goes to the WNBA. The WNBA grows its fan base to include people who traditionally were not watching. And then what is the leap from that fact? More people at games, more eyeballs on games. More eyeballs on players, to a conservative movement seizes upon the WNBA and says, “We’re gonna make something out of this.” How did you see that play out?
It started with the 2023 college national title game, when Caitlin was still in college. And she went up against Angel Reese from LSU. LSU won that game. And after the game, Angel Reese did the “You can’t see me” taunt by John Cena, and it was actually something that Caitlin did [previously] in the Elite Eight. It was taken as trash talk. Angel then repeated that symbol to Caitlin after they won and pointed at her ring.
In the aftermath of that, Angel Reese was called all kinds of things by not only conservative commentators — a lot of this was conservative commentators, but you also had people like Keith Olbermann, who’s a former SportsCenter anchor and probably somebody who’s a little bit more in the middle of the road, calling her classless.
I think a lot of the WNBA fans took those things to be dog whistles, that it was a form of racism. And there was also just overt racism. There were just words that you and I would not say and would not repeat here that were thrown at Angel Reese, who has also dealt with a lot of vitriol since that moment.
That moment changed both of their lives, frankly. And that was really the inciting incident. From then on, I think that there were a lot of people in the new media landscape that recognized that the WNBA was a fault line for a lot of our modern discourse in America.
It is a league that you can use as a proxy to talk about race, gender fluidity, femininity, DEI, labor politics. It is probably the most modern American league that we have.
And if you look back at the history of sports, I think Americans have always used sports as a proxy to talk about things that aren’t actually about the sport. And the WNBA is really just the latest vessel of that.

NEW DELHI
The Delhi High Court directed the Union Government on Monday (August 17, 2026) to take appropriate action within two months on a representation submitted by the Indian Professional Nurses Association (IPNA) seeking implementation of the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission (NNMC) Act, 2023.
Justice Swarna Kanta Sharma said that if no action is taken within the stipulated period, IPNA would be at liberty to approach the court again.
The direction followed a petition filed by the IPNA, represented by advocate Robin Raju, challenging the delay in constituting the NNMC and implementing the Act. The association also sought a time-bound update on the selection and appointment of the Commission’s office-bearers and members of its various boards.
The NNMC Act was enacted to replace the 77-year-old Indian Nursing Council Act and establish a modern system for regulating the standards of nursing and midwifery education, the plea stated.
The NNMC Act received presidential assent in August 2023. The Centre subsequently brought its provisions into force on February 29, 2024, notified the rules on March 13, 2024, and invited applications for posts in the Commission and its boards on March 14, 2024. Despite these steps, the Commission had not been constituted, the petition stated.
NNMC not constituted
An RTI response received by IPNA from the Centre on July 7, 2026, also stated that the NNMC had not been constituted and that no appointment or recruitment had been made for the Commission.
IPNA argued that the delay was particularly significant because national regulatory commissions for other healthcare professions had already been constituted. It contended that the continued absence of the nursing commission was arbitrary and discriminatory and had implications for nursing education, professional standards, and the right to health.
“The delay in constituting the Commission directly impacts quality of nursing education, service standards, and the ‘Right to Health’ of citizens,” the plea said.
The association also raised concerns about the functioning of the existing Indian Nursing Council, including the ineffective Nurses Registration and Tracking System (NRTS) portal, lack of an effective grievance redressal mechanism, and inadequate enforcement against nursing institutions.
The petition said IPNA had repeatedly approached the authorities over these issues. It had also submitted a representation to the Union Health Minister on July 20, 2026, seeking immediate implementation of the NNMC Act, but said it had received no response.
