A car charger is not a complicated device. The best USB car charger is the one that charges your phone quickly, does not overheat, allows multiple devices to charge, and remains compatible with whichever USB cable you (or your passengers) happen to have available. It is usually also a trusted brand, with certification to international standards—not a janky gas station charger that'll blow a fuse with an internal short or offer insufficient protection against dust and debris.
I put car chargers to the test with ammeters and phone apps, and on multi-hour road trips, to make sure each one lived up to its promises. The best car charger I've found is the three-port Anker 167.5W Nano ($38), which combines 100-watt fast-charging capability for auxiliary devices, plus dual-port USB-Cs, USB-A capability, and safety features that include overheat protection.
If you shun dangling cords, I offer the Anker 75W Fast Charger ($30) with slightly lower top amperage but a retractable cable. And for families whose kids can't live without constant tablets in the back seat, there's the DeWalt 72W Front and Back Seat Charger ($45).
For other power needs, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Portable Jump Starters, Best Power Banks, Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations.
The Best USB Car Charger
This three-port charger from Anker offers pretty much everything I want from a USB car charger while remaining hearteningly compact and affordable. The 100W fast-charging USB-C port kicks out nearly 7 amps at top speeds, enough juice to charge my Macbook Air to 50 percent in about 25 minutes, before fast-charging slows down, and does the same for my iPhone. But especially, Anker's PowerIQ technology smartly assesses the differing voltage needs of various phones to avoid over- or under-voltage. I've never actually seen this Anker on sale on Amazon above $40.
It also doesn't hurt that Anker makes some of WIRED's most trusted portable power technology—tech whose reliability we've verified over years of real-world testing. You don't overwhelmingly want a janky cheap charger that blows a fuse. Good insulation and a tiny built-in fan effectively lower overheating versus other fast-chargers, though you'll still notice some heat when charging at 100 watts or above. USB-A capability is welcome for versatility, though my testing showed somewhat lower power than advertised on that port.
Either way, I was able to charge both my top-pick portable jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox ($120), in a little over an hour while also keeping my phone topped off on a road trip—which is pretty much as high-demand as I get while also blasting AC and the radio, and this caused no problems with the 15-amp circuit on my older car. But note that while most modern cars run on 20-amp fuses, the max capacity for this charger when drawing from all three ports does run pretty close to the max load for an older-model car charger. The charger is able to draw quite close to the maximum amperage on a 15-amp fuse.
A similar budget pick: The lower overheating on my top-pick Anker bodes well for longevity, which means it might still be a cheaper option in the long haul. But note that a similar three-port fast-charger from Chinese brand Ugreen ($21) performed comparably on charging speeds. But it also got significantly hotter within 10 minutes of fast-charging.
Best USB Car Charger With Retractable Cord
A retractable charging cable has the distinct merit of keeping your car tidy, without dangling charging cords to get tangled between your foot and the gas pedal. It also obviates the need to remember a cable at all. This Anker model offers a 2-foot cable that retracts quite easily back into its base after a quick tug on the cable, neat as you'd like. The cable's 45W fast-charging capability will max out the charging capability of most iPhones.
Anker is a brand I trust for charging technology. But it's worth noting that retractable cables introduce a couple failure points that could lower longevity. The cable can't be swapped out if it gets worn, and the retraction mechanism itself could wear out. Tidiness has a price, it seems. This said, the charger is not overly expensive, usually retailing closer to $20.
Best Front and Back Seat Car Charger
The modern car family involves a nest of devices—parents in the front seat charging phones, children in the back with tablets, somehow watching the same thing over and over. And nothing ends the peace of a road trip quite like a tablet running out of juice halfway through an episode of Bluey.
This DeWalt is a good solution, offering decent (but not great) 30-watt charging on the USB-C port for front-seat parents, and a couple of auxiliary USB-A ports to keep maintenance charge on backseat devices. DeWalt is a power tool brand, of course, and so these ports were likely designed for a tool or two resting in the back seat. But kids have tools, too, and this'll serve their needs.
It's perhaps frustrating that the back seat chargers are USB-A. But I haven't found a good USB charger with a back-seat USB-C charging setup, assuming your car doesn't have a back seat charger of its own. And so while this DeWalt is a compromise, it's the best compromise I've found so far.
Frequently Asked Questions
How I Selected and Tested USB Car Chargers
For this round of car-charger testing, I looked first for known quantities and trusted charging technology brands like Anker, Belkin, and Ugreen. I also ordered and tested devices that other credible sources had ranked as their favorite USB chargers, making sure that each charger is broadly available and easy to find. Needless to say, I only assessed and recommend UL-certified chargers, and avoided dodgy-looking brands: Short circuits in cars aren't fun, for me or for you.
I then set about testing the claims for each car charger, using ammeters for each port on each charger, testing with an ammeter while pulling max loads. I additionally used the Ampere phone app to test the peak draw for a Motorola Razr and an iPhone 13, and also tested to see whether the charger heated up while pulling max draw—both using the phone app and an infrared thermometer.
I tested with each charger's included cord, where relevant, but also with a fast-charging cable on USB-C devices that advertise this capability. For my top contenders among 100-watt fast chargers, I also tested to see how long it took to charge a Macbook Air M4 and my top-pick jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox.
As with every device tested by the WIRED Reviews team, I subjected my top-pick chargers to real-world road tests. I went on multi-hour road trips with devices plugged in. I charged portable jump starters or laptops while also charging phones. I tested durability in real-world conditions that may also involve grubby fingers. I assessed each device not just for brute speed, but for versatility in different use cases. For now, I favor chargers that offer both USB-C and USB-A capability, so as not to leave any devices out in the cold.
I also checked up on customer reviews for each of these chargers. If I saw any customer complaints, I tried my darndest to replicate them. I jammed chargers in and out of the ports, and wobbled the chargers around in their sockets. I acted the way people act when they're fumbling for a device charger they're not looking at while driving.
Are Cheap USB Chargers Unsafe?
I've put a bit of emphasis on trusted brands while testing USB chargers, and this isn't by accident. The world is full of dodgy gas station or Amazon chargers, and bad cables, with insufficient electrical insulation and inconsistent current delivery.
Bad USB-C cables and electrical insulation are known fire hazards in the worst cases, but inconsistent voltage is also just bad for your phone or laptop battery over time. Poorly made chargers, connectors, and cables can have higher resistance (leading to overheating), bad or inconsistent connections, and poor protections against shorts and surges. All of these things are bad. At worst, they can fry your device or lower your battery longevity.
As a rule of thumb, look for language that a product is “UL-Listed” or "UL-Certified" not merely "UL-Classified" or “Recognized.” The latter two mean that a product has been tested only against specific hazards or under specific conditions. Listed and Certified products have fully passed all tests within a given standard. WIRED will only recommend chargers that are UL-listed or -certified.
Other USB Chargers I Recommend
Scosche PowerVolt 60W Dual-Port Charger for $20: This dual-port USB-C charger from California car brand Scosche is the simplest thing imaginable. Two USB-C ports, each separately rated at 30 watts. Each charges quickly and is reliable. Though this Scosche doesn't offer a fast-charging option for laptops, it's perfectly optimized for a pair of phones—and admirably low-cost. If you're mostly just going to charge a phone, this is a tight runner-up to my top-pick Anker—especially if you're pretty sure you'll never need a USB-A charger in your car.
Anker 40W Two-Port Charger for $20: Like the Scosche, this Anker is a purpose-driven phone charger with two USB-C ports. It's a little lower-powered than the Scosche, with a little less juice than the newest generation of phones can support. But the price is right if you're willing to accept lower charging speeds.
Belkin BoostCharge 42W Dual-Port Charger for $24: This compact, well-insulated dual-port charger from California tech accessory brand Belkin is great as a budget option, with decently fast USB-C and USB-A charging. Just note that the tiny device might be a bit shallow for some deeper car chargers, and that when plugged in, the charger has a nonnegotiable and oddly bright LED light that stays on even when no device is charging. This won't bother you unless it bothers you.
Nekteck 45W Two-Port Car Charger for $32: This basic, bare-bones Neckteck charger is a decent compromise for those who need fast charging on a QC 3.0-compatible USB-A device. While a 45-watt max speed for USB-C charging isn't fast by modern standards, it's still faster than most phones. And the QC 3.0 USB-A charger is significantly faster than most USB-A chargers, for those with older devices.
Lisen 90W Charger With Cord for $20: This charger from Chinese car-tech company Lisen performed reasonably well in testing, though true fast-charging isn't available and the listed charge speeds are a little confusing and don't add up. The coiled cord is not able to be retracted or removed, making this charger a bit ungainly for daily use, but the option on a 60- or 90-inch cord does make this Lisen the rare device suitable for charging a USB-C phone or tablet in the back seat. This said, I tested a shorter cable, and longer USB-C cables are notoriously finicky for high amperage.
Also Tested
The six-port Ai Aikenuo back seat charging kit is useful for keeping a large number of devices charged up for work use or larger families, but it disappeared from Amazon right before this guide's publication. I'll monitor to see if this is a momentary glitch or whether it's been discontinued.

Britain, Australia and Canada have called the decision of the Israeli military authorities not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of aid vehicles in Gaza “shameful”. The strikes killed seven humanitarian workers from the US-based World Central Kitchen (WCK) organisation.
WCK staff from the three countries were among the casualties of the attack, which prompted global outrage.
“This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf. The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,” the countries’ joint statement said.
It continued: “In Gaza, humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.”
On Thursday, Australia’s government expressed “outrage” over the decision, while relatives said that Zomi Frankcom, the Australian among those killed, deserved more than an “internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.”
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision.
The Polish government said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” and called for Israeli authorities to cooperate with Polish investigations into the incident. Damian Soból, a volunteer from Przemyśl, was also among the casualties.
In London, the Foreign Office said the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack.
WCK, which distributed food in Gaza throughout the war, said immediately after the lethal attack that it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air.
“There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.
The IDF said on Wednesday that it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the WCK convoy had deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.
One of the officers who was dismissed had reportedly signed an open letter earlier that year calling for Gaza to be deprived of aid.
The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday that its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing, as well as into the fatal shooting of 15 paramedics in 2025.
Hind Rajab died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.
The IDF repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.
The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”, but experts said criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians very rarely lead to convictions.

A video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi moving around a stage greeting people while the national anthem plays in the background is viral on social media, with users claiming that the Prime Minister was being disrespectful to the anthem.
An user on Facebook, Kumar Raj, shared the purported video on August 15, Independance Day, with Modi circled out. The post has garnered 2.3 million views. It was shared around 14,000 times and has received 30,500 reactions.
Activist Piyush Manush shared the same video on Facebook, which was viewed over 76,000 times.
Several X users also amplified the viral video, amplifying the same claim.
Fact Check
A keyframe in the viral video showed a screen placed on the podium which mentioned the location of the event as Jasauli Kharag, located in Bihar’s Siwan city. The date mentioned was June 20, 2025.
A relevant keyword search led us to the original video uploaded from the Prime Minister’s official YouTube channel. In this video dated June 21, 2025, Modi, seen in the same attire as the viral video, walked onto a stage while he was being introduced by the speaker. Amid cheers from the audience, he waved to them and shook hands with other dignitaries present on the stage. At no point can the national anthem be heard playing in the clip.
Thus, the claim that Prime Minister Narendra Modi disrespected the national anthem by walking around the stage while it played is misleading. The original video shows Modi being introduced by the speaker and waving to a cheering audience, with no national anthem playing in the clip. The anthem heard in the viral version was added later to the original video, altering the context of the footage to amplify a false claim.

Chennai-based agritech startup Fragaria Fruits is in talks to raise ₹40 Cr ($4.2 Mn) in a fresh funding round, sources told Inc42. The funding round will be led by Blume Ventures, and also see participation from Fragaria’s existing investors, including WEH Ventures, Rainmatter, among others, the sources added. The startup could potentially hit a valuation of ₹160 Cr post the investment. Questions sent to both Fragaria and Blume Ventures didn’t elicit any response at the time of publication. The story will be updated based on their responses. The fresh capital infusion comes about 10 months after the startup raised $2 Mn in its seed funding led by WEH Ventures, with participation from Rainmatter, Spiral Ventures, and angel investor Akshayakalpa Organic founder Sashi Kumar. Founded in 2024 by Harish Varadharajan, Timothy Chad Van Niekerk, and Damian López-Salazar, Fragaria Fruits is a Chennai-based agritech startup that uses indoor vertical farming to grow premium, pesticide-free strawberries year-round. The startup operates entirely indoors in high-precision vertical farming systems, where every variable that influences plant growth — light, temperature, humidity, nutrients, and irrigation — is monitored and optimised. Its flagship product is high-quality European strawberries, sold under its consumer brand Oh! Fruits. The brand claims that these strawberries are twice as sweet as the average Indian strawberry, comparable to finest European produce. Following a successful pilot farm in Chennai, Fragaria Fruits has been scaling its operations in Bengaluru since its $2 Mn fundraise, targeting a daily output of 120 kg of premium strawberries. It has been constructing a large-scale commercial farm near Bengaluru and is also developing dedicated facilities for blueberries and raspberries, marking an entry into the broader premium berry category. The brand is targeting the premium niche in the agritech market at a time when the broader industry is growing strongly. According to Inc42 and StarAgri’s Indian Agritech Market Landscape Report, 2025, India’s agritech market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 25% to touch $28 Bn by 2030.

From ‘Indispensable’ Ally to Target of Annihilation
The latest target of Trump’s ire is the low-profile Sultanate of Oman.
When the United States was looking for a way to talk to Iran about a nuclear deal more than a decade ago, it turned to Oman, asking the country to do something it had quietly done for years: make an impossible conversation possible. Because Washington and Tehran had no diplomatic relations, the U.S. felt that the most promising back channel to get a conversation started led through Muscat.
Iran was skeptical but willing to sit down with U.S. officials, provided there was some very particular diplomatic choreography. At Tehran’s request, Oman’s government found a room with multiple doors, so that American and Iranian officials would not be seen entering together. Omani officials took the head of the table, to create the impression that it was more than a bilateral conversation.
That session laid the groundwork for what ultimately became the 2015 nuclear pact. “Without Oman, I’m not sure there would be an Iran nuclear deal,” Jake Sullivan, one of the top U.S. officials involved in those talks, told me.
But today, that pact lies in ruins. President Trump tore it up, then went to war with Iran. Oman has watched its standing with Washington collapse too. Earlier this week, Trump threatened to “bomb the shit” out of the sultanate unless it did what America demanded—adding another longtime ally to the list of countries he has threatened to attack.
Oman, located on the southeastern edge of the Arabian Peninsula, is often overshadowed by its wealthier, more conspicuous neighbors, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, and by its more tumultuous neighbor, Yemen. Yet for decades, Oman punched above its weight diplomatically by serving as one of Washington’s most useful interlocutors in the Middle East, in part because it has maintained relationships with governments that Washington often cannot or will not talk to.
Trump has accused the sultanate of undermining his efforts to strike a deal with Iran and end the war, which began at the end of February and are now in a stalemate. The Strait of Hormuz, which is central to the conflict with Tehran, is also at the center of Washington’s dispute with Oman. The maritime corridor used to carry one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied-natural-gas supplies before the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran began and Tehran closed the strait to traffic through drone, small-boat, and mine attacks. Trump responded with a U.S. blockade, which remains in place even though the deadline for Washington and Tehran to reach an interim deal and set the stage for broader talks over Iran’s nuclear program expired earlier this week, showing no sign of a breakthrough.
Oman and Iran border opposite sides of the strait; their respective territorial waters meet in the 21-mile-wide choke point. The two countries have been in talks in recent weeks to restore commercial shipping, which has dwindled to a trickle. Both countries have floated the idea of a service fee for passage through the strait, but other Gulf nations have objected. Trump has wavered on the issue, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio has repeatedly said that the strait must return to being an open and free waterway. Trump has vowed to declare the strait a U.S. territory. He recently claimed that the strait was reopened and that mines and other hazards have been cleared. Shipping trackers continue to show a rate of passage dramatically below prewar levels.
Omani officials insist that charging for passage is within the country’s legal rights. When asked on Monday in the Oval Office whether he was out of patience with Oman, Trump told reporters: “No, I don’t think they behaved very well, but we’d handle them very easily, just like we do other things.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has separately threatened Oman with sanctions if Muscat facilitates fees for ships passing through the strait.
A U.S. official familiar with the deliberations told me that the administration views Oman’s handling of the negotiations as “dishonorable,” accusing Omani intermediaries of publicly portraying the two sides as nearing an agreement while privately conveying proposals to U.S. officials that the latter viewed as unacceptable. The official also accused Oman of delivering false statements to the press, which Omani officials deny. But this much is clear: The role that Oman used to play for Washington as a useful regional intermediary is over—at least as long as Trump remains in office.
The president’s anger presents an unusually awkward problem for Washington and for Muscat. Oman is not some distant neutral country that wandered into an American dispute. It has spent decades deliberately cultivating its relationship with Washington.
“Oman has decided its strategic importance is to be nonaligned the way Switzerland is nonaligned,” Jon Alterman, the chair in global security and geostrategy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told me. “It’s a relatively small, relatively poor place, surrounded by giants, and Oman has decided it will make itself indispensable to everyone—not because it helps everybody, but because it’s a place that can keep a secret and allows people to meet quietly and resolve conflicts.”
Modern diplomatic relations between the United States and Oman date to 1972, but their history goes back much further. In 1833, President Andrew Jackson’s administration signed a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with Oman, then an important maritime power, as Washington sought to expand commercial ties in the region and protect American merchants operating in the Indian Ocean. An American consulate operated in Muscat from 1880 to 1915. In 1980, after the Iranian Revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, Oman became the first Persian Gulf state to officially grant the U.S. access to its military facilities.
Oman doesn’t host a large, permanent American base like the Al Udeid Air Base, near Doha, the capital of Qatar. But Washington does have access to Omani military facilities and ports. In 2019, the two countries expanded that arrangement to include Duqm and Salalah, two key ports on the Arabian Sea, allowing American ships to operate and resupply outside the Gulf before entering the Strait of Hormuz.
Oman has also spent decades pursuing a foreign policy designed to maintain relationships across the region’s fault lines. It has good relations with Iran, maintains a security partnership with the United States, and has kept channels open to the Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia in Yemen. It has also maintained contact with Israel.
This is often described as Omani “neutrality,” though some of the sultanate’s regional neighbors believe that it favors Tehran. That has sometimes put Oman at odds with its fellow Gulf states, especially Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which view Iran as a major regional security threat. Oman declined to join the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen in 2015 and stayed out of the 2017 regional blockade of Qatar. Muscat also maintained channels to the Houthis, whom Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have long battled. One Saudi official I spoke with offered a skeptical assessment: “Oman’s definition of neutrality has been questionable.”
Oman rejects the idea that its connections to Iran, including its economic relationship with and ties to the Houthis, amount to complicity. Instead, it casts its ties as a relationship of economic and regional importance. Oman serves as an economic lifeline and reexport hub for Iran, absorbing trade activity that previously passed through the UAE. (The UAE announced this week that it is stopping all trade and financial transactions with Tehran.) Iran, meanwhile, supplies Oman with agricultural products and heavy materials.
A senior Omani diplomat I spoke with described neutrality as a practical necessity for a small state surrounded by larger powers. Oman, the official argued, gets criticized from all sides. “The Iranians will tell us, You’re being too soft on the West,” the official told me, while Western governments accuse Oman of being too soft on Iran. “And the Houthis will tell us we’re being too nice to the Saudis, and the Saudis will tell us we’re being too nice to the Houthis. It just goes with the territory.”
But Oman’s independence—its ability to talk to all sides, even if it irritates the others—is precisely what has made Muscat useful to successive American administrations.
Oman’s record as an intermediary is unusually long. The country has helped secure the release of American detainees held by Iran. It has also facilitated contacts involving Yemen. In early 2013, a small group of senior American officials quietly boarded a military plane bound for Oman. For years, John Kerry had been nurturing a diplomatic channel with Muscat, meeting secretly with Omani officials while he was chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in hope of opening back-channel talks with Iran. As President Obama’s secretary of state, he gave the green light to dispatch top foreign-policy officials to Muscat, including then–Deputy Secretary of State William Burns and Sullivan, who was serving as national security adviser to then–Vice President Biden.
Those talks helped form the basis for the 2013 interim nuclear agreement and, eventually, the 2015 Iran nuclear deal. During the Biden administration, Muscat hosted the U.S. special envoy for Yemen, Tim Lenderking, and brokered his first direct contacts and message exchanges with Houthi representatives. Oman “wanted peace in Yemen, and they were willing to travel to Sanaa to meet with the Houthis and pass messages to Houthi leadership and exert their influence where they could to help us achieve a durable peace,” Lenderking, who is now a principal at the Washington-based law firm Squire Patton Boggs, told me. In 2025, the Trump administration again turned to Oman to host negotiations with Iran. Trump subsequently thanked Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, the country’s leader, for Oman’s role.
In addition to serving as an intermediary, Oman offers Washington military access and a stable partner near one of the world’s most important maritime choke points; Oman gets a powerful security partner while preserving the freedom to maintain its own relationships. But that bargain hinges on Oman’s independence.
Analysts told me that this is why the current rupture matters. If the U.S. wants Oman to function as an intermediary, it cannot simultaneously demand that Muscat adopt Washington’s preferred position toward Iran. The very quality that makes Oman useful—the ability to talk to everyone—can look like disloyalty.
That old paradox has now become a crisis. Oman says that it is trying to fulfill its obligations under international law and keep commercial shipping moving, including through Omani territorial waters. The Omani diplomat told me that the country’s lawyers believe that maritime fees can be lawful under international practice and that Oman has no intention of doing anything illegal.
Trump and his negotiators see the issue differently, particularly where any arrangement could give Iran greater control over shipping or legitimize Iranian fees in what Tehran could portray as a victory over its much more powerful nemesis. Other nations have stepped in to play crucial mediating roles in this conflict, thus far to no avail. But Muscat remains one of the few doors available to American negotiators. The difficult question now is whether Trump’s threats will finally slam it shut.

In July, an Alt News post about the upcoming Bollywood film ‘Chauhaan’ was removed twice by Instagram. The post survived when we shared it the third time, but only after two references to Burhan Wani were removed. The episode offers a glimpse into the opaque manner in which content restrictions are being enforced on Instagram in India, and raises key questions amid growing concerns over censorship on the platform.
The original post was a carousel based on an Alt News analysis of the teaser of ‘Chauhaan’ starring Ajay Devgn. The 2.24-minute video shows its protagonist dismissing pellet guns as an ineffective crowd-control measure causing only “limited damage”. This stands in stark contrast to the documented reality in Kashmir, where pellet guns have killed scores, and blinded or permanently disabled thousands. The teaser sparked an online backlash for trivialising violence as entertainment, pairing it with upbeat music. The story can be read here.
Alt News first uploaded the carousel on July 1. Instagram restricted the post within minutes. Since the carousel contained visuals of pellet injuries, Alt News initially suspected that these images might have triggered the removal. The carousel was therefore modified, with some of the visuals changed, and uploaded again.
Instagram removed the second version as well.
Alt News then removed two references to Burhan Wani on two slides in the carousel and uploaded it for a third time. This version was allowed to remain online.
The sequence raises the possibility that the use of Burhan Wani’s name itself may be restricted on Instagram in India — an apparent moderation measure that has not been publicly announced by either Meta or the Indian government.
A search for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram currently yields no results.
What makes the episode particularly striking is that Instagram never explicitly told Alt News why the post was being removed. The platform’s notifications stated that the action had been carried out “through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements” and cited India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.
The notification did not identify the specific legal requirement behind the action, the government order on the basis of which the post had been restricted, or the particular element of the post that had triggered the removal — a point that multiple users affected by the government-ordered censorship frenzy has flagged over the past weeks.
An Opaque Moderation System that Leaves Users Guessing
As for us, Alt News had to figure it out through trial and error. This raises the question — Why should a user have to go through this process to find out why their post has been restricted? If a particular name, word or image is prohibited under a legal order, why does the notification not clearly state so? A user should not have to repeatedly alter and repost content, guessing what may have triggered a platform’s moderation system.
The opacity is particularly concerning because the platform appears to know what triggered the restriction. Its automated system identified the content and removed it within minutes, yet the user is given no meaningful explanation for the action. Instead, the notification offers only a generic reference to an automated system and “legal requirements”.
Besides, a blanket restriction on a name such as “Burhan Wani” makes little sense because names can occur in entirely unrelated contexts. Other people may share the same name, while legitimate references, including news reports, historical discussions or fact checks, could be caught by the same restriction.
Alt News emailed Meta spokespersons asking when the apparent moderation rule relating to Burhan Wani was implemented, why it was enforced without public notification, why users were not clearly informed about the reason for the restriction, and what other names or keywords may be subject to similar restrictions. The company has not responded.
Interestingly, we found that a similar restriction may be in place for ‘Monu Manesar’ was well. A search with these terms throws up the same response. Mohit Yadav alias Monu Manesar, a controversial ‘gau rakshak’ associated with the Bajrang Dal, has been accused in several cases linked to vigilantism and communal violence. He was arrested in 2023 in connection with the alleged abduction and murder of Nasir and Junaid, two Muslim men from Haryana. He has denied the allegations against him.
The apparent restriction comes amid a wider and increasingly opaque censorship controversy surrounding Instagram in India. A recent investigation by The Indian Express found that from March to July 2026, the government sent 1.95 lakh blocking orders to Meta, or one every minute on an average. Over 1 lakh of these were for Instagram.
The Burhan Wani episode illustrates another dimension of this opacity. If the name is itself subject to an undisclosed moderation rule, users have no way of knowing this in advance, or of understanding why content that merely mentions him is being restricted.
And even though the sequence strongly suggests that the references to Burhan Wani triggered the removals, this remains an inference. Instagram has not confirmed that this was the reason.
Fact-Check Posts Restricted
Posts related to an Alt News fact check were restricted in July 2026 on both Faecebook and Instagram.
The report looked at false claims about an old video that showed armed Nihangs clashing with police and breaching barricades. It was being circulated as ‘Khalistanis’ joining the Cockroach Janta Party protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar. In reality, the video was from June 25, 2026, nearly a month before the CJP protests, and showed Nihangs from Punjab marching toward Uttarakhand during a protest. The story can be read here.
Our social media posts on the fact check were restricted in India by both the platforms. And we do not know why.
Readers should note that a click on the ‘How we made this decision’ tab does not bring about any clarity. The response only states, “We are legally required to restrict access to your post in certain locations. We have taken this action based on a local legal requirement.”

With both sides of the aisle keeping an eye toward the 2028 presidential election, Hunter Biden isn’t even flirting with the idea of running.
On Friday, the son of President Joe Biden joked on Real Time with Bill Maher that if he ever launches a campaign, it’s probably because he relapsed, having previously been open about his struggles with addiction.
“No, I haven’t [thought of running],” Biden told Maher. “Here’s my thing; if I announce for president, then somebody should check and see if I relapsed.”
After celebrating seven years of sobriety in June, Biden explained, “My own reason for being out there as much as I am, at least from my perspective, [the media] built this platform to beat the hell out of me for about a seven-year period of time. And when the crowd went home, the platform was still there.
“There’s 50 million Americans that are still sick and suffering every day from addiction, and I get to go out there, and I get to speak to them,” he continued. “Even if it’s one person that sends me a message any day, that says, ‘I saw your message, and I didn’t drink today,’ then I’ve done something that I think is incredibly worthy.”

Having long been open about his struggles with addiction, Biden came under intense public scrutiny in 2020 when the New York Post obtained his personal laptop, which contained images and footage of him abusing illegal drugs.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has notified the ₹62,500 Cr Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) to expand domestic production, deepen local value addition, and support Indian-owned mobile phone brands. The notification comes more than a month after the Union Cabinet approved the scheme on July 15. The five-year programme will run from FY27 through FY31 and succeeds the PLI scheme for large-scale electronics manufacturing (LSEM) , whose tenure ended on March 31, 2026. Under MPMS, the government will offer differentiated incentives ranging from 2.25% to 5% to eligible mobile phone manufacturers and electronics manufacturing services (EMS) providers. Indian brands will be eligible for an incentive of 5%, along with an additional 3% for Indian design and R&D. They will also receive non-fiscal support under the scheme. Companies across both segments can claim an additional incentive of up to 1.5% for sourcing specified components and sub-assemblies domestically. To qualify, localised components must be used in at least 25% of the total mobile phone units manufactured by the applicant during a financial year. MPMS has two target segments: one aimed at expanding mobile phone manufacturing and the other at supporting Indian mobile phone brands. Under the manufacturing segment, applicants must be registered in India and have recorded a minimum turnover of ₹10,000 Cr in FY26. Existing brands will need to generate incremental annual sales of at least ₹5,000 Cr over their FY26 base. A new brand will become eligible after achieving annual sales of ₹10,000 Cr in India and will subsequently have to meet the ₹5,000 Cr annual incremental sales threshold. Under the Indian-brand segment, applicants must have recorded a minimum turnover of ₹1,000 Cr in FY26. Eligible companies may also be granted a gestation period of one year. To qualify as an Indian brand, a company must be registered or incorporated in India, hold its intellectual property and trademarks in the country, and have management control vested with Indian citizens. More than 51% of its shareholding must also be held by Indian citizens, while its design and R&D capabilities must be located in India. Union electronics and IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the government would closely evaluate applicants to ensure that their brands, designs, and intellectual property are genuinely Indian-owned. He added that India could see its first strong indigenous mobile phone brand by mid-2027. The government expects MPMS to drive cumulative mobile phone production of about ₹39 Lakh Cr during its five-year tenure, significantly increase exports, and generate around 60,000 direct jobs. India's Mobile Manufacturing Push The scheme comes as India seeks to move beyond assembling mobile phones and increase domestic value addition across the supply chain. According to MeitY, India is now the world's second-largest mobile phone manufacturer by volume, with 99.2% of mobile phones used in the country being made domestically. Smartphones also emerged as India's largest exported product category in 2025. Companies ranging from Apple and Samsung to Google and Nothing have made India one of their manufacturing hubs. Mobile phone production rose from ₹18,900 Cr in FY15 to ₹6.27 Lakh Cr in FY26, while exports jumped from ₹1,566 Cr to ₹2.60 Lakh Cr during the same period. The government said the growth was driven largely by the PLI-LSEM scheme, which helped establish India as a major mobile manufacturing and export hub.

Sword attack at school in Sweden leaves one person dead and two others injured
Hundreds of students were attending classes at the school when an 18-year-old with a sword attacked multiple people, police say
An 18-year-old with a sword attacked a school in central Sweden Friday, killing one person and seriously injuring two others, according to police.
The suspect in the attack at the school in the central town of Fagersta has been arrested, Police Chief Tommy Alriksson said at a news conference. He was wearing a helmet during the attack, SVT reported.
Shots were fired during the arrest, according to the TT news agency. Police found one victim dead as they entered the school to secure the premises.
The attack took place at the Brinell School in the city of Fagersta, northwest of the capital, Stockholm, while classes were in session for about 400 to 500 students, officials said.
There was no immediate word on the attacker's possible motive.
“We have no reason at this time to believe that there are multiple perpetrators,” said Alriksson, adding that an investigation was continuing.
Police spokesperson Pelle Vamstad, quoted by the TT news agency, said an alarm was received in the early afternoon Friday and that police rushed to the scene. He said officers would check any available camera footage for their investigation.
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, in a post earlier on the X social media platform, lamented the violence in Fagersta “right after the summer break.”
“We do not yet know what lies behind the act, but we know that the police are working very intensively,” he added. “Our thoughts are with all those affected.”
The Fagersta city government said it set up a crisis center in a sports hall near the school. The Vastmanland county government said “many people” were affected and that police, fire services, and healthcare workers were among those caring for them.
Several nearby schools had been locked down following the incident, and roadblocks were set up, authorities said.
Sweden suffered another school attack in February last year in Orebro, also in central Sweden, where a gunman killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself. That was the worst mass shooting in Swedish history.

As Trump courts Kim, Pyongyang ups price while Seoul fears being sidelined
SEOUL - North Korea rebuffed President Trump's apparent bid to reengage with Pyongyang diplomatically this week, issuing rhetorical salvos aimed at Trump's last-minute orders to shorten U.S.- South Korea joint military exercises.
To reinforce its point, the North followed up later in the day with a barrage of about a dozen short-range ballistic missiles launched from around the capital Pyongyang eastward toward the sea, according to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff.
The U.S. and South Korean militaries wrapped up their annual drills six days earlier than initially scheduled on Friday in a conciliatory gesture toward North Korea, though the North suggested the step isn't enough to convince it to return to talks.
In a statement carried by state media, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong said Pyongyang regards the scaling back of the annual exercises as "unworthy of comment," nor does it change, she added, the drills' "provocative and offensive" nature.
President Trump posted on social media on Monday that he had ordered the drills shortened because he thinks they are costly and send a hostile message to North Korea. He later said that he has reached out to Kim for a meeting and received a positive response.
Pyongyang 'raises the price' of reengagement
Kim Yo Jong, however, dismissed what appeared to be Trump's latest overture. Responding to Trump's claim that he had been in contact with her brother, Kim said, "I am not aware of it at all."
But she acknowledged that while U.S. policies towards North Korea remain hostile, "the relationship between the two leaders is still excellent."
The implication of Kim's sister's message is that she is "raising the price of re-engagement, rather than closing the door to a summit" between Trump and her brother, says Kuyoun Chung, a political scientist at Kangwon National University.
Since Trump's return to the White House last year, Pyongyang has repeatedly demanded recognition of its nuclear power status as a condition for resuming diplomacy. Washington has so far been unwilling to do so, because it would negate its long-standing policy of seeking the North's denuclearization, as well as U.N. Security Council resolutions.
As North Korea's nuclear programs have advanced, pressure on them to denuclearize has weakened. Seoul's policy is shifting from demanding denuclearization to seeking arms control, and calls in Washington for a similar approach have gained traction.
While Kim may see little point in meeting Trump, "it is entirely possible, in my view, that there could be a pro forma meeting, in which the two sides shake hands, sit down, have a nice chat, agree to discuss again," and go home, says Joseph Yun, who stepped down as acting ambassador to South Korea last October.
South Korea fears being sidelined again
During the first Trump administration, South Korean mediation paved the way for three Trump-Kim summits in 2018 and 2019. After the last summit failed to produce a deal, Kim bitterly accused Trump of playing him for an "idiot."
That led to a landmark shift in North Korea's foreign policy, which has strengthened Kim's position. In 2023, North Korea formally abandoned the goal of reunifying with South Korea. Kim also signed a mutual defense pact with Russia, and revived ties with China, all but ruling out any role for South Korea as mediator.
Officially, South Korea said it hoped Trump's outreach would lead to renewed diplomatic engagement with North Korea.
But South Koreans have been shocked by this week's events, which have heightened their fears of being sidelined during a Trump-Kim summit. They fear that in order to seal a deal with Kim, Trump could withdraw U.S. troops from South Korea and lift economic sanctions on the North, while leaving their nuclear arms in place.
"The United States would simply reap the diplomatic benefits of the summit," Kuyoun Chung says, "while South Korea bears all the security consequences of the concessions to North Korea."
This week, South Korea sought China's help with North Korea. Visiting Foreign Minister Wang Yi pledged that China would continue to promote "peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula."
But asked whether China could help broker a summit between the U.S. and North Korea, Wang said the two countries should handle that themselves, and the U.S. should drop its hostile policies towards the North.
Transactional approach risks 'eroding political trust'
Trump's curtailing the military drills has fueled South Korea's unease about the future of the alliance with the U.S.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told lawmakers on Wednesday he'd do his best "to make sure the South Korea-U.S. alliance does not weaken" as the U.S. pursues dialogue with Pyongyang. Cho admitted that Seoul was caught off guard by Trump's orders.
But for Trump, Seoul has fallen short on his demands. In the same social media post on Monday, Trump also complained that South Korea had declined his request to join the U.S. in its operations against Iran.
Cho Hyun said Wednesday that Trump's order to shorten drills was intended in part to pressure South Korea to speed up its investment of $350 billion in the U.S., in exchange for lower tariffs.
The administrations of President Trump and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung "actually share several broad objectives," notes Yu Jihoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defense Analyses, a government think tank. They include restarting diplomacy with North Korea and increasing South Korea's responsibility for defending itself.
Where they differ is Trump's transactional approach.
"If South Koreans begin to believe that security commitments or military exercises can be used as leverage over unrelated issues such as Iran, investment, trade, or broader foreign policy disagreements," Yu says, "confidence in Washington's reliability could weaken."
Yu does not believe the South Korea-U.S. alliance is about to implode right away. "The greater risk is the gradual erosion of political trust," he says.
That erosion appears to be well under way. In a recent poll by the Joongang Daily newspaper and the East Asia Institute, 45.4% of respondents see the U.S. as a trustworthy partner, while 46% see it as untrustworthy.
And of the 43.6% of respondents who have a negative impression of the U.S., three quarters attribute it to what they see as the U.S.'s coercive behavior towards allies on issues including trade, investment and defense.

A leading US distributor of China’s most popular humanoid robots and robot dogs now plans to produce its own robots at a facility on Long Island, New York. The business pivot comes amid the US government’s growing crackdown on foreign-made robots.
The company RoboStore had previously become the main North American distributor for humanoid robots and quadruped robots from Unitree Robotics, a Chinese robotics company that produces some of the most affordable and popular humanoid robot models. Universities such as Harvard and MIT, along with tech companies like Amazon and Nvidia, purchased such robots made in China through RoboStore for their own research and development purposes.
“We’ve sold over 1,500 robots and deployed them and worked with customers like Cisco, OpenAI, Nvidia, and over 150 universities,” Teddy Haggerty, founder and CEO of RoboStore, told Ars.
But on August 10, RoboStore announced a major shift in its business strategy with plans to fully open a 66,000-square-foot facility for manufacturing commercial robots by the first fiscal quarter of 2027. It also launched a new company called Robo Inc. to oversee the new robotics manufacturing and systems integration business.
Making the pivot
Haggerty and his team had already started thinking about the possibility of starting up their own robotics manufacturing business about a year ago. While supporting customers’ deployment and integration requests, they had gained insights into how customers were thinking about using robots for specific applications.
They also believed they could help more companies integrate industry-specific robots in ways that made sense for their businesses, rather than simply trying one of the many humanoid robots being pitched as a general-purpose solution for everything.
“Companies like Standard Bots and Universal Robots have a robotic arm for specific use cases,” Haggerty told Ars. “And I will tell anyone that that product is better suited for most businesses, for what they want to achieve, than a humanoid robot.”

Joachim Trier’s Oscar winner “Sentimental Value” became this year’s biggest Amanda Awards winner, taking home eight statuettes, including the top prize for best Norwegian film.
Trier was also awarded for directing, as well as his screenplay written with longtime collaborator Eskil Vogt.
“There’s a lot of stuff going on when you make and release films, and we both like to go back to that safe space and rediscover that calm where it’s just our two voices. We are fortunate enough that our films generate more and more noise that we have to shut out, so when we work, we make it personal and small again,” they told Variety back in January.
“When I write alone, I procrastinate. When I’m procrastinating with Joachim, even if I haven’t done anything, at least I got to spend a day with my friend,” said Vogt, with Trier adding: “Eskil is my longest relationship outside of my parents. We don’t need to be silly romantic about it, but we have to be honest: it’s a real gift.”
Popular on Variety
Paul Thomas Anderson’s hit “One Battle After Another” tok home the Amanda For best foreign film.
On the acting front, Pia Tjelta scored her second Amanda – this time for her performance in “Don’t Call Me Mama.” Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas won for “Sentimental Value,” while Anna Drakopoulou Sverrisdóttir was named Newcomer of the Year for “Brightly Shining.”
“The Battle of Oslo” – last year’s opening film at the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund – won the People’s Amanda.
It depicts the sinking of German cruiser Blücher, under the leadership of Colonel Birger Eriksen, and “is one of the most famous events in our history. Some people are calling it the single most important event during the WWII in Norway,” said director Daniel Fahre.
“We kept it quite accurate, also because it’s such a thrilling story. But we had to look for its emotional side, because there’s no mention of that in military reports. I am sure Colonel Eriksen had doubts, that he was afraid. But nobody wrote about it. I wanted to follow the facts and see what was hiding behind them.”
The Amanda Committee’s Honorary Award went to Per Christian Ellefsen, known for “Elling” and called by the jurors “one of Norway’s most beloved actors.”
“The first film about Elling was released in 2001, meaning it celebrates its 25th anniversary this year, and Per Christian Ellefsen was nominated for an Amanda Award for the title role in the first film,” they recalled, saying that “few characters in Norwegian cinema have been as beloved.”
“While he struggles through three successful films, Per Christian Ellefsen certainly masters the role of Elling to perfection,” they said.
Finally, the Amanda Committee’s Golden Clapper went to casting directirs Mette Holme Nielsen and Jannecke Bervell for their contributions to Norwegian film over more than 30 years.
“Casting is one of the most crucial elements in film and TV production, yet it is also one of the most underrated. It is in the casting process that the script meets the actors, and this is where the foundation for credibility, chemistry, and cohesion is laid,” argued the jury.
“A good casting can elevate an entire production, while poor casting can bring a film down. Casting also plays an important role in promoting diversity, by opening the doors to new voices, new expressions and a broader range of people on screen. It is therefore a profession that requires instinct, an understanding of people, experience and the ability to see potential where others may not.”
Mette Holme Nielsen is known for “Kitchen Stories” and “Utøya July 22,” which earned her a nomination for the International Casting Director Award. Jannecke Bervell worked on “Elling,” “Kon-Tiki” or “The Quake.”

Writer Lauren J. Salkin has accused Taylor Sheridan of stealing his marquee series “Yellowstone” from her 2016 pitch in a lawsuit filed on Friday. 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment are also listed as defendants.
Reps for Sheridan, 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.
In the court documents, obtained by Variety, Salkin alleges that she pitched her own sprawling Western drama, “Sovereign Nation,” to Sheridan’s management company, Elevate Entertainment, in 2016, only to be told: “Taylor thanks you very much for your interest. Unfortunately, he’s unavailable for TV projects.” The suit then claims that “Yellowstone” was greenlit at Paramount “within months” of her rejection.
“Sheridan, however, was not ‘unavailable for TV projects,’” the suit reads, “Instead, he and others used Salkin’s copyrighted works to develop Yellowstone. On June 20, 2018, Paramount Network aired its first episode.”
Popular on Variety
The lawsuit lists several “specific expressive choices” that “Yellowstone” allegedly lifted from Salkin’s “Sovereign Nation.” Those elements, the suit states, include “a tribal casino functioning as the institutional center of political and development power; a signature confrontation staged in the tribal chairman’s casino office over expansion beyond reservation boundaries; the use of trust land, the absence of zoning restrictions, and a 99-year lease structure as the concrete mechanism for that expansion; and recurring master-plan imagery deployed to dramatize the struggle for territorial control.”
Salkin’s lawyers also claim that she “proposed” Danny Huston and Gil Birmingham for “Sovereign Nation” in her pitch deck. Both were later cast in “Yellowstone” and played “materially parallel structural roles: Birmingham as the tribal political leader whose authority and development strategy run through the casino, and Huston as the outside development power broker who supplies the political or commercial path for that expansion.”
The suit later states, “When the works are objectively compared, the same coordinated design repeatedly appears: casino-centered institutions organize political power; the same unusual land-development mechanisms propel the conflict; parallel scenes perform the same dramatic functions; and the same actors appear in materially parallel roles. These are not merely convergences of a shared genre. Taken together with access and timing, they support a strong inference of copying.”

You can't buy anything on these food delivery and shopping sites. Here's why that's the point
Simulated shopping sites offer the thrill of buying without spending a cent
The cart is full. The items have been picked. The checkout button is waiting. You click “place order” — and then nothing happens.
There’s no delivery driver on the way. No charge to your credit card. No package waiting at your door. And that’s the point.
A new wave of mock shopping websites is giving people the thrill of shopping without the bill, as younger, budget-conscious consumers look to curb compulsive spending.
The trend first took off in South Korea, where some turned to simulated shopping sites to recreate the satisfaction of making a purchase without the financial hit, amid high living costs and a culture of consumerism.
Now, the idea is spreading globally. Whether it’s "buying" everyday essentials, adding clothes to a virtual cart or pretending to order a meal, sites such as DopamineCart, FakeEats, DopaHaul and FakeHaul are recreating the familiar rituals of online shopping without anything ever being delivered.
One example is FoodNeverComes, a fake food-delivery site launched in late June that has attracted around 92,000 active users over the last 90 days, according to the site's co-creator Anshul Sharma. They can fill their carts with meals and drinks, go through a mock checkout and follow their order being processed on a virtual map as it’s being “delivered.”
Sharma and his co-creator Purvansh Parmar, both based in Udaipur, India, say the self-funded, ad-free site has recorded about 1.1 million interactions.
The U.S. is its largest user base, says Sharma, followed by China, the U.K. and Vietnam, with Canada coming in third or fourth.
For Parmar, the project hits close to home. He says he struggled with excessive food-delivery orders himself, spending up to 20,000 rupees ($200.70) a week before realizing he had fallen into a cycle of compulsive spending for the convenience.
"I guess it was so easy, you just 'click-click-click,' get the food," he said. "You think you like the food, but in the end, it isn't actually the reason.”
To help users break the habit of online shopping, the duo also shares recipes to encourage people to cook at home instead of ordering in.
The psychology behind the cart
Rhia Catapano, an assistant professor at the University of Toronto who studies consumer behaviour and psychology, says online shopping simulators can activate “the same parts of our brain that doing the actual activity would.”
That's particularly appealing for budget-conscious young people.
“Like playing a video game or dreaming about a vacation that you're never actually going to take, we can imagine a thing,” she said. “In some way, it gives us some of the same psychological benefits.”
But whether the sites are truly helpful depends on why someone is using them, says Catapano.
They may be useful for someone trying to replace purchases they can't afford or don't really want, but not if they’re used to escape negative emotions.
Ajay Shrestha, a professor at Vancouver Island University who studies internet safety and young people, says people should also be vigilant about entering their personal information into the sites.
“When something is humorous, entertaining, gamified or deliberately made to feel consequence-free, people can naturally lower their guard."
Shopping without the environmental cost
The Imaginair store launched online at the end of March offers everything from clothes and footwear to accessories. Users can browse, add items to their carts and go through a mock checkout.
But woven into the familiar experience are environmental messages, like a pair of sweatpants described as “Protect the planet, in comfort," and a leather belt with a description "To reduce consumption, just tighten your belt."
Yves Gauthier, operations and mobilization manager at Earth Day Canada, says the site is intended to raise awareness about the environmental impact of online shopping, for an Earth Day campaign.
Indicative of how deeply consumerism has taken hold, the campaign proved popular, attracting about 30,000 visitors, with roughly 7,000 people spending "more than a minute going around the pages clicking on things." About half of those users, he says, went on to complete the mock purchase process.
Gauthier says platforms like Temu, Amazon and Shein have made it easier than ever to buy almost anything at the touch of a screen, fuelling a culture of overconsumption.
The site, he says, draws attention to the environmental costs of mass production, excessive packaging and transportation-related pollution, while encouraging users to pause before buying something new.
Users are prompted to consider alternatives such as shopping second-hand, exchanging goods with neighbours or repairing things they already own.
If everyone in the world consumed like the average Canadian, according to the Global Footprint Network, we would need the equivalent of 4.49 Earths to sustain that level of consumption.
A way out of the cycle?
The sudden popularity of these sites, says Catapano, shows just how deeply consumerism has become integrated into our everyday lives, with people willing to spend time and effort browsing and “shopping” even when they know nothing will ever arrive.
But she sees a glimmer of resistance, too.
Some people, she says, are realizing through these sites that their shopping habits aren’t serving them — and are looking for ways to consume less and make more intentional choices.
“They recognize that what they're doing is not good for them, so they're trying to make changes.”

In FocusAs natural disasters rage, does China’s ‘top-down’ climate model provide a way forward?
As Beijing enacts a state-led approach to climate adaptation, Washington leans on the private sector and Brussels tries to chart a middle way
A punishing drought is draining Europe’s great rivers, pushing the Loire, the Danube and the Rhine towards record lows. At the Kaub gauging station, the reference point for shipping on the Rhine – Germany’s economic artery – the water level fell to 17cm (6.7 inches) this month, a low unseen since measurements began in 1880.
But this is not a story unique to any one continent or hemisphere. In recent weeks, smoke from intensified Canadian wildfires drifted down the American east coast, leaving New Yorkers struggling to breathe, while China has battled a prolonged heatwave and persistent floods while bracing for what could be the strongest El Nino cycle in the past 150 years.
“Compared with the Western system, China’s greatest advantage in these areas is its very strong capacity for top-down implementation. That is the root of all of this,” said Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow in the Environment and Society Centre at Chatham House.
Governments everywhere face the same three challenges on climate adaptation, according to Guo.

Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav on Saturday said his party would not break alliances, asserting that its fight was against the Bharatiya Janata Party, which he accused of pursuing policies benefiting big business groups.
Addressing presspersons at the party headquarters in Lucknow, Mr. Yadav said the SP had always honoured its commitments. “The Samajwadi Party never breaks alliances. When we agree to move forward with others, we stand by them,” he said.
He said the party’s objective is to form a government committed to social justice, based on socialist ideology and solidarity with the ‘PDA’ — ‘pichhda’ (backward classes), Dalits and ‘alpsankhyak’ (minorities).
His remarks came a day after Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said the SP’s definition of ‘PDA’ was constantly changing, referring to the party’s outreach to Brahmins.
Mr. Yadav also accused the State government of deliberately weakening primary education and shutting schools attended by children from disadvantaged communities.
He said an SP government would revive the model schools project initiated during its previous tenure and strengthen school infrastructure and midday meal kitchens.
Youth manifesto
The SP plans to release a separate youth manifesto for the upcoming Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, focusing on education, employability, skill development and digital learning.
Alok Ranjan, former Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary and a SP member, told The Hindu that the blueprint would propose model schools and colleges in districts, upgrading government inter-colleges, filling vacant sanctioned posts and introducing a time-bound recruitment calendar for teachers.
“It will also overhaul school and university education, with a focus on employability in changing times, besides establishing skill-development institutions and promoting digital learning,” Mr. Ranjan said.
The manifesto is also likely to propose an allowance for unemployed youth. Mr. Ranjan said the plan was “rooted in the SP’s socialist ideology”.
Mayawati seeks apology
Meanwhile, a political row erupted over Mr. Yadav’s recent remark that the SP had “turned 25 paise into a rupee” but was later abandoned by its alliance partners, an apparent reference to the Rashtriya Lok Dal (RLD).
Bahujan Samaj Party national president Mayawati on Saturday demanded an apology from Mr. Yadav to the RLD and the Jat community, saying the remark was “indecent” and “shameful” and had insulted the family of former Prime Minister Chaudhary Charan Singh.
RLD chief Jayant Chaudhary also criticised Mr. Yadav, saying the SP chief could have named him rather than making a reference to the Jat community. “Such behaviour only leads to downfall,” he stated in a post on X.
The remarks followed criticism by SP State president Shyam Lal Pal of an unnamed ally for abandoning the party despite its support. Mr. Yadav’s comment alluded to Mr. Chaudhary’s 2022 remark that he was not a “chavanni” who could be easily flipped.

Stomach pain is one of the most common symptoms people experience. It can range from mild discomfort caused by indigestion or gas, to severe pain caused by conditions such as appendicitis, gallstones, pancreatitis or intestinal obstruction.
Doctors say the site, severity, onset, duration and progression of the pain, along with other symptoms, can provide important clues about its cause. However, the intensity of pain alone does not always indicate how serious the underlying problem is.
“Some people with a serious condition may have only mild discomfort, while others with a less serious problem may experience severe pain,” says S. Jennie, professor, department of general Medicine, SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, Chennai.
Where it hurts
The location of abdominal pain can sometimes point to the organ involved. Burning or discomfort in the upper abdomen or lower chest may occur with acid-peptic disorders. Pain in the right upper abdomen, particularly after meals, can occur with gallbladder disease. Severe upper abdominal pain that radiates to the back may be seen in pancreatitis.
Pain that begins around the navel and later moves to the lower right side may occur with appendicitis. Pain in the lower abdomen or side may also occur with kidney stones.
However, these patterns are only clues and should not be used for self-diagnosis, says Arul Prakash, gastroenterologist, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai. “It is difficult to differentiate between a minor and major problem based only on pain,” he says.
Mild, short-lived pain that improves after passing stools or gas, resting or drinking fluids is generally less concerning. In contrast, sudden, severe, localised, persistent or progressively worsening pain should be assessed by a doctor.
Watch for warning signs
The symptoms accompanying abdominal pain often provide a better indication of urgency than the pain alone. Persistent vomiting can cause dehydration and may also occur with intestinal obstruction. Fever may suggest infection or inflammation.
Blood in vomit or stools should never be ignored. Black, tar-like stools or coffee-ground-like vomit can indicate bleeding in the digestive tract. Severe diarrhoea, particularly with high fever, severe pain or blood in stools, also requires medical assessment.
Increasing abdominal swelling, especially when accompanied by vomiting or an inability to pass stools or gas, can indicate bowel obstruction. Yellowing of the eyes or skin may point to a problem involving the liver, gallbladder or bile ducts.
The SHARP warning signs
Dr. Jennie suggests remembering the SHARP warning signs: sudden or severe pain; associated symptoms such as vomiting, fever, bleeding, jaundice or confusion; advanced age, particularly with chronic illnesses; rigidity or marked tenderness of the abdomen; and pain during pregnancy or after surgery.
Chest pain or difficulty breathing along with upper abdominal pain also warrants urgent assessment, as some heart conditions can mimic abdominal discomfort. Dr. Arul Prakash notes that patients have occasionally mistaken heart attack symptoms for acidity and treated themselves with over-the-counter medicines.
Avoid self-treatment
A common mistake is to assume that every episode of abdominal pain is due to ‘gas’ or acidity. Repeatedly taking medicines without establishing the cause can delay diagnosis.
Painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin can irritate the stomach and increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding in susceptible people. They should not be taken casually for unexplained abdominal pain.
An antacid may provide temporary relief for occasional, familiar acidity or heartburn. But symptoms that persist for several days, keep returning or become progressively worse need medical evaluation. Antibiotics should also not be started without medical advice, particularly for diarrhoea, as many common gastrointestinal infections are viral and do not require them.
Children, older adults and pregnant women need particular caution. Children may have difficulty describing their symptoms, while older adults can have serious abdominal conditions with relatively mild or atypical pain. During pregnancy, abdominal pain may have benign causes but can also indicate pregnancy-related or surgical emergencies.
People with previous abdominal surgery, gallstones, inflammatory bowel disease or chronic liver, kidney or other major illnesses should also seek medical advice sooner when they develop new or unusual pain.
Doctors say, is not to judge abdominal pain only by how much it hurts. A new, persistent or worsening pain, particularly when accompanied by warning signs, should not be dismissed as acidity or gas.
