A premium leather bar cabinet in an urban Indian home is more than just a piece of furniture. It reflects a growing shift in how consumers view products that are proudly made in India. For years, premium Indian leather mostly found its way into global brands, while the craftsmanship behind it rarely received the recognition it deserved. Vikash Gupta spent over 15 years on the other side of that story, running a B2B export business that supplied leather goods to international brands. While studying in the US, he also worked part-time at a leather store. It was there that he realised the real gap wasn't in the quality of Indian leather or the skill of its artisans, but in who got credit for the final product. That realisation pushed him to move away from the relatively predictable export business and build a consumer brand of his own. That idea took shape as Three Sixty in 2009, with the belief that handcrafted Indian leather could become a statement piece in modern homes. The opportunity has only grown since then. India's leather goods market touched $14 Bn in 2025 and is expected to reach $20.6 Bn by 2034, driven by rising incomes and growing demand for premium products. The luxury leather segment, in particular, is seeing steady growth as more consumers are willing to spend on high-quality, design-led products. Three Sixty has built its business around balancing traditional craftsmanship with the demands of a modern D2C brand. Many of its artisans have worked with the company for over 25 years, while its "Scalable Craftsmanship" model aims to preserve hand-stitched and hand-finished techniques even as the brand expands across product categories and into Tier II cities such as Bhopal and Patna. Its design philosophy, which blends global aesthetics with Indian leather-craft techniques such as hand-weaving and edge colouring, has also led to collaborations with brands such as Raymond's, BMW, House of Glenfiddich, and Kapil Dev. More than brand partnerships, these collaborations reflect a shared effort to showcase Indian craftsmanship on a larger stage. In a conversation with Inc42, Three Sixty founder Vikash Gupta spoke about his journey from B2B exports to building a premium D2C brand, the thinking behind the brand philosophy of "Live the Leather Life", and his vision of making Three Sixty a global ambassador for Indian leather. Here are the edited excerpts from the conversation... Inc42: You spent 16 years in the predictable B2B exports (Ranvik Exports) segment before launching Three Sixty in 2009. What was the exact operational trigger that made you switch from B2B margins to D2C brand risk? Vikash Gupta: The operational transition was rooted in a personal realisation. While living in the US and working in a leather store to pay for my tuition, I saw premium Indian products selling successfully under international brand names, but with the 'India story' completely erased. That was the trigger. I realised I didn't want to just be an invisible supplier; I wanted to be the architect of a global identity. Moving from B2B to D2C was about reclaiming our narrative and proving that an Indian brand could define luxury on its own terms. Inc42: Premium leather furniture and bar decor is an incredibly niche space in India. What market gap convinced you this could scale, and how do you reconcile the slow rhythm of luxury craftsmanship with the fast-scale demands of a D2C business? Vikash Gupta: The data point is behavioural: we are witnessing the premiumisation of the Indian home. As disposable incomes rise, the Indian consumer is shifting from mass-produced trends to ‘conversation pieces’, products that signify personal taste and heritage. Home entertainment has become the centre of modern social life, and we identified a significant gap for high-quality, leather-centric bar and lifestyle accessories that serve as the anchor for these experiences. We aren't just selling a cabinet; we are selling the setting for the best conversations. As for reconciling craftsmanship with scale, in an era of disposable, fast furniture, our commitment to slow, deliberate craftsmanship is actually our greatest competitive advantage. We don't reconcile these models by compromising on speed; we reconcile them by doubling down on 'Scalable Craftsmanship.' We have built a robust design and supply chain architecture that allows us to maintain the integrity of artisanal skill while scaling our output. We aren't competing for the consumer who wants a quick fix; we are building for the customer who wants a legacy piece. Inc42: How would you describe the 'Live the Leather Life' philosophy, and how does it reflect your own values? Vikash Gupta: 'Live the Leather Life' is about authenticity in an age of imitation. Leather is a character-driven, living material that ages with grace, a concept often lost in a market saturated with synthetic alternatives. Our philosophy is an invitation to educate: we want our customers to understand the difference between disposability and longevity. By organising this industry, we aren't just selling products; we are honouring the resource, the artisan, and the consumer's desire for something real. Inc42: Three Sixty operates in a fairly niche category with products like handcrafted leather furniture, bars, décor and travel accessories. How and when did you realise that this could be a category to build in? Vikash Gupta: My years as a global supply chain partner gave me a unique vantage point: I saw that global brands were building lifestyle ecosystems around leather, not just selling standalone items. I realised that the Indian domestic market was ready for a brand that treated leather not just as a material, but as the centrepiece of home experience. When you see your product being the stage for friendships and celebrations, you realise you aren't just in the furniture business; you are in the experience business. Operating in this supply chain also taught me that the true luxury of leather lies in its longevity and how it evolves with the owner. Unlike mass-produced materials that deteriorate over time, high-quality, handcrafted leather develops a beautiful patina, absorbing the history and character of the home it lives in. By focusing on bespoke bars, tailored decor, and specialised travel accessories, we discovered that our niche wasn't defined by a lack of demand, but by a demand for deeper meaning. Today's conscious consumers aren’t looking for transient trends; they want to invest in enduring, artisanal pieces that carry a distinct soul and tell a story across generations. Inc42: How central is Indian craftsmanship and artisanal skill to the brand's identity, and how do you work with your artisan community? Vikash Gupta: Craftsmanship is the soul of Three Sixty. We have artisans who have been with us for over 25 years; their hands are our institutional memory. For us, ethics isn't a checklist; it's a culture. We prioritise the welfare of our artisans, from banking and financial inclusion to educational support for their children. When I am on the shop floor with them, I'm not just managing production; I am working with the partners who make our India Story possible. Inc42: Tell us more about the design philosophy. How do you balance global design trends with Indian leather craftsmanship? Vikash Gupta: We have a strong in-house design team comprising graduates from NID and NIFT who develop every collection from the ground up. We treat our design division as a research lab. We don't copy; we curate. Our process involves blending global design inspiration with traditional Indian leather techniques, and we encourage our team to travel and collaborate with international designers, bringing those learnings back to the shop floor. The magic happens when the global aesthetic meets the raw, tactile skill of our Indian craftsmen; that synthesis is where every Three Sixty piece is born. This balance is achieved by respecting the strengths of both worlds: global design brings structural discipline, sleek silhouettes, and contemporary functionality, while our local artisans bring soul, texture, and centuries of hand-stitching heritage. We might take a minimalist, mid-century modern frame inspired by European trends and elevate it using intricate traditional Indian hand-weaving or specialised edge-colouring techniques passed down through generations. By treating leather not just as a covering but as a living canvas, our designs tell a story of global sophistication rooted in authentic Indian craftsmanship, ensuring each piece feels at home in a modern metropolitan setting anywhere in the world while retaining its distinct artisanal identity. Inc42: Tell us about the brand's approach to sustainability. Why handcrafted and long-lasting pieces over mass-produced ones? Vikash Gupta: True sustainability is about durability. We have consciously moved away from the fast-fashion mentality that has encroached on the furniture industry. Leather is, by nature, a circular, biodegradable byproduct of the food industry. When handled with expert craftsmanship, it becomes an heirloom meant to be passed down through generations. By focusing on products that last, we are actively reducing the need for constant, wasteful replacements. We are building for longevity, not just for the season. Inc42: Collaborations with Raymond's Chairman's Collection, BMW, House of Glenfiddich and Kapil Dev are notable. How do these partnerships come about, and what do they add to the brand? Vikash Gupta: These partnerships are strategic manifestations of the India Story. Whether it's collaborating with Kapil Dev on his iconic cricket milestones or working with William Grant & Sons for the first time in their 130-year history outside of the liquor industry, these brands choose us because we share a commitment to legacy. We don't look for transactional partnerships; we look for brands that want to co-author a story of excellence and Indian pride. These alliances elevate purpose; they validate handcrafted leather as a premium medium for storytelling. When we designed the limited-edition, signed portable bars celebrating Kapil Dev's legendary 175* knock, or curated immersive interior statements with the House of Glenfiddich, we weren't just creating products; we were designing collectables. Looking ahead, we are exploring deep, multisensory collaborations with visionary creators and luxury lifestyle brands that push the boundaries of where artisanal leather can be found, creating bespoke experiential touchpoints that celebrate design innovation and authentic Indian heritage on both domestic and global stages. Inc42: How would you describe the culture within Three Sixty, especially leadership's relationship with employees and artisans? Vikash Gupta: We are one big family. In a high-growth environment, maintaining an open, human-centric culture is paramount. My leadership style is built on proximity; I believe in spending time on the shop floor because that is where the brand is actually made. When leadership respects the artisans as the true creators, the entire organisation aligns behind the vision of building a global Indian brand. This mutual respect is what transforms our workshop from a production unit into a thriving community. We place a strong emphasis on dignity of labour and continuous upskilling, ensuring our artisans see themselves not just as workers, but as specialised custodians of a rare craft. By bridging the gap between corporate strategy and the shop floor, we create a workplace where a master craftsman's generational knowledge is valued just as highly as a design graduate's fresh perspective. When our team sees that their individual artistry is directly responsible for putting Indian luxury on the global map, it breeds a deep sense of shared ownership and pride that traditional corporate incentives simply cannot replicate. Inc42: Three Sixty has expanded into cities such as Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, Bhopal, and Patna. What's driving this Tier II expansion strategy? Vikash Gupta: The aspiration in Tier II India is palpable. We are seeing a significant shift where consumers in these cities are demanding the same world-class design and quality as metro dwellers, but with their own distinct preferences. We aren't just expanding footprints; we are tapping into the next wave of Indian luxury. The future of the India Story is being written in these cities, and we intend to be right there as the preferred lifestyle partner. Inc42: What does becoming a 'complete lifestyle ecosystem' mean for Three Sixty's future, and where do you see the brand on the global stage in the next five to ten years? Vikash Gupta: Becoming a complete lifestyle ecosystem means moving from providing furniture to curating environments. We are looking beyond the product. We want to define the spaces in which our customers live, travel, and entertain. We are expanding our design language to ensure that from the moment you wake up to the moment you host a guest, Three Sixty Leather is the thread that ties your lifestyle together. On the global stage, the ambition is clear: ThreeSixty will be the primary global ambassador for Indian leather craftsmanship. My goal is for the brand to sit comfortably in the same conversation as the world's great luxury names, proving that 'Made in India' is synonymous with world-class design, ethical production, and timeless luxury. We are not just building a company; we are cementing India's place in the global luxury discourse.

The California sanctuary which has been caring for endangered singing gibbons for 50 years
The Gibbon Conservation Center, which has been running since 1976, is open for guided tours on the weekends
Between morning feedings, the gibbons break into loud song.
Their vocalizations — ranging from screeching and siren-like calls to guttural hoots and low grunts — echo across a sanctuary in the dry, hot hills of the Santa Clarita Valley, just north of Los Angeles.
Over the last 50 years, the Gibbon Conservation Center has grown from housing a modest assortment of animals into a globally recognized facility dedicated exclusively to gibbon welfare and care. Famed for their distinctive vocal calls, they are among the world's rarest and most critically endangered primates.
Currently, the facility cares for approximately 40 gibbons from five distinct species. Their singing can occasionally be heard up to a mile away by the few residents living on the sparsely populated outskirts of Santa Clarita.
The sanctuary was established by the late Alan Mootnick, a self-taught primatologist who became a prominent authority on gibbons while simultaneously operating a home painting and remodelling business.
He published research papers in academic journals, welcomed international researchers, and answered queries from fellow scientists regarding gibbon identification and care.
“Sometimes they would just send him a picture of a rescued gibbon asking what species, or they will play him a vocalization,” director Gabi Skollar said.
Skollar moved from Hungary to the U.S. in 2005 to learn from Mootnick and work at the center. She has carried on his mission since his sudden death from heart surgery complications in 2011.
Skollar, who had initially planned to leave the job to continue her education, said that she could not abandon the gibbons.
“We have to keep going and take care of this place,” she said.
Now, she lives on-site with another caretaker, waking up every morning to the cacophony of gibbons at sunrise. They are her children, she said.
Each gibbon has their own quirks
Having spent decades at the conservation centre, Skollar is intimately familiar with the distinct personalities of the gibbons residing there.
A young northern white-cheeked gibbon named Pepper regularly prompts the group to begin their singing sessions, which are brought to a close by a pileated gibbon named Violet and her partner Truman. Meanwhile, Pierre, a rescued gibbon, harbors a dislike of men.
The small apes vocalize three to four times every day, singing for 20 to 30 minutes at a time.
Skollar, who is researching gibbon vocalization for a doctorate at the University of California, Los Angeles, said: “There’s a lot of things that we can learn in a captive setting that can be shared with conservationists in the field and also with people working in sanctuaries rescuing gibbons.”
The primates face rising threats in their natural Southeast Asian tropical rainforest habitats, where deforestation continues to destroy their environment. The illicit wildlife trade poses a severe risk, as young gibbons are routinely taken from their parents to be sold as pets. Wild populations for some of the species cared for at the centre have dwindled to fewer than 2,000 apes.
Mootnick bought his first gibbon, Spanky, in 1976 after responding to a newspaper advert. Today, the population is maintained both through births at the site and exchanges with other facilities to safeguard genetic diversity in breeding programmes.
The center became the first to successfully breed the endangered Javan gibbon, a species native exclusively to Java in Indonesia, and is preparing to send a pair of northern white-cheeked gibbons to the Pittsburgh Zoo.
Caretakers connect with apes
On a recent morning, on-site caretaker Jodi Kleier was making the rounds with buckets of washed lettuce, steamed sweet potatoes and bananas. She handed a young gibbon, Rocky, a piece of chopped banana as he reached out through the fence.
Rocky was hand-reared by Kleier after being abandoned by his mother after birth at the center, which can happen with first-time mothers if they went through a difficult birth.
Kleier has worked at the center for a decade, and started out as a volunteer. She has a tattoo of Rocky on her thigh.
She fell in love with gibbons after coming to the center for a primatology course in school.
“I love watching any primates play, because I think they’re so natural to us, we kind of see ourselves in them,” she said.
Kleier and volunteers who come by during the week are constantly washing and cooking produce because they feed the gibbons five to six times a day to imitate the pace of their foraging behavior in the wild.
“The Javans, they’re my favorite species and the male Javan is singing … one of my favorite songs,” Kleier said of a ghostly vocalization. “In Javanese folklore, they’re known as these spirits that live in the forest because you can always hear them.”
Schools and tourists can visit
While the center is only open to visitors for guided tours on the weekends, they receive steady interest from schools, tourists and senior centers.
They also work with local organizations such as The Teaching Zoo at Moorpark College to help students receive hands-on experience in animal care. The college takes first-year students on a field trip to the Gibbon Conservation Center every year, and many have gone on to work there after they graduate.
“When I went out there for the first time in the 1990s, I didn’t know what a gibbon was,” said Mara Rodriguez, a development coordinator who's been with the zoo for decades. “Now I’ve raised four gibbons in my career.”
Anyone who visits “will leave with a lasting impression and begin to care about the species,” she said.
Skollar’s long-term goal is to raise more money to build larger enclosures for the gibbons and construct an education center for visitors. She hopes to continue honoring Mootnick’s legacy and dedicating her life to the gibbons — one of which is named after him.
“When he passed away, I just felt that he’s around and helping us keep this center going,” she said.

Amazon devices are the latest casualties of the memory shortage price hikes
Everything from the Echo to the Kindle is going up.
No company is immune to the continuing chip shortage and its effect on pricing, not even Amazon. As first spotted by Fortune, Amazon has increased prices across its Echo, Fire TV, Kindle and eero product lineups without any major announcement. The price hikes are as high as 60 percent in some cases and as expensive as $100 more in others.
The base model Echo Dot saw the highest percentage increase in price, going from $50 to $80, while other Echo products were equally hit with steep changes, like the Echo Show 21 that went from $400 to $500. On the less expensive side of products, the Fire TV Stick HD has been bumped up from $35 to $40, while the Fire TV Stick 4K Max also increased from $60 to $85. Amazon's popular e-readers have new price tags, with the 16GB model of the latest Kindle now costing $150, instead of $110, and the 16GB model of the Kindle Paperwhite now at $200, compared to its previous $160 price.
Amazon's mesh Wi-Fi product, eero, is also now more expensive with the eero 7 that comes with three devices now costing $400, instead of $350. The eero Pro 7 3-pack shot up from $700 to $800. As noted by Fortune, Amazon Ring products managed to avoid any price updates. An Amazon spokesperson confirmed the price increase to Fortune and attributed the changes to "significant increases in memory and storage component costs," adding that Amazon still wants to proviude products at accessible prices as well as offer promotions throughout the year.
Amazon is the latest tech giant forced to adjust prices thanks to the ongoing RAMaggeddon. Earlier this summer, Apple made the same decision to increase prices across its hardware products like iPads and MacBooks. For similar reasons, Roku raised prices across its devices up to $50 in July.

BERLIN — The German government expects it will need almost €12 billion — roughly $14 billion — to build a new arsenal of long-range weapons aimed at deterring Russia, according to defense ministry documents seen by POLITICO.
The weapons would give German forces the ability to hit military targets hundreds or even thousands of kilometers behind the front — including command centers, airfields, missile launchers, and supply hubs.
Internal documents call the effort a top priority for both Germany and NATO.
They say the goal is to allow German forces to strike "far into the rear area of an adversary" and maintain the ability to respond with conventional weapons "below the nuclear threshold."
The plan has four parts, with the first weapons due as early as next year and the most advanced systems planned for the middle of the next decade.
Internal ministry talking points say "almost €12 billion" in budget funds are expected to be needed for the buildup.
The money has not yet been approved. Another ministry document says the costs have been estimated and submitted as part of the government's budget planning process.
Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the figure or individual programs.
"The measures you refer to are generally subject to the approval of the German Bundestag," a ministry spokesperson told POLITICO. The ministry could only comment after parliament had considered them, the spokesperson added.
Missiles as soon as next year
The fastest part of the plan is a new low-cost cruise missile that Germany wants to start fielding in 2027.
POLITICO reported in June that the defense ministry was looking at missiles from US-Israeli startup Covenant Industries and Ukrainian-linked companies as it searched for weapons that could be bought in large numbers and put into service quickly.
The new documents show that effort has moved further.
Germany is in contract talks with two suppliers, with the aim of receiving missiles for qualification by the end of this year. The documents name three candidates: Covenant's Anthem, the BARS missile offered by an unnamed Ukrainian company, and Flamingo from Ukrainian company Fire Point.
Germany is already preparing framework contracts for later mass production.
The documents describe the low-cost missile as a "cost-efficient and, above all, mass-producible" weapon that can be used alongside much more expensive missiles.
That follows a lesson Berlin says it has drawn from the war in Ukraine.
When POLITICO first reported on the low-cost missile program in June, the defense ministry said strikes against important targets far behind enemy lines had become "indispensable for credible deterrence."
"Cost-effective systems can overwhelm enemy air defenses through mass attacks and are therefore of high operational value," the ministry said at the time.
The Tomahawk gap-filler
The next part of the plan is American.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Bundestag in early July that Germany had reached an agreement with the US government during the NATO summit in Ankara to acquire American Tomahawk cruise missiles and station them in Germany.
"We are closing an important strategic gap in our defense," Merz said, adding that Germany would develop its own European systems at the same time.
Germany's internal target, according to the documents, is to have an initial Typhon and Tomahawk capability by the end of the decade.
The purchase would give Berlin a proven long-range weapon while European alternatives are still being developed.
The final two parts of the plan are being developed with Britain.
Germany and the UK are working on a new high-end cruise missile and a hypersonic glide weapon, part of last year's Trinity House Agreement, with the documents showing a targeted initial capability by the middle of the next decade.
The two governments have already said publicly that their new long-range weapons should be able to reach targets more than 2,000 kilometers away.
The hypersonic project accounts for most of the money in Germany's current estimate.
One internal document puts nearly €9 billion toward development and procurement of the hypersonic weapon, plus €182 million for keeping it in service.
It lists another €1.8 billion for cruise missile development and procurement and €97 million for maintenance.
Those figures add up to just around €11 billion. Separate ministry talking points put the overall expected required funding at "almost €12 billion."
For Germany, the missile plan marks a major change.
Instead of waiting for one new European missile, Berlin wants several types of weapons: cheaper missiles that can be produced in large numbers, American Tomahawks available sooner, and more advanced European weapons later.
The buildup is taking place as German military leaders warn that Russia could be able to attack NATO territory by the end of the decade.
Berlin wants to make sure that if deterrence fails, Russian forces would not be safe simply because they are far behind the front.
Chris Lunday is a defense reporter in Germany at Politico Europe.

The President’s Focus
Panelists joined to discuss Trump’s priorities as the national debt reaches new highs.
The national debt reached $40 trillion this week, but the president’s attention seemed directed elsewhere. Last night on Washington Week With The Atlantic, panelists joined to discuss Donald Trump’s recent focuses, and more.
At a rally for Darline Graham in South Carolina last night, Trump opened the event and spoke about the White House ballroom, devoting several minutes to his project. “Not a day really goes by that he doesn’t talk about the ballroom or the Reflecting Pool or the Kennedy Center or the gold statues,” Matt Viser, a staff writer at The Atlantic, argued last night. “I just don’t know that it resonates as deeply with voters across the country.”
Although residents in Washington, D.C., are watching changes to their city unfold, it’s not one of the “pocketbook issues that I think the midterms are probably going to be about,” Viser added.
Joining the guest moderator Atlantic staff writer Vivian Salama to discuss this and more: Zolan Kanno-Youngs, a White House correspondent at The New York Times; Mary Louise Kelly, the host of All Things Considered on NPR; Michelle Price, a White House reporter at the Associated Press; Viser.

The story so far: Last week, the U.S. accused India of violating what it considers fair trade practices. The White House published a report titled ‘The Great Transhipment Scam’ in which it accused about 40 countries, including India, of helping China evade U.S. tariffs.
What is the Great Transhipment Scam?
Over the last nearly three decades, the U.S. and Chinese economies have become deeply intertwined, with the U.S. increasingly relying on China to be its manufacturing hub, and China relying on the U.S. as its market and for investment. This is a somewhat simplistic assessment of their engagement, but it is also the most relevant for the current context.
This relationship has resulted in the U.S. running huge trade deficits with China. That is, importing much more from the country than it exports to it. U.S. President Donald Trump has long spoken about his concerns about vast trade deficits; this is primarily why he insisted on levying tariffs on U.S. trade partners during his second term.
However, China began facing such actions during Mr. Trump’s first term itself. In 2018, the U.S. imposed tariffs ranging from 7.5% to 100% on goods from China such as electric vehicles, semiconductors, and medical products under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, for unfair trade and tech practices. As per the White House report, this resulted in a shrinking of the U.S.’s trade deficit with China in 2019 and 2020.
On July 24, 2026, the U.S. added a further 12.5% tariff for gaps in forced-labour compliance and the lack of comprehensive legal import prohibitions.
According to the report, since 2018, Chinese exporters have increasingly been routing goods through third countries to evade tariffs. “Products that previously moved directly from China to the United States were shipped through jurisdictions where limited assembly, finishing, repackaging, relabeling, or documentation changes could create the appearance of a different national origin,” the report stated.
What is India’s involvement?
The White House has identified more than 40 countries associated with “elevated illegal transhipment risk”, with India among the top “enablers” of China’s evasion of tariffs. The other countries/regions named as the top enablers are Mexico, Canada, the European Union, Japan, and South Korea.
The U.S. has alleged that these countries are importing Chinese goods, modifying them marginally, and exporting them to the U.S. at tariffs below what these goods would have faced had they directly been exported from China. This, the report said, has led to significant revenue loss for the U.S. government.
“The Office of Trade and Economic Analysis estimates that approximately $67 billion in U.S.-bound goods were transshipped from China through the top hubs — Mexico, India, and Vietnam — in 2025, producing an estimated $28 billion in lost tariff revenue,” the report said.
As an example, the report mentioned the Pune-Gujarat-Chennai production belt, saying that the region “absorbs” pumps and compressors from China, thereby affecting industrial supply chains in Cincinnati, Dayton, and Columbus in the U.S.
What does this mean for the U.S.?
Broadly, the report’s findings suggest that the U.S.’s tariff policy has failed to reduce U.S. imports and increase domestic production. While U.S. imports from China fell from $525.8 billion in 2017 to $327.5 billion in 2025, total U.S. imports from all countries rose sharply from $2.41 trillion to $3.50 trillion. In short, the U.S. replaced many Chinese finished goods with imports from other countries rather than with domestically produced goods.
As Ajay Srivastava, founder of the think tank Global Trade Research Initiative, said, “Mr. Trump’s tariffs changed the source of imports but failed to reduce America’s overall dependence on imported goods”.
What are the implications for India?
This is yet another way that the U.S. is finding fault with India’s trade policies. During his first term, Mr. Trump found fault with India’s tariffs on luxury motorcycles, after which India reduced them.
Last year, he blamed India for financing Russia’s war with Ukraine by importing Russian oil; his government hiked tariffs on imports from India to 50% as a penalty.
More recently, the U.S. Senate passed a Bill with Mr. Trump’s backing that would result in tariffs of up to 100% being levied on India for its Russian oil imports. The Bill is waiting to be introduced and passed in the House of Representatives.
Apart from this, the U.S. has also imposed a 10% tariff on imports from India as a penalty for not doing enough to curb the import of goods made using forced labour. Another investigation on excess capacity is ongoing, which could potentially see tariffs being hiked even further.
The latest allegations that India is helping China evade tariffs are not accompanied by penal actions yet, but that possibility remains. Mr. Trump could decide to impose further tariffs on countries he deems are helping China in this regard.
How could India’s economy be impacted?
For India, any penal action would be a blow to its growth story. Over the last few years, rather than predominantly importing Chinese finished goods, India has been importing raw materials and intermediate goods, using them to manufacture finished goods within the country, and then exporting them.
For example, electronic components made up 3.3% of India’s imports from China in the first quarter of 2015-16. This has grown to nearly 13% as of the first quarter of 2026-27. Several other goods used in manufacturing in India, such as electric machinery, chemicals, plastics, have seen their shares rise over the same period.
On the other hand, the share of finished goods such as telecom instruments have fallen from about 18% to 11% over the same period of time. Similarly, the share of manufactured fertilisers have fallen from about 7.5% in 2015 to less than 1% in 2026. The share of consumer electronics in imports from China have halved over the same period.
The ‘Make in India, For the World’ story still relies heavily on inputs from China. If India is forced to curb those imports, its manufacturing costs will rise, making Indian products less competitive globally.

Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
- Published
Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.
For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.
On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.
The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.
The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.
The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.
The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.
The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.
Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.
The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.
Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.
Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task.
"Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.
He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.
The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple.
According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies.
Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage.
All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme.
Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results.
In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme.
Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year.
"As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC.
"This makes some people desperate to get on this list."
One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said.
Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago.
One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list.
"But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said.
He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year.
Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list."
But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira.
"We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government."
One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him.
"Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC.
His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes.
Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride.
24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi.
Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah.
"Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living."
After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began.
But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

US Supreme Court lets Trump continue work on White House ballroom for now
A lower court had ordered construction paused due to a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeking to stop the US$400 million project
The US Supreme Court on Friday allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to continue construction of his White House ballroom project for now, temporarily pausing a judicial order that would halt much of the development.
The court’s action, known as an administrative stay, gives the justices additional time to consider the administration’s formal request to let it continue working on the US$400 million ballroom while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeking to stop the project proceeds.
In an August 14 filing to the Supreme Court, Justice Department lawyers echoed Trump’s contention that the project is a security necessity, citing assassination attempts against the president and other recent threats.
“This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” they said.
The non-profit National Trust for Historic Preservation sued last year after the administration tore down the White House East Wing and began building a 90,000 sq ft (8,360-square-metre) ballroom without seeking specific approval from Congress. Trump has said the ballroom will be “the greatest of its kind ever built”.
The project combines the above-ground ballroom with an extensive underground complex.

India-Bangladesh ties must serve mutual interest: S Jaishankar
On Pakistan-US relations, Jaishankar said the two countries have a "long history" of ties. He said that while India has, to a large extent, developed its own relationship with the United States, Pakistan stands apart for a different reason.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday said any relationship can work only if it meets the test of "mutual interest", as he spoke about the current state of India’s ties with Bangladesh. He also described Pakistan as a "unique" country, saying no other nation uses "terrorism so systematically" and in such a sustained way to attack and pressure a neighbour.
Speaking at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum, Jaishankar addressed questions on ties with Bangladesh and Pakistan-US relations. His remarks on Bangladesh came amid continuing uncertainty over the much-anticipated visit of Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to India, even as both sides are learnt to be continuing back-channel talks to explore the possibility of the trip in the next couple of weeks.
Declining to respond directly to a question on Dhaka’s demand that India extradite former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, Jaishankar said, "What I can tell you is, for any relationship to work, it has to meet the test of mutual interest. It has to work for us."
He added that ties between neighbours cannot be one-sided. "I am not expecting neighbours to only do what is in my interest. There has to be a reasonable degree of my recognising and respecting what is in their interest, just as I expect them also to do so," Jaishankar said.
"It is when you get that landing point, that common ground, relationships work smoothly," he said, adding that "mutuality" of interests underpins overall engagement.
The Ministry of External Affairs announced earlier this month that India has invited Rahman for a bilateral visit as well as to attend the outreach session of the upcoming BRICS summit in New Delhi. Rahman’s expected visit is seen as important for rebuilding bilateral ties, which saw a severe downturn after the collapse of the Hasina government two years ago.
India-Bangladesh relations came under fresh strain after Hasina held a virtual media interaction in New Delhi on August 5. Following the event, Dhaka reiterated its demand for her extradition and sought to link it with Rahman’s planned trip to India.
India later sought to distance itself from the event, saying New Delhi neither played a role in it nor endorsed Hasina’s comments. The Bangladesh foreign ministry reacted sharply and said the country was "outraged" that the interaction was allowed to take place despite Dhaka conveying its concerns to New Delhi over the likely impact on bilateral relations.
On Pakistan-US relations, Jaishankar said the two countries have a "long history" of ties. He said that while India has, to a large extent, developed its own relationship with the United States, Pakistan stands apart for a different reason.
"Now, to a large extent, we have developed our own relationship with the United States, but here is the point: Pakistan is unique not because it is a neighbour of India. We have other neighbours. Other countries have problems between them," he said.
"It is unique because in this day and age, there is no other country which uses terrorism so systematically and in such a sustained manner to attack and pressurise another neighbour, and that has an impact on public opinion in this country," he said.
Jaishankar added, "I am a minister of a democratic polity. I cannot be impervious to what is the public opinion of my country." In his remarks, he underlined that ties with neighbours must rest on mutual interest and common ground, while reiterating India’s concerns over Pakistan’s use of terrorism.

Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
- Published
Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.
But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.
Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.
Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.
There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.
The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.
The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.
We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.
Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".
We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.
It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.
In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.
One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating.
After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.

The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.
It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.
Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.
Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.
We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.
Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.
Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.
The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.
We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.
He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.
He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.
The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.
The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.
The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.
At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.
Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.
So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.
Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.
They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.
Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.
We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.
When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer.
"When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.
On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.
Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.
When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.
He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.
And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.
This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.
New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.
Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".
Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.
The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.
All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.
Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.
The military has refused to hand them over.
In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set.
Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found.
"[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective.
Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."

This month, the Trump administration announced nearly $2 billion for faith-based groups, the largest allocation of global health foreign assistance to faith-based organizations in more than 20 years. The bulk of it, $1.4 billion, funds health services, including an $850 million award to World Vision supporting 2,500 faith-based hospitals and clinics across 17 countries.
Whatever the administration’s ultimate motives, this is an important signal to my public health and humanitarian relief colleagues. Even as the old aid architecture is collapsing, the faith economy is not. Washington has rediscovered faith as a delivery mechanism. The bigger opportunity is faith as a source of capital.
By faith economy, I mean not simply religious charities, but the capital generated, governed, and invested through religious obligations, institutions, and financial systems. Governments and international institutions have worked with faith-based organizations for decades, relying on them to deliver services where public systems cannot. What they have not built is the financial infrastructure to receive, aggregate, and deploy capital that faith itself produces.
In parts of sub-Saharan Africa, faith-based providers deliver a significant share of health care — in some countries, an estimated 30%–40%. But the capital generated through religious obligation sits outside the way development finance is counted. Official development assistance measures what donor governments spend; it was never designed to capture what believers give. As a result, some of the world’s oldest and most durable capital flows remain invisible to the institutions designing global financing.
Islamic finance offers perhaps the clearest illustration because its religious obligations, capital markets, and risk instruments already span the spectrum from household giving to sovereign finance. Zakat is its most familiar instrument: a recurring annual obligation, generally 2.5% of qualifying wealth. Estimates put the annual zakat pool at roughly $200 billion to $1 trillion. But zakat is also the least interesting part of the opportunity.
I’ve seen this before. As a final-year medical student, during Libya’s revolution, I built the Noor Campaign around religious leaders and institutions because they held forms of trust and moral authority that formal systems often did not. A decade later, I encountered the financial version of the same problem in maternal health. In 2022, I realized that despite billions given in zakat each year, no coordinated mechanism was directing it into maternal and newborn health. The need was enormous: Across OIC countries, maternal mortality remains more than 50% higher than the global average — 299 deaths per 100,000 live births against a global 197.
I knew the money was there; the architecture was not. So I created For Mama, now Every Pregnancy, the first zakat-approved Muslim collaborative dedicated to maternal and newborn health. It raised $13 million in its first campaign, and across three Ramadans it has mobilized more than $130 million from over 192,000 individual donors. More than 50 organizations now use it every year to mobilize zakat and Ramadan giving for moms and babies.
Others began to take faith-based solutions seriously before Donald Trump became a convert. The U.N. Refugee Agency (UNHCR) piloted its Refugee Zakat Fund in 2017 and built the governance around it: dedicated accounts, traceability, religious oversight, and independent compliance. The fund is now backed by 18 fatwas and scholarly endorsements, and UNHCR reports that its Islamic philanthropy work has supported more than 9.9 million people. The point is that a global institution standardized religious capital and made it usable at scale. UNICEF, IRC, IOM, and GiveDirectly have since built their own mechanisms for zakat or Islamic philanthropy.
But if development stops at zakat, it will have missed the larger opportunity.
Islamic finance already has instruments that operate far beyond philanthropy. Waqf— an irrevocable endowment under Islamic law — can endow health, education, and other public goods over generations; they can’t be dismantled unlike government aid budgets. Sovereign and thematic sukuk can finance hospitals, housing, and climate infrastructure. Sharia-compliant insurance and risk instruments can shift the cost of a disaster away from a government balance sheet before it happens.
At the sovereign level, this is no longer theoretical. Indonesia pioneered the world’s first sovereign green sukuk and has linked cash waqf directly to government securities. The opportunity is not simply to collect more religious charity. It is to connect capital that already has its own investors, institutions, rules, and sources of legitimacy to the financing needs governments are increasingly struggling to meet.
That matters because some of these instruments can perform functions otherwise financed through public budgets, concessional capital or emergency aid. A sovereign sukuk financing a hospital is not charity filling a temporary budget gap; it is public infrastructure financed through a different capital market. A waqf supporting a hospital over decades is not an emergency appeal; it is a durable source of financing for a public good.
What is missing is the connective tissue between these financial systems. Islamic finance has its own rules and standards; development finance has another set for reporting, rating, and measuring outcomes. They were not built to work together. Until governments, investors, scholars, and development institutions can agree on how eligibility, disclosure, and performance translate across them, much of this capital will remain difficult to deploy at scale. Predictable in aggregate is not yet programmable at scale. Whoever writes those standards sets the terms: which needs qualify, which institutions certify, which populations get counted.
Government does not disappear in this model. Its financing mix changes. Countries become less dependent on whether a foreign legislature preserves an aid line, and more able to draw from capital markets, permanent endowments, and domestic or transnational pools of faith-generated capital.
That is what makes the U.S. State Department’s recent announcement such a useful test. It confirms something the health sector already knows: Faith institutions can be formidable delivery infrastructure. Washington has now put nearly $2 billion behind that idea.
But it is still American money, dependent on American appropriations and political choices. The World Vision initiative alone depends on the availability of funds. And the consortium selected for that initiative is made up of Christian organizations. American Jewish World Service says it was not consulted and learned about the announcement from the State Department’s press release. Muslim organizations, meanwhile, have raised concerns about unequal access to federal security funding at home. Faith remains, in this model, a delivery channel whose support is determined by whoever holds political power.
Funding faith-based organizations is a procurement decision, dependent on whoever controls the purse. Building the architecture to receive faith-based capital is infrastructure.
Faith capital carries its own politics — donors impose conditions, institutions make choices about who deserves help, scholars disagree about what qualifies, and some interpretations are exclusionary toward women. Built badly, it can reproduce every exclusion the current architecture already practices.
But ignoring it does not make it disappear. This capital will continue to move through communities whether global health and development institutions engage with it or not. It can finance health, education, and resilience; it can also reinforce exclusion and practices those same institutions spend billions trying to change. The case for building the architecture around it is not that faith capital is purer money. It is already there, it does not rise and fall on the same political cycle as foreign aid, and properly designed, it can widen the pool of capital available for health and direct more of it toward better health outcomes rather than deeper inequity.
The sector has spent decades treating this capital as either invisible or suspicious. It is neither. It is underbuilt. And the people who build the architecture around it will decide who it serves.
Alaa Murabit is a medical doctor. She is a U.N. high-level commissioner on health, employment, and economic growth, and a Lancet-Georgetown commissioner on faith, trust, and health. She created the first zakat-approved Muslim collaborative for maternal and newborn health, Every Pregnancy, and founded Voice of Libyan Women.

More than one in two anti-tuberculosis prescriptions assessed in healthcare settings outside India’s National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) did not conform to recommended treatment standards, according to a new systematic review and meta-analysis.
Published in the Indian Journal of Tuberculosis, the PRAMAN India study analysed 34 studies conducted between 1991 and 2024, covering 3,834 real-world anti-TB treatment records. The pooled prevalence of faulty prescriptions was 53.3% (95% CI: 42.2–64.1%).
The study also found a significant long-term decline in faulty prescribing. Weighted linear regression showed an average reduction of 1.38 percentage points a year (P=0.013). The crude prevalence fell from 68.6% in studies from 1990–1999 to 32.6% during 2020–2024.
Millions of prescriptions affected
The researchers estimated that about 2–3 million anti-TB prescriptions could be incorrect every year in India’s non-programmatic healthcare sector, based on private-sector treatment volumes. This translates to roughly four to five potentially faulty prescriptions every minute.
The estimate is not a direct count of prescriptions issued nationally, but an extrapolation based on the volume of TB treatment provided in the private sector.
The burden was not uniform across the country. In the regional analysis of 3,817 prescriptions, Madhya Pradesh, Haryana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Maharashtra and Uttarakhand recorded faulty-prescription rates above the overall crude prevalence of 50.8%.
Five of the 10 States with the highest TB case notifications, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Delhi were among those with rates above this overall prevalence. The study notes that these States also account for a disproportionate share of private-sector TB drug sales, giving them particular importance for TB control.
Differences between providers
The study also examined whether prescription quality differed according to provider type. Faulty prescribing was 59% in studies that included both allopathic and indigenous practitioners, compared with 51.1% in studies involving allopathic practitioners alone.
However, the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.74), meaning the study does not establish that one provider group had a higher rate of inappropriate prescribing.
Gyanshankar P. Mishra, associate professor of respiratory medicine at Indira Gandhi Government Medical College, Nagpur, and corresponding author of the study, said the reasons for inappropriate prescribing may be more complex than deliberate deviation from treatment guidelines.
“Some gaps may reflect evolving evidence, changes in treatment guidelines and inadequate access to updated recommendations,” he said.
This is particularly relevant in TB, where treatment recommendations have evolved over time and standardised regimens are periodically updated.
Need for intervention
The researchers also used machine-learning-based modelling to estimate future trends. For 2025–2030, the projected prescription error rate was 49.7% ± 9.0%, with a median of 50.7% and a modelled range of 37.1% to 62.1%.
The authors stress that this is a model-based projection and not an observed national prescription rate.
The concern is not only whether a prescription matches a guideline. The study’s discussion notes that faulty prescriptions can compromise treatment efficacy, prolong infectiousness and contribute to drug resistance, potentially undermining TB elimination efforts.
The researchers therefore recommend strengthening links between private providers and the NTEP, including Public-Private Mix models, continuing medical education, prescription-quality audits and feedback, digital clinical decision-support tools and timely referral to programme-based services.
“For every patient with TB, irrespective of where they seek care, the treatment needs to be standardised,” Dr. Mishra said.
He said sustained engagement with private providers and dissemination of updated treatment recommendations could help address prescription gaps.
